subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE

speechtext: Order of the Day-Special Order.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond) moved:
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend The Oleomargarine Act, chapter twenty-four of the statutes of 1919 (second session), and the amending Acts, by providing that notwithstanding anything contained in The Dairy Industry Act, 1914, or in any other statute or law, the manufacture in, and importation of oleomargarine into Canada, and the offering for sale, the sale and the having in possession for sale, of oleomargarine, shall henceforth be permitted, subject to the provisions of the said Oleomargarine Act and to such regulations as are now or may hereafter be established by the Governor in Council.
He said: Mr. Speaker, no doubt you viewed with alarm my entrance into the Chamber this afternoon. Probably you thought that I must be armed with a very large array of papers and that the House would be subject to a long and tiresome speech from me. I want to assure you before I go any further that my speech will be brief, but I trust it will be logical and replete with facts. The question of the manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine has been before parliament for a number of years. In 1886, on a motion by a member of the government to place a tariff duty upon the importation of oleomargarine, a debate took place which considerably affected the standing of the commodity in this country. At that time there were no regulations in force regarding the manufacture of oleomargarine, and in the course of the debate statements were made to the effect that this commodity was manufactured out of dead horses, rats and other unwholesome ingredients. A few years later legislation was passed to ensure the purity of dairy products, culminating in the Dairy Act of 1914, which was amended in 1916 to provide for the manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine in this country.

Under this act various regulations were put into effect to protect our people against adulterated products, and to-day I hope we shall not have repeated the well-worn argument that oleomargarine is harmful or unwholesome, for the reason, Mr. Speaker, that the manufacture of this commodity has been under the direct control of the Department of Agriculture and it is generally acknowledged that the gentlemen in charge of that department are very careful indeed to see to it that there is nothing dangerous to the public health in the ingredients which enter into the manufacture of oleomargarine.
Without entering into details regarding these ingredients, I will content myself by saying that there is a difference of opinion both in the country and in this House as to whether or not we should allow the further manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine. We must approach this question in a fair and honest frame of mind and should not use arguments which, while they may have been effective up to 1916, can now be safely discounted in view of the fact that the Department of Agriculture exercises very stringent supervision over thi3 manufacture. But while there may be a difference of opinion on the desirability of allowing oleomargarine to be still manufactured and imported, we cannot ignore appeals from various influential organizations which to-day are asking parliament to make effective an Oleomargarine Act such as I propose to introduce if this resolution passes. We must consider this question not with the eye of 1886 but with the eye of the present day. If I cite the Canadian Lumbermen's Association as being in favour of the continued manufacture and sale of oleomargarine, I shall perhaps be told that this organization is looking for cheap food for its labourers. And when I say that the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada is also asking that my proposed bill be brought into effect, I shall be told that this organization, too, is interested from a financial standpoint. But, Mr. Speaker, I have stronger authority still in the fact that 200,000 of our women have shown by the votes which they cast in their respective organizations and by their circular letters that they are in favour of the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine being continued. As I say, the motives of the Canadian Lumberman's Association and of the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada may be questioned on the ground of their being pecuniarily interested; but will any hon. gentleman dare rise in his place and tell us that the mothers and sisters and daughters

Oleomargarine-Mr. Carroll
of the Canadian people are engaged in propaganda that will hurt their offspring, their kith and their kin? The stand taken by these women is one of the strongest arguments, it seems to me, that can be used in favour of the continued manufacture and sale of oleomargarine.
But to return for the moment to the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada. I presume that as business men they are not interested either in poisoning our people or in bringing about the ruin of our daily farmers. What do they say about this matter? In 1916, when an order in council was passed under the War -Vftasures Act to permit of the manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine, this association undertook to investigate this commodity. Their investigation convinced them that oleomargarine was not the menace to the health of our people which the propaganda of its enemies had sought to make out. Here is a circular which the association have sent out to the members of the Senate and of the House of Commons, and I may be permitted to read one paragraph, as follows:
Before our members undertook to offer it for sale to the general public we made exhaustive enquiries as to the ingredients it contained and its method of manufacture. We consulted with the chief analyst for the Dominion government and he pronounced it a perfectly good food, and he stated that it contained no harmful ingredients, and, as on each package is stamped the approval of the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion of Canada, our retail grocers, butchers, produce dealers and general store merchants throughout Canada felt perfectly justified in stocking it and offering it for sale. If our customers did not [DOT]want it there would be no sale for it, but our experience shows that they do want it, and, seeing that it is a non-injurious and palatable product, and contains nothing that is unheal thful, we are of the opinion that they should be allowed to buy it if they so desire, and no law should be passed to prevent them from having it.
I reiterate, Sir, that whatever may have been said regarding the harmful properties of oleomargarine should no longer be repeated, because parliament in 1917 recognized this commodity as a healthful article of food, and up to the present time millions of pounds have been sold throughout the country with the approval of the Department of Agriculture. Again I appeal to hon. members not to use the argument that oleomargarine is harmful food, because by so doing they will in effect be casting a slur not only upon the Minister of Agriculture and his predecessors but upon the departmental officials as well. Surely before the approval of the department is placed on this article which goes out in small packages, the precaution is taken to
ascertain whether or not it is a healthful article of food.
Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, regarding the injury which oleomargarine may have been causing to the dairy industry of this country. Well, I do not believe the manufacture of oleomargarine has been in any way injurious to the dairy people, because every pound of butter they manufacture has a ready sale; the milk from every cow they raise is sent out in the shape of butter and cheese. But they tell you that oleomargarine is used as a substitute and that in its sale as such the persons handling it make their customers believe that they are buying butter. I do not think there is any force in that argument, for this reason: Every package of oleomargarine that is manufactured in or imported into this country has stamped on the product itself, in letters that may be seen and read by all, the word "Oleo." Every parcel is also enclosed in a wrapper which indicates in the clearest way that it is oleomargarine and not butter. Moreover, the Department of Agriculture exercise supervision over and make regulations respecting the manufacture of this product in Canada as well as its importation. Now, follow me. This product is manufactured here, or is imported. Surely the officers of the Agriculture department are sufficiently alive to the interests of the people to see to it that not an ounce of oleomargarine leaves the factories in this country or is imported without there being stamped upon it the word "Oleo." Then it goes to the wholesaler. I hope that the Agriculture department have been sufficiently alert in performing their duty to the people during the last four years to see to it, through their inspectors or other officials, that the wholesaler who gets this bulk of oleomargarine for distribution to the retailer does not attempt to impose upon the people by erasing in any way those distinctive letters which indicate that the product is oleomargarine and not butter. Then we come down to the retailer. I do not argue that the Department of Agriculture have a sufficient staff to see to it that no substitution or erasure is made at that stage. But, Sir, I have sufficient confidence in the honour and honesty of the retailers of this country to believe they are not doing that kind of thing, and it will take a very strong line of evidence to make me think otherwise.
When did the dairy industries of this country suggest, after 1917, that we should have a prohibition against the manufacture or sale of oleomargarine? It is a very peculiar thing that in 1921, in their petition to the government of the day, they did not ask for



Oleomargarine-Mr. Carroll
the prohibition of this article of food. What they did ask for was a "standard colour of oleomargarine"; for the printing on each package of the word "oleo"; for a differently shaped package "from that now used for oleomargarine"; "for the prevention of deception or dishonesty in making purchasers believe they are actually getting butter or an article of the same food value as butter."

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: May I ask what my hon. friend is quoting from, and the date?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I am quoting from a copy of a petition sent to the Dominion government in 1921 by the Dairy Council of Canada. Now, if they saw in 1921 that they should not ask for the prohibition of oleomargarine, or, to put it differently, if they did not ask for it, what has changed their mind in the meantime? Is there any evidence that dealers have been deceptive in the matter- that they have attempted to make the people believe they were getting butter when they were really getting oleomargarine? I do not believe it, Mr. Speaker. Taking this matter as a whole, I think we should use the arguments that may be used as from 1917 in respect to oleomargarine and not hark back to the times when people were afraid of anything new and when they believed that oleomargarine was made up of such ingredients as I mentioned in the earlier part of my.remarks.
I wish to impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, and upon the members of this House the fact that the parliament of Canada put the stamp of its approval upon oleomargarine in 1917 and has kept it there ever since. It has indicated its belief that oleomargarine is a nonharmful food, a food that is wholesome. In casting your votes in this connection I want you to remember that fact; I want you not to be led away by any other thought but that there are thousands of people in this country who want to use oleomargarine and who have the right to use it. I hope you will not think me a plagiarist if I use the words: Is this an article of commerce? And- If this is an article of commerce, why should we prohibit it? I am using the words, Sir, of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in a former debate in this House. He is one of the few people who have the happy faculty of placing a whole argument in a nutshell.
I ask the members of this House to give fair consideration to this whole question. I ask them to think of the millions who are asking this parliament that they be permitted to put this product on their table as an article of food. I ask them hot to be led away by

their own personal interests; we are not here for that purpose. I do not make any accusation-I believe that every member of this House will use his best judgment in the matter-but I do suggest that we be not led away by any selfish motives. Let us seek away down in our hearts and ask ourselves: Are we going to prevent the people from using oleomargarine if they wish to use it? If we are, then it is just as well that parliament should to-morrow say to the people that they shall not use shoes unless they are up to the standard; that they shall not use an article of clothing unless it is the very best; that they shall not purchas? any horse food that is not up to or, perhaps, above the standard. It may be said that oleomargarine is a cheap article of food, but it is not deleterious; it is not unwholesome. But I say, give the people of this country who wish to use that article of food the privilege of using it. I reiterate: If this parliament takes it upon themselves to refuse the common people of this country that which I consider a benefit, they will hear from them in the very near future.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to second this resolution I do so with the understanding that I may suggest certain changes or in my opinion improvements to it as I go along. Under those conditions I am glad to second this resolution.
This matter has been discussed, as has been pointed out by the hon. member (Mr. Carroll) who has just taken his seat, on a number of occasions in this House in the past, and I for one sincerely hope that we shall decide finally on this occasion whether we are going to have oleomargarine in this country or not. The subject has taken up a very great deal of the valuable time of this House in previous years. On this occasion I can hardly refer to the subject without saying a word as to the way in which this resolution has been put off from the early part of the session until now when we are in its closing days-a resolution of the very greatest importance not only to the dairymen of this country but also to the consumers and to a certain group of manufacturers. I feel that this matter should have been given attention earlier in the session if possible, and should not have been avoided and side-stepped in the way it has been. I rather think the question has been evaded to a certain extent, but I shall not speak any more of that phase of the question beyond referring for a moment to what the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) said yesterday when discussing oleomargarine and in uttering the word "cuckoo" we will all understand what I mean.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
This measure was first introduced as a war measure on account of the great scarcity of fats overseas. It will be remembered that there was a considerable demand for fats on the other side of the Atlantic during the war, and oleomargarine was introduced at that time and found very useful indeed over there. In fact, our Canadian troops went all through the war using only oleomargarine as a spread for bread. It has been suggested that on account of its having first been introduced as a war measure it should cease now that the war is over. But let me point out that the people of Canada have expressed their wishes through their representatives in this House on several occasions and have extended the time year by year, and at the present time oleomargarine is now recognized as one of the staple articles of food in many sections of this country. I think the government should carefully consider this in bringing down any measure or in giving support to any measure for making oleomargarine permanent in this country.
What is oleomargarine? In the first place it is made from selected beef fats, neutral lard, vegetable oils, pasteurized milk, salt, pure water, and sometimes includes butter. It is all churned together and then made into blocks and offered for sale. It is manufactured only under the strictest sanitary conditions. It is first necessary for anyone desiring either to import or to manufacture oleomargarine in Canada to obtain a license from the Minister pf Agriculture for that purpose, and the minister may at any time cancel that license for cause. It is made under the very closest inspection, the inspection of our Meat and Canned Poods branch of the Department of Agriculture, and their certificate and brand on any goods sent out of this country is accepted in all parts of the world. With the United States we have an exchange of certificates between our Health of Animals branch here and the Bureau of Animal Industry at Washington.
The question is often asked, is oleomargarine wholesome? We find that its digestibility is about the same as butter, about 97 per cent, and its energy value is also about the same. With regard to its palatability we find that the British or English-speaking people throughout the world have a preference for fats showing the lactic acid flavour, as a result of the fermentation of milk and cream from bacteria working upon it. Oleo-maragarine will never be as popular as butter in this or any other country because it will never be as palatable, not possessing that peculiar lactic flavour I have just referred to, and anyone who understands or has an appreciation of real good butter can never
224i
be misled by any oleomargarine. He can tell the difference both by taste and odor.
One feature of this oleomargarine question that has been stressed to a very great extent in the discussions in this House in the past year is the vitamine content of oleomargarine. You will find that authorities differ a great deal on this point, some claiming that the other animal fats contain just as many vitamine soluble A as the butter fats themselves. Let me quote. William Clayton, Master of Science at Liverpool University, in a book published in 1920 says:
The published work on "The Nutritive value of Oleomargarine and Butter Substitutes", with reference to their content of the fat-soluble accessory growth substance, is due to Halliburton and Drummond whose conclusions were: That the fat-soluble accessory growth substance is present in beef fat and also oil and is present in margarine prepared upon such a basis. Such margarines are nutritively the equivalent of butter.
We find, too, that butter varies a great deal in its vitamine content, and this is indicated very greatly by the pigmentation or colouring of the butter. For instance, in winter time we find that the butter is very light in colour, and then it has a very low vitamine content as compared with the rich, bright yellow butter of June or July during the height of the grass season. Now, the butter maker is permitted to colour his butter in the winter time so that it will look like June butter. As has been pointed out by scientists who have investigated the matter very carefully, the vitamine content is shown by the height of colouring, but the butter maker by heightening the colour of his butter gives no indication to the purchaser of the vitamine content or its value as a food in that particular respect. Let me quote in this connection from Sherman and Smith's book " The Vitamines," 1922, by H. C. Sherman, Professor of Food Chemistry, Columbia University, and S. L. Smith, Specialist in Biological and Food Chemistry, United States Department of Agriculture. They say:
In recent years butter has occupied a unique position because it appeared to be conspicuously the richest in vitamine A among the commercial food fats. Further work in this field indicates, however, that the value of butter in this respect is subject to rather wide variation.
Steenbock, as previously noted, found that paleness of butter fat indicated paucity of vitamine A, byt the present system of artificially coloring butter makes it impossible for the consumer to apply this criterion. The burden of responsibility for the maintenance of the vitamine value of butter lies with the producer. By intelligent and liberal use of feeds rich in vitamine A, such as alfalfa, and care in the manufacture, transportation and storage of the product, both butter and other animal fats may in time be standardized as commercial sources of vitamine A.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
Quoting again from Mr. Clayton, of Liverpool University, lie says:
In conclusion it is well recalled that butter owing to the influence of food, storage conditions and temperatures used in the renovation of inferior products, and even the method of use of the produce in the home, may not exceed a good oleomargarine in nutritive qualities.
The whole question seems to depend upon the adequately varied and balanced diet of the individual. Children should preferably be fed on butter, but adults, with their stronger digestive powers, may with absolute impunity replace butter with either oleo or vegetable margarine, provided they consume sufficient amounts of the vegetative green parts of plants since these furnish an ample supply of all three vitamines.
You will see here that the diet of a man being very varied, a paucity of vitamines in any particular article of food may mean that the whole ration was short in that particular respect. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, a few of the common articles of food.that contain vitamines. I will only mention a few of them so as not to take up too much time of the House.
Butter; cream; margarine prepared from animal fats other than lard; milk, condensed, evaporaited or dried; nut butter; mutt-on and beef fat; heart; brain; sweetbread; cod liver oil and other fish livers oils-
Which, I may say, is one of the richest in this vitamine.
-herring oil, salmon and cod oil; liver; onions, kidneys; potatoes; fat fish, as herring, salmon fish roe; eggs-
And some forty-two others, including many vegetables.
This will indicate to you how very freely these vitamines are distributed among the common articles of food. We have also had rather sweeping statements made about the entire absence of vitamines in oleomargarine. You will see, however, that this is not the line of argument pursued by those men who are experts in this particular direction. In a bulletin issued by the National Dairy Council entitled "Health vs. Wealth" I find the following statement:
You may wonder when milk and butter contain vitamines why beef fat does not. Vitamines are in green, leafy substances, grass, leaves, twigs, whole grain and many things that a cow eats. The cow requires some for her own use and stores some in her liver, but all the rest is given off in the milk and are never deposited in the flesh. As oleomargarine is chiefly made from the waste products of the animal at the slaughter house it could not possibly contain vitamines.
This is a very broad statement indeed and is opposed by many. Now let me quote from a statement by H. Steenbock, of the Department of Agricultural Chemistry of the University of Wisconsin. He says:
In our work a somewhat similar product, the oleo oils from beef fats, prepared in commerce for the

manufacture of oleomargarine, were in some instances found richer in fat-soluble vitamine than many butters. Subsequent to the publication of these results we became aware of the fact that vitamine content as determined in our feeding experiments with these samples seemed to vary directly with the intensity of pigmentation.
Pointing out again that you may form an opinion as to the presence of vitamines by the colouring of the fat material. Now, in this particular article on "Health vs. Wealth" it is indicated that most of the vitamines are lost except those given off through the milk, but the author does not state what becomes of the vitamines fed so liberally during the grass season to those animals which are not giving milk; and we could hardly expect that nature will be so improvident, as in the case of the steer and the dry cow, as to cause an almost entire waste of this particular and valuable ingredient of food. If we accept Steenbock's theory for a moment we will recognize, as I pointed out a moment ago, that the excess of vitamines is clearly indicated by the high colour of the butter fat. Those who are familiar with the beef aspect of the question will remember that grass beef is also very much higher in colour than beef produced in winter time, indicating that there are vitamines stored up in the beef fats particularly at that season of the year.
Now in some of the American literature which has been distributed in the propaganda against oleomargarine we find pictures of white rats indicating some rats fed on vitamines which are of a very lusty character and other rats fed on a diet wholly lacking in vitamines which appear very weakly. It must be admitted that growth is due to certain chemical changes which take place in the body, and that the very best results are obtained where you have a ration that is chemically well balanced. In many sections of the country there is a paucity of certain ingredients in the soil which causes certain diseases-, for example the disease known as rickets. I know of certain sections of British Columbia where cattle, young animals particularly, pastured on certain lands soon after exhibit rickets, or a bending or softening of the bones, due to the absence of calcium and phosphates. By the feeding of cer-
4 p.m. tain food rich in calcium and phos1-phates, however, these conditions are avoided and you can produce healthy cattle on this very same land. I know certain sections of British Columbia where, during the calving season many calves live only for an hour or two after birth, a severe loss resulting from this mortality. This again is due to the absence of iodine, showing again how necessary it

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
is, in the case of growing animals, particularly that the rations should be well balanced.
I may say that during the war our Canadian troops, as I pointed out a while ago, had nothing but oleomargarine as a spread for their bread. This was also used by the British troops. The Danish army and navy is also supplied with the same material. In many Danish institutions oleomargarine is a regular part of the diet. It has been pointed out in some literature I have seen that it is necessary to have milk in some form or other for the proper growth of the human being. I do not think that this theory has been thoroughly supported by evidence. Take the case of the North American who never used dairy products in his life. Yet you see Indians out on the prairie six feet one inch in height and weighing two hundred pounds, fine lusty fellows. If we were to look into the matter very carefully we should probably find that not more than one half of the people of the country use milk or milk products.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I should like to know if
the hon. member has proof that the mothers among the savages do not nurse their children.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman's question is very appropriate. Every human being is probably nursed in that way, but I am talking about the individual when he reaches the period when the individual can use butter spread on bread. I am quite sure the Indians in the West have never used any butter. If they have, the practice has only commenced within recent years.
We also had very strong criticism of the vegetable oils used in the preparation of oleomargarine. I know that, either last year or the year before, we had some vivid word pictures drawn here of perspiring natives toiling in the jungles of Africa gathering the various seeds and plants from which these oils are obtained. I thought at the time the picture was rather overdrawn. I may say that the principal ingredient in the vegetable oil line used in the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada is simply cotton seed oil. While we hear many complaints about the use of cotton seed oil in the preparation of oleomargarine we find it is used in many other articles of food such as shortening, and in salad oils, without the least bit of trouble. Evidently the oil is regarded as quite suitable in those cases but apparently is objectionable when used in the manufacture of oleomargarine. In addition to that we find that even annatto used for the purpose of colouring butter is1 mixed with cotton seed oil and bv the use of this particular colouring, as I
pointed out a while ago, January butter is made to look like June butter and as though it were rich in vitamine contents.
Now, we find that the consumption of oleomargarine increases as butter goes up in price, and it lessens as butter goes down in price, because no person with a decent palate or a good taste would for a moment think of eating oleomargarine if he could secure butter at a reasonable price. Oleomargarine, though, furnishes a greal deal of relief to people in families where economy is an absolute necessity under certain conditions that are liable to occur from time to time. To indicate that oleomargarine is in demand, let me quote a telegram received from the chamber of commerce in my constituency, the city of Victoria :
We strongly urge you support resolution introduced by Mr. W. F. Carroll, M.P., Cape Breton, to make permanent legislation permitting manufacture and sale oleomargarine in Canada. Public opinion in Canada overwhelmingly favours such permanent legislation. Will you please forward copy this wire to Prime Minister and Mr. Carroll mover of the resolution.
May I say that Mr. Spencer, in addition to being chairman of the chamber of commerce, is the owner of a very large departmental store where they handle all lines of food products. I have had similar wires from women's organizations, including the Local Council of Women, but I will not take up the time of the House in reading them.
We usually find that oleomargarine is lower in price than butter, and I have in my hand these quotations of last week in Ottawa:

This shows a difference between creamery butter and oleomargarine of 13 cents wholesale and 15 cents retail, and a difference between dairy butter and oleomargarine of 6 cents wholesale and 8 cents retail.
I was informed only yesterday that it paid the grocer in many cases to sell oleomargarine, because he made a greater profit from the sale of oleomargarine than from the sale of butter. This would hardly be borne out by the figures I have cited. The profit shown in dairy butter is about 7 cents between wholesale and retail; on creamery butter, 7 cents between wholesale and retail; and on oleomargarine only 5 cents between wholesale and retail.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Is the hon. member prepared to state the source of the figures he has cited?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
These figures were obtained from the city market in Ottawa last week, on the day it was expected that this ques-
Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie

tion would come up. I did not think it necessary to get new figures to-day.
The argument has been used that we should wipe out oleomargarine in this country, because some of our logging camps give it to their loggers to spread on their bread in place of butter. I do not think we should be inconvenienced simply because of that. That is something that should be arranged between the logging camp men and their employers. In British Columbia, as I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) will agree, you cannot put on the table of the logging man anything except just what he demands and he sees that he gets it.
Many families throughout the country are from time to time using oleomargarine in order to keep down family expenses. We have the man who gets out of work; we have the man who has sickness in his family and who has to incur an extra expense; we have those families where economy is an absolute necessity, and this occurs from time to time in the everyday life of the people of this country. The people have every right to decide for themselves in their own intelligence whether oleomargarine is to be purchased by them or not, and this House is taking upon itself a very great responsibility when it tells the people that they should not have the same privileges as are enjoyed by the people of every other country in the world.
We have three groups that are chiefly interested in this oleomargarine question. We have the great consuming group which is the first consideration; then we have the dairy man; and, third, we have the manufacturer of oleomargarine. Therefore, this is not entirely a question pertaining to the dairyman. If the poor man or the man who desires to lower his cost of living, cannot obtain the cheap oleomargarine and cannot afford the price of butter, it will be necessary for him to use ordinary beef or pork dripping, and I am sure oleomargarine would be more palatable for his use under such conditions. We should leave this matter entirely to the judgment of the people. It is not the place of the government of this country to prohibit the manufacture of oleomargarine; rather it is the duty of the government to protect the people, to see that oleomargarine is made in a very wholesome way; that there is no possible criticism along that line, and then that it is not sold for something which it is not. As I pointed out a moment ago, oleomargarine, on account of its inferiority in flavour, will never interfere with good butter.
We have also had the argument put forward I hat if the manufacture of oleomargarine is

once made permanent in this country, oleomargarine will greatly increase in quantity. I think that argument is not borne out by our experience since 1918 when it was first introduced. We find that we have had free access to the American market, and not only the ingredients which are made up into oleomargarine in this country, but the manufactured article can be imported from the United States absolutely free of duty. So, if there had been a greater demand in this country for oleomargarine, we would have had it entering Canada in very much greater quantities. The truth is that since 1918, when oleomargarine was first introduced into Canada, there has been a steady falling off in the quantity consumed in this country; but it has been very clearly shown that when butter gets cheaper in price, the consumption of oleomargarine lessens to a very considerable extent. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The hon. member will notice that under the Liberal administration we have been using more butter than oleomargarine.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I am sure the Liberal government can take credit for some things, but that is rather a long step.
In the meantime creamery butter has shown a steady increase, and only last year it increased something over 15,000,000 pounds. At the present time the consumption of oleomargarine amounts to only about 2 per cent for the spreads used for bread in this country. That is, 98 per cent of the spreads consists of dairy products as compared with 2 per cent of oleomargarine. This shows that the situation is not at all a dangerous one. The dairyman of this country, therefore, might very well look at this question in a broad, liberal way.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Would that condition continue if oleomargarine became permanent in this country?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I presume the hon. member will admit that his figures give no intimation as to whether the coeval existence of oleomargarine would not have still further reduced the Canadian export of butter in the term of years he has referred to?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I contend that the decline in our exports of butter was not due to the presence or the absence of oleomargarine at all; I say that if oleomargarine can ruin our butter business in Canada, then Denmark should have been ruined by now, for the reasons I have stated.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, I suppose, would concede that the decline in our exports of butter would have been more , disastrous than it was if the industry had had to compete with oleomargarine throughout the period he mentioned? It is mere conjecture as to whether or not the absence of oleomargarine helped to keep the industry.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I am not claiming that the absence of oleomargarine kept it up at all. What I claim is simply that we are not making progress, and instead of fiddling around discussing a question of this kind in connection with a great industry such as the dairy industry, we should be busily engaged this afternoon trying to discover some means of improving the condition of that industry in Canada to-day.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I contend that there is absolutely nothing in the hon. gentleman's figures to show that the absence of oleomargarine had any effect on butter one way or the other in Canada.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I pointed out that from 1880 to 1921, the period covered by the fig-

Oleomargarine~Mr. Tolmie
ures I submitted, throughout almost the whole of that time except for the last three or four years, we had no oleomargarine at all in Canada, and our butter exports were on the decline all the time. These figures, I think, indicate quite conclusively that we have nothing very much to fear from the manufacture and consumption of oleomargarine in this country. What we need immediately is a well-considered, a carefully worked out, and a broad and comprehensive plan for the development of our great dairy industry; and we should be discussing the more important phases of that business rather than wasting our time on this question.
The dairy industry of Canada has a hundred times more to fear from the manufacture of poor butter than from the manufacture of oleomargarine. The reports brought back by the officials of the Department of Agriculture who recently visited Great Britain go to show that the fact that we do not obtain as much for our butter as the Danes do is due to the poor quality of our product, its poor colouring, its poor keeping qualities and its flavour. I was asked only yesterday whether I expected the people of this country to adopt the standard of living of the Danes. Now, I do not know anything about the standard of living of the Danes, because I do not know Denmark; I have never been there. I do know, however, a number of Danes who have come to this country and settled both west and east of the mountains, and I can say that they are among our very best settlers. At any rate, they are men who are willing to work; and they work with results. J can recall one man whom I met in the city of Calgary, who came here with nothing at all-he had 25 cents in his pocket when he landed. To-day he turns out butter every week at the rate of tens of thousands of pounds. Another man of this type told me last year at the Calgary exhibition: 'Tolmie, you can break me if you like and I shall be independently rich in this country in five years.'' And, Mr. Speaker, he said this in a section of the country we hear decried so much in this House.
Let me quote some figures to show what we have to fear from the manufacture of bad butter, as compared with the production of oleomargarine, in Canada. I would ask hon. gentlemen to pay particular attention to the figures with reference to oleomargarine, because we hear it stated so frequently that this article is being sold for butter in a wholesale way in Canada. In 1919, the convictions for infractions of the Dairy Act, that is, for the sale of bad butter, were 111, while the convictions under the Oleomargarine Act

were eight; in 1920, the convictions for butter were 126 and for oleomargarine 12; in 1921, the convictions for butter were 126 and for oleomargarine 14; and in 1922, for butter they were 126 and for oleomargarine 14.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Is not that due to two facts -first, the far greater quantity of butter sold; and secondly, the fact that there is a very strict standard of butter making while there is none whatever for oleomargarine in this country?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I do not think the hon.
member will find any very strict standard of butter making extensively applied to dairy butter throughout this country. I have been a dairy inspector myself and a good many times I have seen butter that was anything but desirable. Quite apparently there was no standard at all except to get the butter into solid condition and sell it to someone.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Would not my hon. friend say that probably the reason why more oleomargarine people escaped than butter makers was due to the fact that the former were represented by more able attorneys?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I do not think so. I am not trying to argue in favour of oleomargarine as against dairy products. I am trying to quote exact figures, and it is a very poor showing indeed if our dairymen, or whoever are responsible for the administration of the Oleomargarine Act, can find only fourteen convictions from Halifax to Victoria in one year if infractions of the law are nearly so general as they are stated to be.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman tell me how many firms in Canada are making oleomargarine compared with the number of our dairymen?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend the number of our dairymen, they are here by the thousands, but I think the oleomargarine manufacturers are confined to two firms. If I am not mistaken, we have two factories in Toronto and one in Edmonton.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: What are the names of those two firms?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The Swift Canadian Company and the Harris Abattoir Company.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: They are American firms?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
One has the same name and is I presume a branch of the Chicago firm, although I have no evidence of that, but the other is a strictly Canadian firm as far

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
as I know. I am acquainted with both proprietors and they look like Canadians anyway.
To indicate how carefully the dairyman is protected in this country with regard to the manufacture of oleomargarine, I will quote the regulations. I do not say that this protection is ample, and I have already intimated that there may be further restrictions we can apply so as to prevent the sale of oleomargarine for anything other than what it actually is. Before oleomargarine can either be manufactured or imported the dealer or manufacturer must have a license from the Minister of Agriculture. The minister may cancel this license at any time for cause. All packages must be clearly marked "Oleomargarine." I have a package here on which will be noticed the word "Oleomargarine" is deary marked. We also have the word "Oleo" stamped directly into the material itself in letters one and a half inches high. Oleomargarine must be manufactured in an inspected establishment and, as I pointed out, the inspectors are highly qualified men who in addition to being skilled veterinarians have also passed a further examination before being taken into the employ of the Department of Agriculture. The sanitary arrangements must be first-class in every respect. The manufacture of oleomargarine in butter establishments is strictly prohibited. All materials must be inspected and analyzed if thought necessary. Oleo oil and neutral lards used for this purpose must be from inspected establishments. Importations of any of these materials must be accompanied by certificates from recognized authorities in the country from which they come. Milk from nonreacting cows or pasteurized so as to be free from tuberculosis must be used. Butter free from rancidity and bad odour must be used. I may say that some of the manufacturers are using no butter at all at the present time. No preservatives other than salt are allowed. No unlicensed person is permitted to mix oleo with butter. No colour is to be used or given away with Oleomargarine. Manufacturers of oleomargarine must not use the words "butter," "creamery," "dairy," or the name of any breed of cattle in advertising or describing oleo or on any package containing oleo. Pure vegetable oleo must be so designated. It must be sold only in its original package. In all restaurants where oleomargarine is sold there is to be a placard displayed, "Oleomargarine sold here." Now. we have heard a great deal about how oleomargarine is sold in some places for butter. I have made careful inquiry among the butter
distributors in this city, who say that that is not the case, that our restaurants here buy and use butter of the best quality. I have also asked a prominent gentleman connected with the Dairy branch who also agrees that not much oleomargarine is disposed of, at any rate under these conditions.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman ever seen one of those placards in any restaurant in Canada?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Not where I eat. There are very severe penalties imposed for any infractions of these regulations. I am quite sure that frequently oleomargarine gets a reputation for certain things that it is not guilty of at all. For instance, a gentleman, connected with the Department of Agriculture at that time, travelling from Montreal to Ottawa received on the train some very bad butter. He was very much disgusted with it and very angry, and after "calling down" the waiter he placed the butter in a paper package and had it analyzed, claiming very confidently that it was not butter at all but oleomargarine. The analyst found that it was just bad butter-some of that butter I was describing a few minutes ago.
There are certain propositions being put forward for the further control of oleomargarine even more stringently than at the present time, so as to make it impossible for it to be sold for butter. It has been proposed to give it an artificial colour. You will note, Mr. Speaker, here is a sample of oleo oil used in the manufacture of oleomargarine which is of a distinct yellow colour. Here again is some cottonseed oil, which is a vegetable product and which also is a rich golden colour, indicating that the natural colour of any product made from these two articles would be yellow. It is proposed now, however, to change this colour. Whether a proper standard can be arrived at or not I do not know, but if the manufacturers are agreeable I see no reason why this proposal should not be carried out. I feel we should place this matter on the soundest possible basis, I think we should encourage our dairymen in every possible way, and if I for one moment thought that this oleomargarine manufactured in Canada would interfere with the dairy industry-last year there was the miserably small quantity of less than 4,000,000 pounds of oleomargarine manufactured compared with 240,000,000 pounds of butter-if I thought it was going to seriously interfere with our dairymen I would certainly oppose its continued manufacture. But after a very careful study during the past three or four

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
years I have been unable to find any reasonable argument along these lines.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman himself engaged in dairying?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Oh yes, I am engaged in the dairy business, and I also have two pure bred herds of very valuable dairy cattle. My principal customers are dairymen. However, I feel that when I come down here as the representative of Victoria City I would not be justified in allowing my private interests to interfere with my public duty.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Of course-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I would remind hon. members that these interruptions are only allowed with the consent of the hon. gentleman who is addressing the House. They must not be too profuse.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I want to ask the hon. gentleman two questions. If a greater number of people were engaged in the manufacture of oleo might not conditions be different? Also, if permanent arrangements are made does he not think there will be a great increase in the amount of oleo manufactured?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
No, I do not think there would be any difference at all, because ever since 1918 our people have had an opportunity to eat all the oleomargarine they want. Our figures show that instead of an increase in consumption there has been a steady falling off with the decrease in the price of butter, that is, the consumption of oleomargarine has fallen from 14,000,000 pounds to less than
4,000,000 pounds last year, which I think is a pretty fair indication that the people are getting tired of it. Had there been a duty on oleomargarine it might have affected the figures, but this commodity can be got just as cheap from the United States as in this country, and the people have shown that they have no great desire for it.	-
The butter maker is asking the oleo maker to colour this product, made from two yellow articles, either pink, green or black. I think it would be unreasonable to ask for that change in colour; it would be entirely foreign to the natural colour of the products from which the finished article is made. Remember this: The dairyman to-day-and the oleomargarine man does not object to it-is allowed to colour his butter so that he can make January look like June; he can make it look as if it were rich in vitimines when perhaps it is not. In Great Britain they permit ten per cent of butter to be added to their oleomargarine product; in Denmark fifteen per cent is allowed. In this country some of our

packers are using as much, I think, as eight per cent. This can hardly be called adulteration-the mixing of a small quantity of higher priced material with a lower priced material Adulteration, as I understand it, is quite in the opposite direction.
As have pointed out, on every package of this product "Oleomargarine" is clearly marked. I am strongly in favouf of improving that in any way possible so as' to prevent the article from being sold as butter, or so as to obviate any misrepresentation in connection with it. I am a firm believer in putting a duty on oleomargarine imported into this country and on such of its ingredients as are already manufactured here. I see no objection whatever to the standardization of oleomargarine and the placing of a statement on each package indicating exactly what is contained in it. Holland has built up a great oleomargarine industry, the product being largely exported to Great Britain. Here is a chance in our country for development along similar lines. I feel that we should take up any line of work that will increase our industry, add to the wealth of the country and enable us to overcome the difficult conditions that exist as a result of the war. I believe in the firmest and closest policing of the sale of oleomargarine and dairy products in general. Unless we put our goods on the British market in the best possible condition we are not going to get our share of the market over there.
The suggestion has been made that oleomargarine affects dairy prices in this country. I do not think that its sale affects the price of butter here at all, for the reason that we get rid of our surplus in an export market: If the dairy industry of Canada is to increase we must continue to develop our export market. Naturally the price of butter in Canada is set by the price of butter in the market in which we dispose of our surplus product; and do not forget that that butter is sold in a market where oleomargarine also is sold in huge quantities. If we cannot compete with the little bit of oleo sold here, how on earth can we ever hope to compete in the British market, where oleomargarine is s*old in such large quantities? One thing is sure, if we are going to compete over there we shall have to reduce our cost of production to such a level as will enable us to meet the Danes and our other competitors on that market; otherwise we cannot hope for good results.
It has been stated that the farmers all over this' country are firm believers in the wiping out of the manufacture and consumption of oleomargarine. I have had talks with several farmers in the West, and when the whole con-

Oleomargarine-Mr. Tolmie
dition is explained to them, as I have attempted to state it to-day, they have felt that there was no unreasonable ground for fear of the competition through the manufacture of oleo. But here is a very interesting thing: At the last session of the Alberta legislature a resolution was brought up to wipe out oleomargarine, that is, to recommend that the manufacture, sale and importation of oleomargarine in this country be made to cease. This resolution was put to a vote and that farmers' legislature voted it down by a majority of 30 to 12. I want to congratulate those farmers on the broad-minded view they took of the situation. If the dairymen throughout Canada were fully informed concerning this matter we would not have all this row about oleomargarine at the present time.

There should be a campaign in this country to increase the consumption of dairy products, to advertise their value, and so on. I think also that in connection with our export it would be well to adopt the words "Canada, approved" on our Canadian products wherever possible. These are the words that appear on our pork, bacon, ham, and so on that are sent out of this country. By having these words attached to all our products we should set up and maintain a nigh standard; we would keep up our volume of exports and maintain the quality of our goods, thus being able to get our share of the British market in a comparatively short time. I know it would do me more good to take the other side of the question, as I said before in reply to an inquiry by an hon. member-to take the side of the dairyman. But I do not feel justified in
doing so; I feel that this House has no right to tell the people of Canada that they have not the same intelligence as the people of other countries and that they cannot be allowed to buy oleomargarine if they wish to do so. The whole thing hinges on that one point, in my opinion we have to leave a little to the people. We told them a while ago what they should do with their money when they went to a certain place of entertainment; now we are going to tell them what to put in their mouths, and in doing so I think we are going a little too far. Last year the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) espressed great astonishment at my stand in this connection.
I studied this question very thoroughly, both when Minister of Agriculture-when I was able to get information more easily than now-and subsequently; I have examined it carefully from all points of view, and I have come to the conclusion that the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in this country is not hurtful to our daily industry at the present time and will not hurt it in the future. Instead, therefore, of wasting our time on a question of this kind we should be busy trying to develop the dairy industry along proper lines.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (.Mr. Carroll), has been less belligerent to-day than he wps on a former occasion, I trust that I shall have no difficulty in keeping within the rules of parliamentary debate. I am not going to follow his argument very far, but he made one statement that I think is hardly fair. He said that oleomargarine had the approval of the staff of the Department of Agriculture. I think he has no warrant for that statement. The law was passed by this House and these gentlemen, however much they may be against oleomargarine, are in duty bound to enforce the provisions of the law.
The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) in the beginning of his speech found lault with the government for what he termed the long delay in giving an opportunity for the discussion of this resolution. It struck me as rather curious that he should criticise the government in that respect, because if my memory serves me correctly, in 1921 when he was Minister of Agriculture a bill providing for the extension of the oleo legislation stood on the order paper from the early days of the session and was not discussed until within the last two weeks of the session.
This question has been _ discussed in this country for a great many years. The first
Oleomargarine-Mr. Kay

legislation enacted on the subject was I think in 1886, when oleomargarine was first prohibited. In 1903 the provisions of that restriction were re-enacted, and this occurred again in 1914 under the Dairy Industry Act. During all that, period from 1886 to 1917, a period of thirty-one years, oleomargarine was prohibited in this country, and we have not heard that there was any public demand or any demand whatever for its introduction. In 1917 the members of the House will remember that we as well as all the allied countries were beginning to feel the pinch and the stress of the Great War, and all the peoples of the allied countries were then willing to submit to any sacrifice which would help towards winning the war. Many things were done, Sir, not only in this country but in all the allied countries at that time which no one would have dreamt of as possible under normal conditions, and one of these extraordinary things was the enactment in 1917 of the order in council permitting the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada. Before that order in council was passed the matter was fully discussed by the Canada Food Board, an organization of the government, and by a special committee of that Food Board known as the Special Milk Committee. Upon that committee were representatives of the dairy interests, and when the great need of the boys at the front and of the allies for more butter and fats was pointed out to the dairymen they consented gladly, as patriotic citizens should, to allowing oleomargarine to be manufactured, imported and sold in Canada provided that it was as a war measure only and a temporary one. In order to show that that was the view of the government I will read the provisions of that order in council, dated October 23, 1917:
Whereas attention is drawn to the abnormal demand for butter due to war conditions and to the very great probability that such abnormal demand and consequent high prices will prevail for this product for some time to come;
And whereas it is in the public interest, under the special conditions above named, that other fats should be available in Canada under strict and reasonable conditions as a substitute for butter,-
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under and in virtue of the provisions of the War Measures Act, 1914, is pleased to make and enact and doth hereby make and enact the following regulations providing for the importation to Canada and the permitting of the manufacture, sale and possession within Canada of oleomargarine and establishing the conditions of such importation, manufacture, sale and possession, such regulation to be in force and to have effect for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue, the conclusion of such period to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council, as provided in the said regulations, and as a war measure onlv.

That, Sir, as I have said before, was agreed to by the dairymen of this country, but it was agreed to on the distinct pledge of the government of the day that the measure should not be made permanent. On the expiration of the War Measures Act in 1919 the government of that day did not consider that the special conditions mentioned in the order in council, a return to normal conditions, had arrived, and therefore in the second session of 1919 a bill was introduced intituled "An act to permit the'temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada." Since then, Sir, as you well know, year by year, a temporary bill has been introduced, and I claim that the fact- that the bill has been a temporary measure, for twelve months only at a time, is an indication that the government still considered that a pledge had been made to the dairymen of the country.
Let me remind the hon. members of the House of a pledge made during the war by the British government with reference to the removal of the embargo on Canadian cattle. I need not remind this House and the people of the country that without exception we made a demand that that pledge made during the war should be carried out. The people of England, notwithstanding their great objection to the admission of Canadian cattle, felt that they were bound by the pledge which their government had given to ours, and so last year a government in Great Britain which was not the same government which had made the pledge, but the government of Bonar Law, removed the embargo on Canadian cattle, and to-day our cattle are admitted to England. I ask you then, Sir, is it not equally the duty of this government to fulfil and carry out the pledge which was given by the government of that day to the people of this country that when conditions became normal the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in this country would again be prohibited? Feeling that this is so, feeling that the pledge of the government of that day is the important point to discuss, I have refrained from taking up the pros and cons of the question of oleomargarine, and therefore,
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell):
That all the words after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck Out and the following substituted therefor,-
In view of the distinct assurances given at the time that the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine was suspended by order in council in 1917 under the War Measures Act of 1914, such suspension being but temporary and a -war measure only, should now be removed and the question

Oleomargarine-Mr. Euler
left, without prejudice as to its merits, in the same position as before the enactment of the said temporary suspension.	.

MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
At the outset of the brief observations I propose to make I should like to say immediately that I am heartily in favour of the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll). This subject has been discussed session after session, and the same old straw has been threshed and re-threshed again and again, almost every session since I have been a member of this House. I deem it unfortunate that time has been unnecessarily spent from year to year in attempting to solve a simple problem which should properly be solved only in one way, it seems to me, if the members of the House choose to approach it in a fair and unprejudiced manner. Last year the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) introduced a resolution into this House which called for the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. That resolution was very exhaustively discussed, and finally was lost by a substantial majority. I contend that that vote itself was a declaration on the part of this House that it did not believe in the principle of the prohibition of oleomargarine; and I contend further that it was a direct mandate to the government to wipe off the statute book the law which provided for the prohibition of the sale and manufacture of oleomargarine. I regretted at the time that the Minister of Agriculture did not accept the vote in that way, and that he did not take steps to put himself in line with the expression of the opinion of the House as contained in that vote. As it was, the principle of the prohibition of oleomargarine was still recognized as the will of this parliament when exactly the reverse was the case, as expressed in the vote on
5 p.m. the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Missisquoi. Therefore,
Oleomargarine-Mr. Euler

in September, unless something further is done in regard to this matter the old law becomes operative and oleomargarine is prohibited. Now, we are under the necessity of discussing the whole matter again.
I accept as true the assumption that oleo is a wholesome food. I am quite content to take the word of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), who knows a good deal about the subjeot that it is. I have read a little about it myself, and I have personally come to the conclusion, and have the conviction, that oleomargarine is a wholesome food and contains nothing deleterious to health. That being true, my position is as it has always been in previous discussions on the question. If oleomargarine is wholesome and if it is sold for what it is, then I say this parliament has no moral right to declare that another person may not purchase, as he or she pleases, an article of commerce according to the price which they care to pay. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the issue here is a matter of personal liberty. I do not think that it should be possible for parliament to dictate to anyone as to what lie or she may purchase provided the commodity to be purchased is a sound article of commerce. Herfe is a palatable, wholesome food, a substitute for a more costly article. When butter is selling at 70 or 80 cents a pound in the winter, who dares say that the mother, we will say, of some eight or ten little children-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Make it twenty children.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I will make it twenty if you like; in the province of Quebec it may be twenty-five or more-who shall say that the mother of these children, with a small income, shall be prohibited from buying the only substitute for butter which she can afford? I think the suggestion is entirely indefensible from every point of view. It is an outrage in principle, and it is unworthy of a people that calls itself advanced and progressive, and having respect for ordinary human rights and freedom.
It should not be necessary at all to make an extended argument in regard to the matter. One would almost judge from some of the statements that have been made by opponents of oleomargarine and the indignation with which it is regarded, that those of us who favour oleomargarine are trying to force people to eat it. That is not the case at all. Those who do not like oleomargarine can buy butter. All we are contending for is freedom of choice and liberty in the matter.
fMr. Euler. 1
The point has also been raised by some friends outside of the House in conversation, that because butter is more nourishing, therefore oleomargarine ought to be prohibited. If that principle is to govern, we might as well say that a good porterhouse beef steak is more nourishing than a bit of veal or a piece of the shank of the animal. That argument could be carried to absurd lengths. Cream is better than milk; milk is better than skimmed milk, I suppose. Are we, therefore, to say that the inferior article cannot be used at all? Will an interfering parliament say that one must buy steak instead of sausage or the cheaper meat which is, perhaps, the only thing a family can afford? Some people like to wear real silk, not the artificial silk that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is trying to promote. Some people cannot buy real silk for their dresses or hosiery, they are forced to buy cotton. Are we justified, for the sake of the manufacturer of silk goods, in prohibiting people from buying cotton or any other class of goods which they may choose to buy?
We have talked almost with horror of substitutes for butter. It seems to me that the fact that the people of this country or any other country have been able to devise substitutes that serve their purpose at lower cost, is simply an indication of their ingenuity in adapting themselves to the needs of the moment or general conditions. So long as there is no deception, there should be no objection to substitutes. Cotton is a substitute for wool. Would you, therefore, abolish cotton, especially because it is imported? There seems to be antagonism to some of the ingredients of oleomargarine because they are imported from other countries. Concrete building blocks are a substitute for cut stone and are made to look like it as much as possible, and why should they not? I am even told that carrots and other vegetables sometimes appear, after they have gone through certain processes of manufacture, as the finest of strawberry jam or something of that kind. In my town thejf used to make, and I think they still make leatherette, a very good substitute for leather, and they make it to look as much like leather as they possibly can. Why should they not as long as this leatherette is not sold as something it is not? In my town they make a great deal of furniture, and sometimes possibly a member of this House will purchase what appears like a very fine article of mahogany furniture, when after all he has purchased only birch which is finished like mahogany and it is perfectly good furniture. Let me take even such a matter as linen collars. Possibly members of the House think

Oleomargarine-Mr. Euler
they are to-day wearing linen collars. As a matter of fact, I think they are all wearing cotton collars, and these wear longer than linen collars anyway. Therefore, the argument of substitution, in my opinion, constitutes- no argument at all. If there is butter in oleomargarine and that improves oleomargarine, why should the butter not be used? It is said that oleomargarine is made to look like butter and that is objectionable. One might almost as well say that butter looks like oleomargarine. Butter is made for man and not man for butter, and I cannot quite understand the veneration with which some of our hon. friends speak of butter and the sacred cow from time to time.
It surely must be significant that every other civilized country in the world permits the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr Tol-mie) has already made reference to the butter industry in the country of Denmark. To-day at luncheon I had the honour of sitting at the same table with a gentleman who came originally from Denmark and who has been living in this country for some time. He toi.1 us there, when the conversation turned to the matter of oleomargarine, that he could not understand for one moment, why anybody could possibly object to the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. He said: "Denmark is the greatest butter country in the world"-and perhaps he is right-and he added: "No one there thinks of objecting to the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine." I think he even said that they make more oleomargarine than butter, and I believe he said further that many of those who make butter eat the oleomargarine and sell the butter.
We talk of protection, and there has been a good deal of criticism in this House with regard to the matter of high tariffs, or, as ir is often called, "high protection." Sometimes I have been a recipient of some of those criticisms although I am entirely guiltless. Those who would prohibit the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine go far beyond the limits of high protection. They apparently believe in monopolies. Tariffs are usually directed against the outsider, the foreigner, the foreign product; but this is actually an attempt to put out of business a legitimate industry within our own country in order that another industry may benefit.
When one examines the arguments of opponents of oleomargarine-and I say this with all goodwill-there is really only one motive in the movement, and it is this:	That
all competition in connection with the commodity of butter may be removed by act of parliament, so that certain producers may
make more money at the expense of the consumers. Broadly stated, I believe that and nothing else to be the fact. All this solicitude for the poor children who will not be allowed to eat butter and who will be forced to eat oleomargarine is, as one gentleman said to me to-day, just so much eye-wash. This is a purely commercial proposition. I do not blame those who are makers of butter throughout Canada for desiring to make as much money out of butter as they can. That is business; but I do not think it is right for the members of this House who are representing all the consumers of Canada, to taka an attitude of that kind, advancing the interests of one class at the expense of another.

Can this parliament afford to recognize a principle of that kind? I say that it cannot. I would even go so far as to say that the man who raises cattle ought to object to anybody breeding hogs for fear that pork might come into competition with beef. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I will leave the hon. member for Victoria City to stand behind his own statement; I did not make it. Another argument has been advanced and it is the only one which to my mind carries any weight; and, at that, I do not think it goes very far.
Oleomargarine-Mr. Forke

It is that the prohibitory law was suspended on the strength of a pledge given by a former government that it was only for the duration of the war, and that the old conditions should be restored at the conclusion of hostilities. A pledge is a pledge, and I do not think that it should be violated or viewed in any light that would be regarded as a reflection on national honour, on parliamentary honour, or on the honour of any government. But surely a former government cannot perpetually bind succeeding administrations. This is a parliament elected by the people of Canada since the war, and it undoubtedly has a perfect right to legislate as it sees fit in the interests of the whole people. If that principle were not admitted, then any law that we now have on the statute books, enacted by the last government or any other before that, would necessarily have to be maintained by this parliament. That is absolutely unthinkable. This House has a right, moral, legal and in every other way, to legislate with regard to oleomargarine precisely as it deems fit in the interests of the people of all Canada.
Finally, I do not think that the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine is going to injure the dairy industry. The hon. member for Victoria City dealt with that aspect of the subject better than I possibly could because he is much more familiar with it. When butter is low in price or comparatively low- because it is never very low now to those who live in the towns-I do not believe that people will buy anything else to any great extent. When, however, it is extremely high, going up to 75 and 80 cents, as it does in the winter time, and is readily and profitably sold, there should be no objection on the part of those who sell it to the use of oleomargarine by people who cannot afford butter. Surely when butter is selling at these high prices, the men who are out of employment or who have scant employment, with a small income, should be allowed to purchase this substitute. I do not think that any hon. member of this House would say to any man or woman with a large family who cannot afford butter that the purchase of this wholesome substitute for butter shall be prohibited, so that their children may be deprived of something to eat with their bread.
I would add, before concluding, that no one can deny successfully that oleomargarine when properly made is thoroughly wholesome. And it is cheaper than butter. It is sold as oleomargarine and nothing else; and I would say that if the government or the Minister of Agriculture feels that oleomargarine is still being sold as butter, or feels that it should be surrounded by further restric-

tions, provided it is not actually prohibited, I am ready to support any measure that will ensure fair protection for the dairy industry. Let the manufacture of oleomargarine be surrounded with all sorts of safeguards in the public interest. But if oleomargarine is wholesome-as undoubtedly it is-and if it is properly safeguarded, then we have no right to forbid its manufacture and the use of it by the people. Such prohibition is an interference with the right of citizens and cannot be justified on any grounds. In my opinion the government should bring in a bill to repeal the old prohibitory act and then if necessary, introduce another providing for the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine under proper conditions and with adequate safeguards.
