speechtext:
I had not intended making any speech on the motion and the amendment thereto, but after listening to the remarks of the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Euler) I feel that I should offer some explanation of the way in which I propose to vote. The closing sentences of his speech practically state all that I intend to say at the present time. The amendment declares that at the time the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine was suspended by order in council in 1917, under the War Measures Act of 1914, the assurance was given that as such suspension was but temporary and a war measure only-
-it should now be removed and the question left, without prejudice as to its merits, in the same position as before the enactment of the said temporary suspension.
An order in council is not merely a scrap of paper that carries no consequences whatever, and it seems to me that the proper step to take now is to remove that order in council, "without prejudice," so that the matter might stand where it stood before. Then, if the government will bring down a bill dealing with the subject of oleomargarine I shall be prepared to discuss it. In the meantime I shall vote for the amendment, because I believe it proposes the proper step.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with my hon. friend (Mr. Forke) in what he has said and in the attitude he is taking. I should not like at this time to go into the respective merits of the prohibition or the importation of oleomargarine, but I do think that an undertaking was given a large interest in this country, under circumstances to which this House and parliament should pay attention. As has been mentioned by

Oleomargarine-Mr. Mackenzie King
the hon. member who introduced the amendment (Mr. Kay), during the period of the war, there appeared before the Milk Committee of the Food Board members of the dairy industry, to whom it was represented that the interests of the country rendered it advisable on patriotic grounds that the government should be given a free hand in the matter of permitting temporarily the importation of oleomargarine. The dairy interests acquiesced at the time, freely and willingly, in the belief and on the understanding, backed up by the government of the day, that when the circumstances had passed which had given rise to the necessity for this temporary arrangement, the measure permitting the importation of oleomargarine would be repealed. I think it would be a great misfortune if any large interest in this country, any large body of our citizens, had reason to feel that the government had not to the fullest measure lived up to any obligation assumed under circumstances such as then existed. Reading the order in council which was passed at the time, I think there is no room for any difference of view whatever as to the exact ground on which the importation of oleomargarine was then permitted. It has been read by the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) but I may requote the first few paragraphs. It is dated October 23, 1917:
Whereas attention is drawn to the abnormal demand for butter due to war conditions and to the very great probability that such abnormal demand and consequent high prices will prevail for this product for some time to come:
And whereas it is in the public interest, under the special conditions above named, that other fats should be available in Canada under strict and reasonble conditions as a substitute for butter.-
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council under and in virtue of the provisions of the War Measures Act 1914 is pleased to make and enact, and doth, hereby make and enact the following regulations providing for the importation int/ Canada and the permitting of the manufacture, sale and possession within Canada of oleomargarine and establishing the conditions of such importation, manufacture, sale and possession, such regulations to be in force and to have effect for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue, the conclusion of such period to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council as provided in the said regulations and as a war measure only.
I think this clause in the order in council makes it abundantly clear that the action taken by the government at that time was in the light of war conditions, and with the distinct understanding that when the war was over and, to use the words of the order in council, "the present abnormal conditions cease to continue," the order in council would be repealed and the dairying industry would
be put, as respects the importation of oleomargarine, exactly where it had been prior to the time it acquiesced in this particular order being passed.
Now, there is further evidence it seems to me which is conclusive in large part, and that is the legislation which extended the period of permission for importation. The act assented to on 10th November, 1919, 10 George V, Chapter 24, is entitled, "An Act to permit the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada." Why was that word "temporary" inserted in the title unless it was to emphasize the fact that the conditions which were set forth in the order in council had not, in the view of the ministry of the day, yet fully ceased to exist, and that this period of extension was to go on for another year.
All subsequent legislation on this subject has been in the nature of an extension year by year. I agree with what the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) says about a government not necessarily being bound by all the acts of preceding administrations. I think every case has to be considered in the light of all the circumstances surrounding it, and I confess that had I seen or known of the existence of this pledge last year, I should have been inclined to attach very great importance to and place strong emphasis upon it, and to have seen that it was referred to in the course of the debate. As nearly as I can gather, no reference whatever was made to this particular pledge in the debate last session. When a deputation representative of the dairy interests waited upon members of the government some little time ago, they stressed very strongly what they had conceived to be the representations of the government of the day and what they had represented to other members of the dairy industry as a consequence, and I felt at that time doubly convinced-I had previously learned of this pledge, and having learned of it decided to see that some recognition was taken of it- I felt strongly convinced at that time that the dairymen would not in all probability have acquiesced as they did in the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine during the period of the war if the pledge had not been given; and inasmuch as their action was taken for patriotic reasons, I feel it is the duty of this parliament to see that that pledge is carried out. Once it is carried out, I think parliament should be perfectly free to take whatever subsequent action it may deem fit with respect to the continued importation and manufacture of oleomargarine.



Oleomargarine-Mr. Meighen

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Might I ask
my right hon. friend where he stands in the matter of the pledge given by his government?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I will stand by any
pledge given by the late government. But I must say that I find the Prime Minister a lot more anxious and solicitous about a pledge given, as he says, by the late government, than he is about any pledge given by his own. Pledge! Really this talk about a pledge appeals to my mind as so insufferable that I can hardly command patience or find language to address myself to it. We are told by the Prime Minister that the late government gave a pledge that oleomargarine would be swept away when the war was over, and that we would return to a policy of no oleomargarine as we had before. He leads that pledge into an order in council, which was passed in the year 1918 and by which he states this parliament is bound. Well, I will have to try to address myself to that question before coming to a discussion of the merits of what really is before this House. What is before this House is whether we are going to have oleomargarine or whether we are not. Does any hon. member think that	if we	accept this amendmentin that way and slip the question outside the door this government is going to come forward with a bill to restore oleomargarine or indeed with any bill on the subject at	all?	Let	us all	rememberthat oleomargarine dies if this parliament does nothing this session. The legislation passes out of existence.	Now let	us be assured first	of all,	that	once we	vote for
this amendment and thus get rid of this resolution we are in effect shoving the subject out of doors because, take my word for it, this government is not going to come in with any bill once they have the excuse of the passing of the amendment.
But I said I would address myself to the question as to whether or not there was a pledge that binds us to support this amendment. In 1918 the government of the day, having behind it a War Measures Act passed in 1914, which virtually gave them power to legislate instead of parliament in respect of 
all matters that concerned the war, even indirectly, passed an order in council under the authority of that act whereby oleomargarine was admitted whereby the statute was suspended which had forbidden the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. Naturally the government did this as a temporary measure, and plainly stated in the legislation that it was a temporary measure. As a matter of fact the government had no power to enact other than a temporary measure under the War Measures Act. We had no power in the world permanently to alter an act of parliament; we only had power to do so temporarily in so far as we felt it justified and called for by the emergencies of the war by which we Nvere then surrounded. Consequently, we made it plain in the order that this was to be considered by the people of Canada as no permanent commitment on the subject but merely as a temporary measure resorted to by the government under the authority of a temporary act. We made this clear in our order in council. Not satisfied with that, next session we advised parliament what was done and recommended that the temporary measure which we had put into effect by order in council be made a temporary measure by legislation. Thereupon, by an act of the parliament of this country, the order in council was merged in a statute, and we no longer rested on the order in council. We rested from 1919 onwards on the statute of this House. Consequently-although I do not impugn for a moment the sincerity of the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke)- there is now no order in council to wipe away. Does anybody honestly imagine that there is to-day an order in council in effect? It has no more existence or effect than a piece of blotting paper?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The question was voted upon last year and the decision was in favour of the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. That was a decision of the House last year. Will the passing of this resolution have any more effect than that resolution had?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I doubt it very much. I doubt, even if we pass this resolution, whether the government can then make up its mind. It could not last year, and I have not seen any evidence of additional virility this year. I doubt if it would; but we must do our duty when a resolution is before us- whether the government is able to do its duty or not.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
We want to clear the way, anyway.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Meighen

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: There is no order in council to get out of the way, nor is there anything else to get out of the way. The order is as dead as Julius Caesar; it was dead a year afterwards. It was merged in a statute which provided that oleomargarine should not be forbidden to enter, nor forbidden to be manufactured for a period of time thereafter, parliament thereby taking the ground that under the conditions then prevailing, which were undoubtedly abnormal, we should not legislate in a permanent way; we should legislate in a temporary way only and leave parliament absolutely free when the temporary period was over to legislate just as it desired. What I am seeking to impress on the House is that at the expiration of the period fixed by parliament in the legislation of 1919, parliament was left free to act either one way or the other, as it might see fit. Parliament was free from all pledges of any kind. There had been indeed no pledge of any kind, affecting anyone, the moment the legislation expired.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Can my right hon. friend tell me when that period was?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I think it was last year. No; the first period expired in 1921.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Was it a fixed period?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Yes, it was a period fixed; it expired in 1921. The government of the day came in with a bill to extend it permanently and recommended that bill to parliament. There was a very great difference of opinion in the House-a difference of opinion as to its merits, confined not at all to the opposition alone but manifested by some on the government side. We finally, in view of the opinion of parliament, modified the bill to have it last only for a year and recommended to parliament that a measure to this end be adopted. The operation of the act was to expire one year from then, leaving parliament at the expiration of that period quite free to act as parliament might in its wisdom see fit. That law expired last session and this government being without any policy of its own at all placed the subject in the hands of parliament to be decided on a motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). Parliament on that motion declared emphatically against a policy of forbidding the admission to and manufacture in Canada of oleomargarine. One would have thought that the government then would have introduced a bill pursuant to such vote of parliament, but it did not; it introduced a bill providing for prohibition for one year and one only.
I have recited these events in order that parliament may understand its position now, in order that no hon. member of this House may feel that his vote or his decision is in any way restrained or his rights as a member of parliament abbreviated by any action of any previous government or by any action of any previous parliament. There is no excuse for any hon. member shelving this question to-day because of anything that has heretofore taken place. No hon. member I know is bound to vote for the admission of oleomargarine because of anything that was done before; every hon. member is just as free to vote against the admission of oleomargarine as if nothing at all had been done by the late government or by the late parliament. Surely it is not necessary to emphasize again that an order in council which is dead and which made no pledge at all save that its own life would be temporary, as necessarily it was, forms no hindrance to the free action of this House. Surely it is equally unnecessary to say that a statute which was declared to be temporary, to exist for a limited period only, forms, when that period is over, no obstacle to the free exercise of the rights of hon. members of this House. As I said at the beginning, the whole thing is so absurd, it is so beyond the pale of reason, that one can scarcely have the patience to hover round such a subject now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
May I ask another question? I think when I asked my right hon. friend before about the period expiring he had in mind the expiration of the particular act. He has just said the order in council contained no pledge. I would like to read these particular lines:
Such regulations to be in force and to have effect for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue,-
That was a pledge.	,

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
the conclusion of such period to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council.
That was another pledge. I will ask my right hon. friend if that period was ever determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Yes. undoubtedly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Where is the record?
.3528

Oleomargarine-Mr. Meighen

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I will have to go over a little of the ground again, I see. Undoubtedly a pledge was given that the order in [DOT]council would be temporary. Well, was the order in council not temporary? Is not the order in council dead long ago?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: It was the prohibition that was temporary, not the order in council.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Certainly the prohibition was temporary and the order in council too. There were hundreds of prohibitions passed under the War Measures Act that were just as temporary. Was parliament by those acts tieing anybody's hands after the temporary period was over? Were its hands tied, can anyone seriously argue, against freedom of legislation at the expiration of that period? Why, the Prime Minister can go through the records of the orders in council and I will guarantee that he can find two thousand of a like temporary character. Parliament was just as free at the expiration of these orders to legislate in regard to the subjects covered by them as in regard to any subjects within the purview of this House. The only pledge if you call it a "pledge" was that it would be temporary; that does not mean that parliament is not free later to make it permanent. The Governor in Council determined the period of the existence of the order in council the moment the subject was brought before parliament and a statute passed. We .brought it before parliament and parliament passed a statute for a temporary exclusion, .[DOT]and at the end of the expiration of that period parliament is free either to make it permanent or to do away with it for good. I do snot doubt that every hon. member of this -House, as an intelligent man, knows that parliament is to-day as free as if there had never been previous legislation, either orders in council or a statute of any kind. So I banish from my mind the suggestion that in any way we are tied by a pledge; we are not. We have to act; we are wholly free; what should we do as free men and a free parliament?
I have no hesitation in saying what I think should be done. I do not find, however, that any member of the government, upon whom now is the responsibility and who ought to take the initiative in this House on public questions, seems equal to the task of declaring what he thinks should be done. I think oleomargarine should be admitted. I do not for the life of me see any argument why an article which is a food and which unquestionably-at least it is unquestioned-if properly made is a wholesome food, should be forbid-

den entrance to or manufacture within this country. The only argument attempted against it is that it so resembles another article of production-butter-that there is danger of its being mistaken for that article, confused therewith, to the damage of and injustice to the producers of that article. I am ready to agree that it is no more than right and justice that the producers of butter should have ample protection against such confusion and against substitution. If I were convinced that it was impossible to give ample protection, to provide those safeguards that would make the conditions of produc- ' tion fair for dairy butter, then I think the lesser evil would be to vote against the admission of oleomargarine. But I have never heard anything so to convince me. I am not convinced that even under present conditions, the regulations are such as do not sufficiently protect dairy butter. I am not convinced, on the contrary, that they are sufficient-I do not know enough about it-but I am thoroughly convinced they can be made sufficient. And if it were necessary to go to the extent of providing a colour standard up to which the producers of oleomargarine might go and beyond which they might not go, I would support the establishment of such a colour standard and I guarantee this, that if you compel the oleomargarine maker to keep the colour of his article below a certain standard, you will never have it mistaken for butter and never do any injustice to the dairy industry. I am not saying it is essential to have that done. I do say it is practical to have it done, and I do say, if the Minister of Agriculture or the government feel that it is essential in order that the distinction may be defined and clear and unmistakable, then they ought to go ahead and do it. It can be done; it has been done.
Consequently with the burden on the administration to so frame and enforce regulations as will prevent confusion, as will prevent unfair substitution, I say there should be no objection to its admittance. Now I am going further.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Was the right hon. gentleman of the same opinion in 1917?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I was of the same opinion.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Then might I ask further, instead of passing a temporary measure under the War Measures Act why did he not pass a law to admit oleomargarine permanently?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I thought I had told the hon. gentleman. I had told the House. Under the conditions of those times, which were abnormal, we did not feel that in

Oleomargarine-Mr. Meighen
matters of general policy affected by those passing forces we should legislate permanently. We came to parliament and committed ourselves to permanent legislation in 1921. We were quite prepared as a government, indeed we actually did recommend to this House the permanent admission of oleomargarine under proper regulations. That is where I stand to-day.
Now I would go further. I believe as regards oleomargarine the same as regards other articles produced in this country or substitutes for which are produced in this country, that we ought to have a fair protective tariff against importation, and I say so more with regard to the needs of the dairy industry of this country, because it is not asked for so far as I know by the makers of oleomargarine-I say so more in justice to the dairy industry of this country than I do with regard to any producers of oleomargarine. We ought to have a duty against the admission of oleomargarine. I want to know why the farmer of this country should in this market which he helps to build up, to which he contributes every time he pays a dollar of taxes or buys a dollar of goods, be subjected without any restraint to competition of others from other countries who do not do anything to build up the market of Canada. We ought to provide a duty against the admission of oleomargarine and against the admission of the ingredients that go to make up the element of oleomargarine. If anyone can provide me with a reason why there should be a preference given in the tariff of Canada to the admission of oleomargarine I should like to hear it; it should be treated the same as other products against which duties are placed on their admission into this country-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Would the hon. member place a duty against the ingredients of oleomargarine?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Yes. I do not see how we could be fair to the butter makers if we did not.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: On cottonseed oil, for instance?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: There may be some ingredients you should not tax, but there are others you should. You cannot be fair unless you impose a duty against some of the ingredients anyway.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Would not that duty take away the cheapness of the argument that has been presented in favour of oleomargarine?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
You mean the cheapness of the article. It would not affect the cheapness of the argument. I do not think it would affect the cheapness of the article, or I should say, would not substantially or permanently affect it. It would in some measure for a time, but permanently I doubt very much if it would. But why should we in this country subject the farmer who produces his butter to the free admission of a competitor when the man who produces butter across the line has an eight-cent-a-pound duty against butter and an eight-cent-a-pound duty against oleomargarine? That is the condition today? The United States farmer has his market. He has a preference there because he helped to build it. He has his own country as a basis to rely on, on which to build his industry. He has a duty of eight cents a pound against butter and a duty of eight cents a pound against oleomargarine. We here have a four-cent duty against butter, and nothing against oleomargarine. That is an unfair position for the producer of butter in Canada. That is a position that should last no longer, and I venture to say that if you place the Canadian butter producer in a position comparable with his American competitor, you are not going to find him unreasonable on the question of oleomargarine. Do those two things-provide by more stringent regulations, because certainly more stringent regulations can be provided, against the possibility of substitution, that is to say, of the palming off of one article for the other; provide against that, put oleomargarine in the same position as other importations into this country that compete with productions in our own country and in our own market, do those two things, and, of course, make sure that only wholesome food ingredients enter into its production, which I understand is provided for already-and then if these three conditions prevail I know of no argument against the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine.
Mr. ROBB. How long has oleomargarine been allowed to enter Canada free under the Customs Act?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Oleomargarine was entirely forbidden up to 1918, and since 1918 the ingredients have been free.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: And oleomargarine.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
And oleomargarine too,
as I understand its history. We should have placed a duty on oleomargarine before. We should place a duty on it now and place a duty on such ingredients as compete with

Oleomargarine-Mr. Fielding
Canadian products. We should place these articles in the same category as other products of our country. Then see that the oleomargarine is manufactured only from wholesome substances, see that the restrictions are such that it cannot be unfairly substituted for butter, and these things done I do not know how we can argue against the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. There may be difference of .pinion on this subject; there is room for difference of opinion. But that is my view and I deem it my duty to state it to the House and state it clearly.
On the other question as to our being under some compulsion to vote for this amendment because of the 1918 order in council, there is no room for any difference of opinion at all. There is no room for sensible argument. It is a mere sham or screen erected in order to enable those who desire to do so to evade a fair and square issue that is before parliament.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE

-I would like to be
permitted to finish, if I may, before six .o'clock. May I first direct myself briefly to the constant complaint of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that the government as a government does not deal with this question. He has repeatedly emphasized that, indicating that he attaches great importance to it. Let us have a little common sense on this question.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: There is a difference of opinion among members of the government on this question. My hon friend, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has one view, I have another view. Does my hon. friend contend that on a matter of this kind one or the other of us should resign? Is it a matter of such vital importance as to justify a member in leaving the cabinet because he differs from some of the others? Surely he would not take such an absurd position. We take the position that inasmuch as there is a difference of opinion in the cabinet, the commonsense view is to ascertain the opinion of the House of Commons and be content to accept its judgment.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: You got that last session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
But only for a short
time.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
You got the view of
the House of Commons last session. I would take it that it would be for all time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
We are taking the
position to-day that inasmuch as there is a difference of opinion among ourselves, the commonsense view is not to make it a matter of vital importance and break up the cabinet, but simply to invite the judgment of the House of Commons and accept it whatever it may be. What has my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition done about it? In 1921 he took the noble stand that we were going to make this permanent, no longer any question about it, and he introduced a bill. Noble soul! But immediately he abandoned the bill. He made a change. He agreed to a bill that was not permanent. He agreed to temporize. He agreed to play safe for another year. If that be the case, if my right hon. friend felt perfectly free to do that at that time, cannot he give us the gracious privilege now of having a difference of opinion in the government and being content to accept the judgment of the House of Commons.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The difference is this: The former government, as a government, took a stand without any previous direction from parliament. This government had before them a previous direction from parliament last session, but they refused to take a stand, and they still refuse to take a stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: My right hon. friend says his government took a stand. They did not do so very strongly and they did not stick to it very long. My right hon. friend practically abandoned one bill and took another bill.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
That is practically what my right hon. friend did. A good many years ago when oleomargarine was an unsought product, it was prohibited in Canada. For many years I had the pleasure and duty of introducing the budgets of the country, and I want to say this: To the best of my knowledge and belief the question never arose as to what was to be done with oleomargarine. So long as butter could be got at a reasonable price nobody wanted oleomargarine, and nobody cared about it. And to-day if you can get butter at a reasonable price nobody wants oleomargarine. With the progress of time oleomargarine seems to have improved in character. It seems to be a product now which eminent physicians and health authorities certify is all right; there is no objection to it, it is a wholesome and useful product. I believe that if anybody had drawn attention to it

Oleomargarine-Mr. Fielding
in earlier years the prohibition would have been removed. I state again that oleomargarine remained on the prohibited list, not because anybody agitated for prohibition, not because anybody demanded it, but because the subject was not at all considered. Nobody wanted oleomargarine so long as he could get good butter.
I think I am correct in saying that Canada is the only civilized country in the world which refuses to allow the use of oleomargarine. I know of no civilized government in the world which prohibits oleomargarine except Canada. Hon. members know the old story as to the man who differed with his brethren on the jury and who said "that he never met such stupid men in all his life as those eleven fellows." Are we the only intelligent people in the world? Is the whole world, outside of Canada, wrong in its policy on this question? I think myself that the real question bdfore parliament to-day is simply this: Are the Canadian people as intelligent as other people? If we admit that the Canadian people are as intelligent as others, why cannot you give to these intelligent people the right to buy an article which is wholesome when they want it? It is not a question between butter and oleomargarine. Nobody wants oleomargraine to-day if he can buy butter at a moderate and reasonable price. I submit, as the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) put it, that the issue upon this question is: Are we an intelligent people? Are we to be trusted with the duty of looking after ourselves? Is there a doubt lest we shall not always take care of ourselves wisely in a matter of this kind? Now, there are some things as to which we have prohibition-I will not say prohibition but restriction. To-day, for example, there are explosives which are dangerous. We do not prohibit them, we put restrictions upon them; we say they shall only be sold in a certain way. Then there are narcotics and drugs. We do not prohibit them but we say they shall be sold subject to restriction and to restraint. Oleomargarine is the only thing in the commercial world which the people of Canada cannot be trusted to buy if they want it. It is an awful accusation to make against the people of Canada that they cannot be trusted to buy oleomargarine.
To-day nobody condemns oleomargarine on its merits. We have this extraordinary position-I say that with great deference to my respected leader-that it is claimed we are under an obligation. I cannot admit that for a single moment. If that is so when is this pledge to end which was given in 1917? We have had a new election, a new parliament.
What a preposterous thing it is to claim that the members of this new parliament are bound by something that was done by a previous government and a previous parliament. We are free to vote as we like, and let us vote as we like on the merits of this question. We are bound by nothing that happened in a previous parliament. "Ah!" it is said "in the cattle embargo a pledge was given; a change of government took place but nevertheless the pledge was carried out." Yes, the Right Hon. Bonar Law was a member of the government that gave the pledge, and he was called upon to fulfil the pledge given by the government of which he was a member. I have never joined in the argument that because of that pledge Canada's case was very strong. When you want to make a case before a rival or competitor you bring every argument you can. I think that in England there were some excellent men who did not want to admit Canadian cattle who used that pledge as a convenient excuse. I do not quarrel with them for doing so, but I decline to admit that the members of one House of Commons are bound by the act of any previous House, and I am bound to say that I see no foundation whatever for the statement that in this matter there exists a pledge that binds us. If there is a binding pledge I have a right to ask when does it end? If it binds us now it binds our successors, we are no longer a free parliament. No, the real question is not as between oleomargarine and butter. The people who want oleomargarine only want it when they cannot get butter at a reasonable price. If they cannot afford to use butter they will use oleomargarine; they want a substitute which is wholesome. Do not let anybody be deluded by the cry that oleomargarine is not wholesome. The highest medical authorities tell us that it is wholesome. I cannot for the life of me see why the intelligent Canadian people cannot be trusted to decide for themselves what they want. If we are as intelligent as any other people in the world give us the right to exercise our intelligence.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of detaining the House with any lengthy discussion of the proposition before us. There are, however, some features that I think have not been

Oleomargarine-Mr. McConica
touched on and that we might well consider. We are asked to allow the permanent manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada. What is oleomargarine? Nobody knows. You may search the statute books of Canada from end to end, and you will find no definition, no formula, no restriction, no anything that indicates what oleomargarine is. The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) gave us a formula, but does anybody follow his formula? We have no evidence that people do. There are a dozen or twenty different kinds of grease that they say may go into oleomargarine, but in what proportion and with what other constituents we have no means of knowing.
My objection to oleomargarine is that it is not presented upon its merits; that it does not stand on its own legs. We are told that men should have a right to buy as they see fit, and it is quite possible that most of us who buy oleomargarine know what we are buying. That is not the point. The question is:	Does the fellow who eats it know
what he is eating? That is the thing we want to be instructed on. Your Chinaman may go to the wholesale establishment to buy oleomargarine, and it has a government wrapper on it, with a label with oleomargarine in large letters printed on the side. He slips it in through the back door of the kitchen; the wrapper goes into the stove; the case knife wipes off the big letters; he mixes up about five pounds of it with one pound of butter; then he sells that to you and to me and to his other patrons as butter, and we pay for it as butter. I venture to say that 90 per cent or more of the oleomargarine that is consumed in Canada today is consumed as butter. The ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) was asked: Did he ever see a sign up in a restaurant or a hotel that they sold oleomargarine? He said that he did not eat in such places. How does he know? Do any of us eat there? We do not know. I would not be surprised if he had eaten a ton of oleomargarine.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I do not think I look like that.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
It may have that effect on some people; I do not know. I have an idea that if he knew how much of that stuff he had eaten when he went home after prorogation, he would be ashamed to look his own cows in the face. When he eats oleomargarine, what is he eating? He does not know. He knows he is not eating butter. He knows that oleomargarine, in its natural state, does not look like butter; that it does not taste like butter; that is does not smell

like butter. He knows that certain greases, what kind he does not know, are taken and treated chemically, then deodorized, decolourized, and mixed up into some sort of a conglomeration which is called oleomargarine. We have had a statement from scientists that they have analyzed it. Does any man state what the food value is? Does any man put down a table stating that butter is so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so, and that oleomargarine is exactly or very nearly the same? Certainly not. When a man eats that stuff, thinking it is butter, he is taking into his system something that is entirely foreign, something that his system does not require. Experience shows that milk is the natural food of the human being; that milk products are naturally adapted to building up the human system. What about this oleomargarine? We do not know. For that reason I do not think this is a question whether a man shall have the right to sell it or not. The question is:	Shall a man have
the right to feed it to some other man under false pretences? That is the point, and that is the one thing that, I imagine, is the vital point in this discussion.
An hon. member suggested that to prohibit oleomargarine from coming into or being sold in Canada is protection, similar to tariff protection, and he argued that we on this side should never support the prohibition of oleomargarine for that reason. I am not a protectionist, and I hope the time may soon come when nations will conclude that protection is a mistake. I very much doubt the right of a nation to tax one private individual for the benefit of another, and that is what protection is, in essence. When one man is protected someone else protects him, because there is no magic by which the passing of a protective law will create wealth for the fellow who is protected without imposing a burden on some other person. I repeat, if one man is protected some other man has to protect him. For fifteen years I have been selling my farm products in western Canada, and I do not think I ever sold a dollar's worth that brought me one single cent more because of a protective tariff; while I have not bought anything for which I did not pay more by reason of such a tariff. That is something I do not believe in. But if protection means to protect the people of Canada against fraud, against paying for something they do not get, against buying one thing and having to accept in lieu of it a rank imitation and counterfeit, then I am a protectionist.
I am not here urging this as a matter of protection to the dairy industry or to the

Oleomargarine-Mr. McMaster
farming industry generally. I urge that we prohibit the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine from the standpoint of the people of Canada, who are the consumers. We have the statement of the lumber boss that he is in favour of it; have we anything from the lumber jack? That is the point. Where is the man who eats it that is asking that this stuff be allowed to come into Canada or be manufactured and sold here? There is not one word from any such person. Did anyone ever hear of any hotel keeper who advertised: "Nothing but high grade oleomargarine used in this hotel?" Why, the effect of such a pronouncement would be to empty the dining-room in a day. No; the trouble with this thing is that it is not sold on its merits; it does not stand on its own feet. It is an imposition on the people who use it, and for that reason I shall certainly support the amendment offered to the House.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
The question now before the House has occupied our attention on several previous occasions and it is to be hoped that on this occasion, after a full discussion, we may make up our minds and act accordingly. So far as I am concerned, I am not in favour of the prohibition of any wholesome article of food. I cannot take any other stand, holding the principles I hold; and therefore I am in favour, not necessarily of oleomargarine, not necessarily of butter, but of liberty and freedom of choice for the people of Canada. I do not think that anything has been proved before the House to show that oleomargarine is not a wholesome article of diet; and once the fact of its wholesomeness is established, the whole burden of proof is thrown upon the shoulders of the restrictionists and those people who believe that liberty of choice should be interfered with.
I take it for granted that there should always be a presumption in favour of liberty. What is the object of eliminating oleomargarine? The eloquent member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McConica) has placed his opposition to oleomargarine on the highest
ground. Ear be it from me, he says, to advocate anything for any special interest; it is the welfare of the people that I am considering; it is to protect the people against this deleterious substance that I wish to see legislation passed. May I observe that, if oleomargarine were an unwholesome article of diet, we have a distinguished doctor in charge of the Department of Health of this country who would see to it that 6uch an article was prohibited. No, Mr. Speaker, the object of the propaganda is, as I trust I shall be able to show, the mistaken idea that by prohibiting oleomargarine you are going to enhance the price of butter, or at least to stabilize it. That is the real object lying at the basis of this propaganda against oleomargarine. But we are not here to represent merely what we may imagine are the views of our constituents. We are here to look at matters from the point of view of the national interest.
Let me just examine for a moment the real, though unavowed object of those who are in favour of the elimination of oleomargarine, that is to say, the raising of the price of butter. Will it raise the price of butter to eliminate this substitute? I do not think it will. The price of butter, of which we have a large exportable surplus, is determined not in Canada but on the markets of the world. There the butter enters into competition-if there is such competition-with oleomargarine, and the price of our butter will not be affected by oleomargarine in this country. This was most conclusively argued by the member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) two years ago when the matter came before the House. I do not believe that oleomargarine is a competitor of good butter; I believe it comes into competition only with butter of an inferior grade. If that is the case, as I believe it is, What is the result of the prohibition of the manufacture in or importation into this country of oleomargarine? Well, the first result will be to give an example of class legislation which will redound very little to the credit of those who support such a move. I say class legislation; it is not even class legislation, because it cannot be imagined, for instance, that to prohibit oleomargarine will help the farmer who raises beef cattle, and for whom the market for oleomargarine helps to maintain the price of what he produces. If this prohibition is to help any one it will tend to help-I do not believe it will succeed in doing so, but that is what is aimed at-only a section of a class, that is, the dairy farmer. Nor do I believe that it could help this section.

Oleomargarine-Mr. McMaster
Furthermore, it would deprive the people who cannot afford to buy good butter of a wholesome spread for their bread. Now, I know that in appealing to the members of this House I am appealing to gentlemen who are humane and reasonable. Can they place themselves in the position of an unorganized workingman in a city? Organized workingmen, through combination, are generally able to raise their wages to a reasonable height; but the vast majority of people working in cities are unorganized, they have to sell their labour for what they can get. There have been those who have justified the manufacture of oleo as a war measure. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there are those who under the present organization of our society are always at war with poverty and with debt, and they have a right to be supported and to have liberty to exchange their labour for what they want as long as they are not buying what is poisonous or positively deleterious. I ask those who support the idea of the elimination of oleo to put themselves in the place of some poor working man with a large family. He comes home at night after this legislation is passed, after oleo has been driven off the market, and not being able to afford good butter-in the winter time good butter goes beyond the price Which the poor can afford to pay-he finds his children with dripping on their bread, perhaps lard, and if they say to him, "Father, why cannot we have that nice stuff that we had on our bread last year?" "Oh well," he answers, "the representatives of the dairy farmers have said you cannot have it." Is there a supporter of the prohibition of oleo who would like to overhear that conversation? I do not think so.
Now, there are others too, there are the clerical classes, there are the school teachers, there are the ministers of the Gospel who find the cost of living pressing heavily upon them. Are you to tell them that they shall not have oleo if they want it to spread upon their bread? And let me say this-and I make the plea very strongly to those who agree with me on tariff matters-if you vote to eliminate oleo you are placing in the hands of the protectionists a rod for your own backs. For if you vote for the elimination of oleo, how in the world can you expect anyone to listen to	you when
you protest against the imposition of duties which raise the price of what you must buy?
I would implore hon. members who agree with me on tariff matters to think very deeply before they commit themselves to an attitude which will be in direct contradiction and IMr. McMaster.l
repudiation of the principles they have advocated in this House. They will be regarded as inconsistent people-and we are told that consistency is a jewel.
And let me with all frankness and with all courtesy expose to those who think differently from me what posture they will appear in before the people of Canada, before the vast numbers who live in our towns and cities and who are not interested in having oleo eliminated. First of all, those who vote for the elimination of oleo will place themselves before the nation as the representatives of a class who are thinking of their selfish interests and not of the public weal. No one is obliged to eat oleo unless he wants to, we are not forcing oleo down anyone's throat, but we who believe in the principle of liberty do feel that there should be liberty of choice.
Then may I make this argument also? I think it is a sound one. Those who in Great Britain fought for fiscal freedom made their appeal first to the workman in the town, then to the manufacturer, subsequently to the farmer on the land, and finally to the landlord, and they got the vast majority of the British people to agree with them. They could not carry on the battle successfully themselves, they had to get the cooperation of other people. Now, in the fight which many of us wish to make for lower tariffs, for greater freedom of trade and commerce, we need the help of the consumer in the town, we need the help of the workingman in the factory, and if by our vote we restrict the liberty of those classes in the towns who wish to purchase something which they think they need, we will be in a poor position to ask for their help. The matter is not of tremendous importance in one way; it is of tremendous importance in another. People have got to be guided either by expediency or by principle, and it is hard for me to understand how anyone who desires to have his conduct guided by principle rather than by expediency can one day vote for lower tariffs, for greater freedom of exchange-because in the long run that is what it is, allowing a man to exchange the product of his own toil, his own capital, for what he lacks-and then next day say that so far as a certain exchange is concerned the possibility of making that exchange shall be cut off.
You are a student of history, Mr. Speaker, and no doubt you will be interested to note the similarity of the idea underlying this proposed legislation to eliminate oleomargarine with the ideas on trade and commerce which obtained in the time of the Stuarts. I have before me the Encyclopaedia Britannica,

Oleomargarine-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
and I read with interest that by an act passed in the reign of Charles II it was decreed that all dead bodies should be buried in woollen shrouds. They must not be buried in linen shrouds, nor in cotton shrouds, they must be buried in woollen shrouds. Why? Because the lawmakers of those days wished to favour the interests of the woollen manufacturers. And I say with all courtesy that legislation which would prohibit the manufacture and sale of wholesome articles of food in this country is legislation on the lines of that which prevailed in the time of Charles II. I think perhaps with that historical allusion I had better leave the question to be decided, I trust, by the enlightened intelligence of the members of this House.

Mr. Speaker, as the representative of an agricultural constituency I do not wish to give a silent vote on this question. Oleomargarine is unknown to the people I represent; they eat good Canadian butter. The only requests I have received from my constituency to vote for the continued manufacture, importation and sale of oleo were from a couple of lumbermen so they might be able to supply it to their shantymen in the winter time. Therefore I am free in the matter. My electors are consumers of good butter, and I hope will continue to be for a long time to come, and I should like to see the majority of Canadians following their excellent example.
We are dealing with an aftermath of the war. Nobody ever dreamt of allowing the importation, manufacture and sale of oleo in Canada previous to the war. Our parliaments before that time-and they were made up of reasonable men-never thought of allowing this product to be sold to the Canadian people. But during the war it was allowed in under the abnormal conditions which then prevailed. Those conditions are now at an end, and I think we are free to act in the matter. I am going to cast my vote to re-establish the embargo on oleomargarine, and thereby I am satisfied that I shall have done my duty towards my constituents and the people of Canada generally.
There is one great problem in Canada which must be solved and solved soon if Canada is to remain the country that it is or is to have the future that we hope for it; the people must go back to the land. That is the main salvation of Canada. In the first ten years that I had the honour of representing my constituency in this House its population increased by five thousand people; in the second ten years the increase was only five hundred people. Their explanation is that the young people are leaving the farms and going to the cities because farming no longer pays. I have heard the agricultural question discussed from the point of view of the West; the condition that exists there exists in the province of Quebec just as acutely, but little is heard here of the grievances which our farmers have. But the people of my province are a patient and long suffering people. The progenitors of some of them were there some ten generations ago, and they have passed through many of the crises experienced by Canada during that time. They have stood the burden and heat of the day and are willing to stand it yet, but I say frankly to this House that unless we do something immediately to induce the people to return to the land we are facing a great crisis in this country.
I know of no industry in the province of Quebec that is of more importance in every respect than the dairy industry. Quebec occupies an enviable position in that respect. We have a land which is eminently suited to the purpose of dairying and a climate which is exceptionally favourable to the raising of cows and the making of butter. I would therefore, dislike to see this House give a vote which would jeopardize what I consider to be the leading industry of eastern Canada-the dairy industry. I was pained and surprised to see that a large number of agricultural representatives from western Canada last year forgot the agricultural interests of eastern Canada to the extent of voting against the dairy products of eastern Canada in favour of oleomargarine. After all, oleomargarine is a mere fancy; it never existed in this country before the war. Nobody thought of it then, and it was allowed in under certain well-defined rules, with a positive engagement that as soon as the abnormal days disappeared the privilege then granted would be repealed. There were too many substitutes of various kinds during the war; it is difficult now to go into a store in any part of Canada and buy an article which is not a substitute of one kind or another. Manufacturers and others during the war lent themselves too readily to the making of substitutes of this kind or that, and I am not in favour of encouraging any more of them.
I do not see why the farmers of Canada, the dairy farmers especially, those who have the courage, and, I may say, the patriotism, to stick to the land when so many others are deserting it, should be given a slap in the face by this House of Commons in favour of an article which, after all, is consumed by very small numbers of people. We are told the consumption is only 4,000,000 pounds annually, its use being confined mostly to the
Oleomargarine-Mr. Lewis

cities; in the agricultural districts it does not exist. I should be surprised to see the representative of an agricultural constituency vote in favour of the main motion now before the House. I will say nothing further, Mr. Speaker, than this:	I will vote for the
amendment, and in casting that vote I think 1 am acting in the genuine interests of the farming community of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in regard to the situation by which we are confronted. I do not feel that the amendment is necessary; the defeat of the resolution offered by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) would have accomplished the same purposes that the amendment has in view. However, now that the matter is before the House I wish to make my position clear.
During the by-election in Moose Jaw-and I want to speak as kindly as I can in regard to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell)-he stated that when the vote was about to be taken last year on the subject of oleomargarine I, with about five or six others in this corner of the House, immediately slipped under the bam and the only part of me that could be seen was my feet. Well, I hope the whole of me will be seen when the vote is taken on this occasion. But what the minister said was not quite correct, and as the charge was repeated in a paper in my own constituency, I wish to answer it. It is true that the Minister of Agriculture spoke to me in the afternoon-not a short time before the vote was taken, but in the afternoon -in respect to oleo, and also about the conditions in southern Saskatchewan and the need of entering largely into dairy farming. With all of that I quite agreed. But about eleven o'clock in the evening I asked the whip, when the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) was1 speaking, how many more members were going to speak, and he said, "Oh, possibly ten or eleven." I wanted to speak on the subject, but he did not think the vote would be taken that night and I left the House about eleven o'clock. I understand, however, that the vote was taken some two hours afterward. So that I did not slip under the bam just a few moments before the vote was taken. As I said, I understood that the vote was1 not going to be taken that night.
Now, I wish to speak only about three or four things. The second thought that came to me when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking was this: Since when did he become solicitous about the keeping of pledges? It is only a few weeks since the party of which I am a member
[Mr. Marcil.J
presented an amendment because they felt, either rightly or wrongly, that the Liberal party were not implementing their pledges of 1919. It seems to me that a government should think about keeping its own pledges before concerning itself about keeping the pledges of the government that preceded it. At all events, so far as the pledge was concerned, it may have been a pledge, as the hon. member for north Waterloo (Mr. Euler) said this afternoon, to the dairy interests. So far as it was a pledge to them, it should be kept; but I think there is a greater pledge to the Canadian people, and they have spoken since that time in no uncertain voice.
The third point I wish to make in regard to the amendment is this: To me it appears to be somewhat of a camouflage. I went upstairs immediately after I had heard the amendment read and I looked over the resolution that was proposed last year by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). It did seem to me that that resolution superseded any pledge that had been given to the Canadian people in 1917 or any time afterwards, because it assorted that it was in the interests of the Canadian people that oleomargarine should not be imported into or manufactured in Canada, and the House voted against it. The majority was not large, it is true, but at the same time it was a majority, affirming the view that the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine should be permitted. So it is that we have heard the expression of the representatives of the Canadian people in this parliament; they have spoken definitely; they have expressed the opinion that the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine should be permitted.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE

I shall answer that in a few moments, because I was charged by the Minister of Agriculture with shirking the vote. If I shirked the vote I shirked it in good company, because the right hon. the Prime Minister himself was absent and about eighty other members, probably not expecting the vote to be taken that night, and that is the reason why I feel justified myself in regard to that matter.
As far as the resolution is concerned, it does seem to me that parliament, although eighty members were absent when the vote was taken, wanted the sale of oleomargarine. But let us go one step further. The laws we pass here are not the laws of the Medes and Persians, and if this year it is necessary to change that vote, and if we think it is in the interest of the primary industries, but not in regard to a matter of principle, that that vote should be changed, I think parliament is competent to change it without being inconsistent at all. What I do feel is this: It seems to me that there is a certain lack of courage on the part of the government after the resolution passed last year by the vote
it obtained, in not bringing down a measure and shouldering the responsibility. I think it was the duty of the government to have done that, to have shown that it had backbone enough to bring in a measure of that character. I hate to cast my vote in regard to a camouflaged motion, and after hearing the speech of the hon. member to my left (Mr. McMaster) it is very hard for me to reconcile any position I may take to-night, because we are not really fighting or voting on the merits of the question.
There is one thing I do want to urge upon the government earnestly, and it is this: If this amendment carries and the importation and sale of oleomargarine is defeated, I feel that the government should insert a clause whereby people in Canada can at least manufacture oleomargarine for export, and thereby use up the by-products in some of these large concerns. If it is the will of the Canadian people that we shall not eat oleomargarine, well and good; I am willing to abide by that, but it does seem to me that these manufacturers should have the privilege of competing with Belgium and other countries in the British market. That is all I have to say on this resolution, but I hope that a measure will come before this House where there will be no side-stepping at all, and where we shall be able to vote on the merits of the question.
Just before I came up to the House I spoke to a washerwoman with a large family and said, "Possibly to-night we shall vote for the elimination of oleomargarine." She said, "If you do what are we going to do in winter with butter at sixty-five cents a pound? I shall not be able to put anything on the bread for my children." That is the situation as it seems to me at the present time. We are not forced to eat oleomargarine, and as far as the West is concerned, when I was out there I went into many and many a store to find out if they ever sold oleomargarine, and I never came across one village store in my constituency that sold it, so that I cannot see that it enters into competition with butter. Furthermore, I want to say as a member of parliament with the family I have that I have bought oleomargarine as a test for my children, and as far as some of them were concerned they could hardly tell the difference between oleomargarine and butter, especially in regard to that cottage roll the minister speaks of. I am not saying it is a good thing for the children, but it does seem to me that the people of this country have a right to say what they are going to eat, and if it can be proved that this is a wholesome food I do not see why we should restrain

Oleomargarine-Mr. Dechene
this trade in any way. As far as I am concerned, I would like to see this question fought on its merits, and not on a camouflage or an amendment such as is before the House at the present time, on which we really cannot get a consensus of opinion in regard to oleomargarine.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
