Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much pleasure to the greater part of this debate on oleomargarine. I was already well acquainted with the views of most of the members and nothing new has transpired in the present discussion, unless it is the word "camouflage" which was freely made use of. The last speaker (Mr. Lewis) clearly proved to us that there existed camouflage among a greac number of members sitting around him. In fact, last year, when this debate took place, the interests of the large packing houses were strongly emphasized and we were told: "These packers allow us, we from the West, a better price for our beef when the manufacture of oleomargarine is permitted, because they can make use of a large portion of the beef fat, which gives them some return." Now, we know, through the circulars of these gentlemen which have been distributed to all the members, that there is about twenty-five to thirty pounds of beef fat or such per head used in the manufacture of oleomargarine, the price of the former being four or five cents per pound, this would mean that the manufacturers would pay for beef about SI or $1.25 more per head. This would amount to very little for the cattle-breeders of the West, and even this slight advantage would not exist in the eastern provinces. For over twenty years, the governments of the eastern provinces have exerted all their energies to promote the dairy industry. Large sums of money have been paid to agricultural and co-operative' associations, and also to farmers, in a word, to all those who took an interest in the growth and improvement of the dairy industry in our provinces.
Every year, parliament is called upon to vote large sums for the improvement of the dairy stocks of the different provinces. Every year, the provincial legislative assemblies vote large amounts for the same object, always, with the idea of fostering lively competition among the farmers, and, bearing in mind the improving of the dairy herds and at the same time benefiting the farms and the commonwealth. What would be the object of having spent such enormous sums, if by a majority vote of this House, we allowed the manufacture of oleomargarine on a large scale.

We are told: There are but three or four million pounds of oleomargarine sold yearly, it is very little compared with the 270,000,000 pounds of butter produced and sold yearly, in Canada, or by Canada. This may be true to some extent, but one must not lose sight that last year parliament passed an act extending for one more year the right to manufacture, to have in one's possession and sell oleomargarine. Evidently the large manufacturers of this article did all they could to keep down this trade, so as to show how small it was and not to frighten the other industries. However, I think that the majority of members will not be deceived by this camouflage of the manufacturers who, to-morrow, should the law permit them and the markets be thrown open, would spread over the country a product of an entirely inferior quality.
The hon. member (Mr. Lewis) who has just taken his seat, told us that he made, last year, the experiment of oleomargarine on his children. I do not think that he is much to be congratulated on this matter. If he had had some experience with this product, he would not have tried it a second time and I am certain that his wife would not have wanted him to bring oleomargarine home again. Most of the experiments made consist in placing oleomargarine or butterine on bread. If these gentlemen would only go to the kitchen and place this oleomargarine on hot toasts, or else, do some frying with it, I think they would much prefer not to be the cook when this is happening; it is healthier to be in the open air or pace up and down in front of the house while the wife is leaning over the pan. I do not think that all those who have a delicate sense of smell and like to eat well, bear a love for oleomargarine to the extent of putting up with the smell of tallow on their toasts or again in cooking. There is nothing so unpleasant as the odour of suet or oleomargarine in the frying pan and I have heard this as a fact from more than one person who has given it a trial. It is a substance which disintegrates with the heat and that is why when it is used on toast or in cooking it is abominable. When you are told, Sir, let the workman give it to his children to butter their bread, I think, that is a very poor argument. Here is another weak reason given in behalf of the labourer: How do you expect the working class in winter to purchase butter at 65 cents a pound? They forget to tell us, however, when these prices prevail, oleomargarine has increased in price and is sold from fifty to fifty-five cents a pound,

Oleomargarine-Mr. Warner
and even much dearer, with profits ranging from 100 per cent to 125 per cent. The price of manufacturing oleomargarine is 12 to 15 cents per pound and it is sold at 24 and 25 cents per pound; it is sold just sufficiently low enough to compete with butter, but not in keeping with the workman's purse. Very few working men, if not influenced, buy oleomargarine. It is forced upon them. It is forced upon them when the large companies feed their men with it. It is forced upon them in all restaurants of cities, where meals are served at cheap prices, without mentioning if butter or oleomargarine is supplied. This article is coloured and given the appearance of butter, it is served to those who come and eat in such places at a rate of 5, 10, 20 or 30 cents per meal, but great care is taken not to mention that as the hon. member who preceded me in this debate stated, we serve only oleomargarine of the best make. This is simply camouflage. Another reason that certain speakers invoked this evening and which I feel certain cannot but have astonished you, is the freedom of choice. Here is an article which is not worth much, everybody admits- perhaps it is worth nothing-however we are free to purchase it, we are told. Is this the only instance, in our country, where a citizen is not allowed to purchase what he finds good to his taste? Have we not in Canada a temperance act which applies to the whole country, and have we not in this province where we live, at present, a law which decrees: You shall not have the right to drink beer and you shall neither have the right to drink wine? Do we not know, Mr. Speaker, that beer plays a very important part in the Enalish workman's diet?
There was almost a revolution in England, during the war, when they tried to stop the workman's beer. Do we not refuse -in certain parts of the country, not only to our workmen but everybody the right of drinking beer, even though it may be a pleasure to them? Is beer a deleterious product? Evidently not. It is a product made from malt which is recommended by the medical profession but one must not make use of it to excess. Neither would it be wise to eat too much oleomargarine.
In France^-as you are better aware than I am, Mr. Speaker, wine is part of the diet, not only for the well to do classes but also for the working classes, and cider is also part of the diet of the farming class. Even here, in certain parts of the country, is not the use of wine prohibited? In this province we are allowed to make wine, to sell it by the dozen bottles, but you are not permitted to
purchase it by the bottle. What becomes of individual liberty? When it does not suit the purpose, we abolish it. This is not a serious argument. I therefore state, Mr. Speaker, that we should brush aside that part of the reasoning in favour of oleomargarine and treat it laughingly.
One last word before closing my remarks. We were told a short while ago that this was part of our political platform, that we even made promises that the greater number of the members of the government would be bound by these promises of the Liberal party and should vote against oleomargarine. It is not the first time that the Liberal party places on its programme this question regarding oleomargarine. I remember-when I was still at the university or college-when the Liberal party under Sir Wilfrid Laurier prohibited the importation of oleomargarine. What was the result? Oleomargarine was prohibited shortly after 1900 and immediately the dairy industry improved and expanded, and a few years later our country had become known abroad as an exporter of butter and cheese. The prohibition which Sir Wilfrid Laurier had then imposed on this article had been favourable to the trade development of our country. We have the experience of the past, why not follow in the same footsteps? This plank in the programme of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in 1900, is still part of our programme; and I am, to-day, happy to adhere to it as well as to many other measures by asking that imports of oleomargarine be banned and by strongly supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Missis-quoi (Mr. Kay). _

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as short speeches have been the order of the day in this debate I hope I shall not speak at undue length. Although there is quite a lot I should like to say I will try and make my speech as brief as possible. I wish to say that I want to discuss this matter from, perhaps, two viewpoints. First, as to the effect of the use of oleomargarine on the young folks that we expect from this time on to grow up and become citizens of Canada; second, as to whether the government should or should not carry out their pledges; and, perhaps, I shall have something to say as to the possible financial effect on Canada, of a question of this kind if we do not act wisely.
One thing that is always present in our minds is what is best for the children of our country. The state, it will be admitted, has the right to say something with respect to the conduct of parents or people who are taking care of children. If parents, through

Oleomargarine-Mr. Warner
carelessness, negligence or other cause, do not send their children to school the law steps in and declares that those children must be given a certain amount of schooling in order that they may develop into proper citizens. Some people may regard that as unfair towards the parents. Nevertheless such is the law. Is it any more unfair or unreasonable to go one step further and provide
9. p.m. that the parents or guardians of children shall give them nourishing food in order that their physical development may be of the right character. It has been stated many times in this discussion that it has not been proven that oleomargarine is not a healthful food. I challenge that statement especially for children. Let me tell hon. members who have been quoting authorities, that some of the authorities that have been quoted have been quoted on both sides of this subject. I have under my hand several quotations. One is from Dr. McGill, until recently Dominion Government Analyst, who says that one pound of butter is equal in producing value to four and one-half pounds of beefsteak. He gives a long list of comparisons, but the important thing is in the next paragraph of his remarks:
In addition to providing heat and energy for the body butter promotes growth and health to a remarkable degree because it is rich in that vital element called vitamines (fat soluble A) which is absolutely indispensable to health and growth and as a factor in the building of bone and teeth. There is no problem before the country of greater importance than the one of properly feeding and nourishing it* people.
Statistics in the United States show that one out of every four in that country is suffering from under nourishment, and that 350,000 of them die every year from no other cause than poor or deficient food. It is not a case of poverty, so much as a case of ignorance. The food now given those children costs even more than proper food would cost. Similar figures are not available for Canada. While the condition of our children is doubtless not as shocking as the United States because a greater proportion of our people live on the land, where the children are fed on milk and butter in greater abundance, still children suffering from mal-nutrition are far too numerous in our centres of population.
It is the sacred right of children to be given wholesome nourishing food, that they may grow up to be strong and healthy men and women.
The next is Mr. Herbert Hoover, a member of the United States government, who won so much honour for himself and his country as United States Food Administrator during the war. He puts the case clearly when he says:
The basis of child welfare is health and physical development, the foundation of child health lies in proper feeding. In its broad aspects the proper feeding of children revolves around a public recognition of the interdependence of humans upon dairy cattle. The white race cannot survive without dairy products.

That is Herbert Hoover's idea. Professor E. V. McCollum of Johns Hopkins University, Who is one of the greatest authorities on the use of foods, for the preservation of vitality and health, in his book, "The Newer Knowledge of Nutrition," at page 16, after alluding to certain experiments in diet, says:
With this diet the interesting observation was made that growth could be secured when the fat in the food mixture was butter fat, whereas no growth could be secured when the butter fat was replaced by lard, olive oil, or other vegetable oils. Under these conditions, why should ignorant parents be permitted to give oleo instead of butter to helpless little children merely because it may be a few cents cheaper when butter is an essential to the health of the v-ild and the welfare of the nation?
I might say that is proof-and I have more -that it has not been proven that oleomargarine is a proper food for children. It has been proven that it is not.

speechtext: What is that from?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I got this statement from the secretary of the Dairy Council, who obtained the information from the parties who have been quoted. I wish to quote from Dr. Wiley who has been quoted on both sides as I think these other authorities have. I wish to quote a statement by Dr. Wiley copied from a letter that Mr. Love, secretary of the Alberta Dairymen's Association, got from Dr. Wiley himself. This is what Dr. Wiley says:
Originally my objection to oleomargarine, and this is quoted by the dairy interests, was based on the fact that it imitated butter. Not only did the makers of this product seek to resemble butter in colour, but also in flavour, and for this reason in the making of oleomargarine it is, I believe, universally churned with cream or milk. I have always been opposed to this process in the manufacture of oleomargarine. I believe that the churning of oleomargarine with milk or cream is solely for the purpose of simulating butter in the taste or flavour. For that reason it masquerades, or seeks to masquerade, under assumed properties which are possessed by butter itself.
Since the oleomargarine problem first presented itself in this country-
He is speaking of the United States.
-there has come a new discovery of supreme importance to the health of our people, namely, the vital factors, commonly called vitamines, in foods. Investigation shows that butter fat of all known fats has the most abundant supply of vitamines. Next to butter fat comes the fat of eggs and the fat which attaches itself to the vital organs of the animal body. For this reason animal fats which are used in the manufacture of oleomargarine are far inferior to butter fat, and to this extent oleomargarine is inferior in wholesomenes3 to butter. There are some animal fats used in the manufacture of margarines which contain no vitamines at all; for instance, lard. The same objection holds in regard to vegetable fats used in the manufacture of margarines.
It has been stated, further, that the feeding of oleomargarine to children or young animals

Oleomargarine-Mr. Warner
is distinctly injurious because a lack of development ensues in many ways. Here is what Dr. Margaret Patterson has to say on this point:
In Denmark (one of the best dairying countries in the world) the high price obtainable for butter induced the people to ship all the butter out of the country. The butter-fat was extracted from practically all the milk used in the country. The children were given plenty of separated milk, (a very valuable food for it contains all the lime salts, in fact, the only lack is the butter fat). This lack of fat was supposed to have been made up in fats of other kinds. The proper number of calories were given, but after a time the children developed a very troublesome type of sore eyes. The eyes showed no signs of improving under the most skilled physicians and had it not been for the research work carried out by Dr. McCarrison in Britain, and Prof. McCollum and others in America, the cause and cure of the disease might have remained unknown, and hundreds of children would have lost their eyesight.
This doctor goes on to say that as soon as butter fat was given to the children, and without any further treatment, a noticeable recovery followed. An hon. member has informed the House that we do not know what oleomargarine consists of. I do not believe we do. I have here a statement from the Dominion Cold Storage Commissioner in which he quotes Mr. Love, the secretary of the Alberta Dairymen's Association, in reference to the question as to the formula for oleomargarine. I read the following:
We asked J. A. Rudick, Dairy and Cold Storage Commissioner of our country, for the formulae to make oleomargarine and he was forced to reply as
follows:
"We have these on our files as well as the formulae used by most of the American manufacturers, who are exporting oleomargarine into Canada. These were supplied to us by the manufacturers on the undertaking that the information should be considered as confidential, and we are, therefore, not able to pass this on to you."
We can see how the thing is covered up so that no one can tell what oleomargarine contains. No one knows anything about it apart from the cold storage authorities who take charge of it. To continue:
Compare Mr. Ruddick's statement with the law of Canada on butter, as found in section 21, page 27, of the Food and Drugs Act, Department of Health of Canada, 1920, which read as follows:
"Butter is the clean, non-rancid product made by gathering in any manner the fat of fresh or ripened milk or cream into a mass, which also contains a small portion of the other milk constituents, with or without salt, and contains not less than eighty (80) per cent of milk fat, and not more than sixteen <16) per cent of water. Butter may also contain added colouring matter of harmless character."
The oleomargarine manufacturer does not even have to make his formulae public, so that the public may know what to look for in his product and help the government of our country to prosecute violators of the law, the same as is done in the butter business.
Everybody in Canada knows exactly what the contents of butter are, but no one can possibly tell you of what oleomargarine is made.
However, we have the printed portions of two parchment wrappers off oleomargarine and margarine prints sold in California, U.S.A., which read as follows :
"Milcoa Brand Oleomargarine.-Ingredients:	77.50
per cent cocoanut oil, 5.50 per cent peanut oil, 12.00 per cent moisture, 2.50 per cent salt, and 2.50 per cent milk solids.-Morris & Co., Los Angeles, California, U.S.A." and
"Nuco:-Ingredients: 76.00 per cent cocoanut oil, 5.00 per cent peanut oil, 2.50 per cent milk solids, 2.50 per cent salt, and 14.00 per cent moisture."
Now then, the people who are talking about oleomargarine being made from animal fats are under a delusion as well. The practice is becoming more and more general all the time to make oleomargarine out of vegetable fats, and these are imported. I do not wish to weary the House by reading it, but I have under my hand a statement by John Burns, manager of one of the biggest packing plants in Alberta, and perhaps in Canada, in which he says that they do not pay any more for an animal on account of the oleo oil they expect to get out of it.
The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) stated this afternoon that only about 2 per cent of the spread for our bread was oleomargarine, the other 98 per cent being butter. He also quoted the convictions of men for wrongful handling of these two commodities. He said that for one year there were 126 convictions in the case of butter as against 14 convictions in the case of oleo; the following year the figures were 106 and 11 respectively. Now then, when we analyze these figures we find that the convictions relating to the handling of oleo constitute 9i times more than those relating to the handling of butter. I do not believe it will he possible to control the manufacture, importation and sale of oleo once we remove all restrictions.
Now I shall take up another feature, that is, as to whether our dairymen were misled by the government at the time they acquiesced in what was considered to be purely a temporary war measure. I am told that it is not a good argument to say that the dairymen are holding the government to their pledge, but I claim, Mr. Speaker, that such a pledge was made and still stands. If for no other reason, it is plain to me that the temporary nature of the legislation demonstrates that such a pledge was given by the government of the day. I have in my hand a letter from the wtorthy Minister of Agriculture at the time this temporary legislation was intro-



Oleomargarine-Mr. Warner
duced, the Hon. Mr. Crerar, in which he says in part:
You have doubtless noticed that an order in council has been passed providing for the admission of oleomargarine into Canada under certain provisions during the period of the war.
That is, during the period of the war alone. Further, he says:
I think you can rest assured that it will not be the policy of the new administration to do anything that would in any sense permanently injure the dairy industry.
That is what Mr. Crerar wrote me when he was Minister of Agriculture in 1917. I wired him at that time on the request of the Alberta Dairyman's Association, and that is the answer he gave me. I have before me the first act which is entitled:
An act to permit the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada.
Now, that is all temporary and the government have never denied that the legislation was intended to be of a temporary character to meet the abnormal conditions arising out of the war. The dairymen understood, and I understood, when I got that letter from Mr. Crerar, that that is what the government, meant, and I believe the people of Canada still entertain that view. Therefore I am going to support the amendment to restore the old condition of affairs before there was any order in council or any other action to permit the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. I believe that is where this commodity ought to be, and I should like to see the government take the responsibility of dealing with the matter in accordance with the pledge given by the former administration.
Regarding the value of dairying and its national importance, I have been in the dairy business all my life, since I was old enough to milk a cow, and I think I understand it from one end to the other. I know from experience how hard it is to keep people in this business. I also know how important it is to Canada to have our farmers continue as dairymen. It is worth something to Canada to encourage our farmers and help them to make a success of the dairy business, and thereby help to bring about national prosperity. For this is what it means. I have heard some people view this problem merely from the standpoint of the profit that is made out of butter. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that is only a detail. The pork which will be produced by increasing our dairy business will be equal to the amount of money derived from our dairy products. Denmark is one of the greatest dairying

countries in the world, and she is also one of the greatest bacon producers in the world, as everyone knows. Now then, are we by allowing this substitute for butter to cut off two valuable lines of production? You can call it protection or what you like, but I say that it is not a proper thing to put oleomargarine in competition with butter when we have spent so many millions of dollars to develop the dairy business of Canada. I do not think it is good policy to do so. I think I know enough about business to understand that Canada needs every dollar she can get from every honourable and legitimate source, and our farmers need the elimination of oleomargarine to place them in a position where by increased dairying operations there may be a corresponding increase in bacon production, which will enable them to do their share in bringing back this country to a prosperous condition.
I have been studying this problem ever since Mr. Crerar wrote me the letter from which I have quoted. I come from the United States where they have always been unable to control the oleomargarine business. I do not wish to use harsh words or harsh illustrations, but I want to tell you that these corporations that are putting oleomargarine on the market are just as hard to control as the bootleggers in the liquor business. I do not believe we can control it.
I appeal to hon. members for support to this amendment; I believe that such an attitude on our part will give renewed confidence to the farmers. The government are thinking of an immigration policy; are they going to permit the "sale of a substitute for butter that will make it harder for the people who come to our country to go into the best business we have? I do not believe the government can afford to do it; speaking for myself I hope they will not do it.
Now, just a word in regard to whether the prohibition of oleo would or would not be protection. We are not asking for protection on an article that enters into fair competition with another article. I think I have shown that oleomargarine is not a proper food for children. It is a substitute for butter, the best you can make. If it were a question of butter coming into this country and we were asking that a tariff be put upon it to shut it out, that is what I would understand as protection. I am looking at this matter, not from the monetary point of view, but from the point of view of the welfare of our children, I have references here which show that children attending school who had been fed with butter on the one hand and oleo on the other ad-

Oleomargarine-Mr. Fortier
vanced in knowledge and in physical weight where they had used the butter and lost where they had used the oleomargarine. That was demonstrated by actual test; I could read the Quotation, but I do not need to. Let me point out also that we compel the parent who might otherwise be negligent to send his child to a school to get an education. Are we going to say that he may, without perhaps knowing the actual effects, feed to his children something that will prevent them from absorbing the instruction that is given in our schools? Are we going to be as inconsistent as that? There is enough butter in Canada to enable everyone who wants a proper spread for his bread to get it; there is no question about that. Science tells us that the parent who buys oleomargarine to give to his children would do his family more good and would make a better investment of his money by buying butter with it, thus getting a natural food and a perfectly wholesome product. I think, Mr. Speaker, I have said enough on the subject; I shall not take up any more of the time of the House.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) and I shall endorse with pleasure the amendment to the resolution brought down by the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay).
I disapprove of oleomargarine and I favour butter, good butter; I wish to see our farmers succeed, to help in promoting both the development of our farms and this always increasing industry known as the dairy industry.
This question of oleomargarine has been discussed in every possible way and examined under different aspects by the hon. members of this House ever since the beginning of this debate. For my part, I shall briefly touch upon it. One of the phases to which my attention has been drawn the most, is the economic aspect of the question. It was said with a great deal of truth that every pound of oleomargarine Which is imported, manufactured or sold in this country, has for object the replacing of one pound of butter. Those who supported the resolution of the hon. member for Cape Breton South also stated that, for the last few years, the sale of oleomargarine had considerably diminished in this country; that three or four years ago, if I am not mistaken, the sale amounted to about 14,000,000 pounds and that last year it only amounted to 4,000,000 pounds, and they seemed to infer from this fact, that we had nothing to fear from the sale of oleomargarine, we, the advocates of the dairy industry, because, as we are aware, the sale of this article decreases from year to year and tends to disappear. If such is the case why legislate with the object of continuing the sale of this product? If it tends to disappear, if the public has taken an aversion to oleomargarine, in my opinion, there is no use passing a law allowing to place once more on the market this famous substitute for our Canadian butter.
It was the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), I think, who so ably discussed the economic aspect of the question. He represents one of the most beautiful counties of the province of Quebec, a flourishing region of Gaspe. May I be permitted to tell him that the electors of another district of the province of Quebec, the district of Labelle, who have devoted themselves to farming and have opened up, in the heart of the Lauren-tian hills, a beautiful and large domain, are: fully in accord with him this evening, because they share the lofty views he so well expressed. As the hon. member for Gaspe so ably stated, it is more than time that the people give their thoughts tc the land, and develop their agricultural industries, for agriculture will certainly be the salvation of the country, and, among these agricultural industries, the dairy industry has not its equal. Indeed, we are passing through, at present, a period which is perhaps more critical than the one we went through s few years ago; however, those who are in touch with history, will remember that about the year 1S82, our rural districts were being depopulated; a constant emigration from our country was taking place and many of our farmers disheartened, abandoned their farms to cross over to the United States. We are facing at the present moment a situation somewhat approaching the one our fathers experienced. At that time the public men of the province of Quebec were moved by the sad state of things, even the clergy came to the rescue and all proclaimed: We must save our farmers. It was then that we witnessed the development of our dairy industry in that province, the organization of numerous dairy associations. Eminent men took up the good work in the province and from that date we rejoiced in seeing the farmer take an interest in the land and produce in greater quantities butter and cheese. He paid his debts, cleared his mortgages and made the land productive. In my opinion, it is the dairy industry that saved Canada. We should be attached to this industry. If the people were so much attached to it in the old centre of the St.
Oleomargarine-Mr. Fortier

Lawrence valley or in the old provinces of Canada, should we not be so, we the representatives of those colonization districts. I should like to see in my region of Mount Laurier industrial dairy associations; lecturers to teach the people, the settlers, how to make a success of these farms and keep them to some extent, away from the bush, the home of shanties, so as to enhance the agricultural industries in all those valleys. I should like to see subsidies granted to the county that I have the honour to represent, for the establishment of butter and cheese factories, and to obtain better herds of milch cows. I think that this would be one of the most important acts that the government could accomplish. This work of the dairy industry, I may say is the first, the one that dominates to-day.
I therefore take pleasure in stating that I am absolutely opposed to the sale of oleomargarine which is placed on the market to replace butter. It was advanced in support of the motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that oleomargarine is a product which is sold cheaper than butter and that consequently it might have a certain attraction for the poor and labouring classes. We must not lose sight of the fact that oleomargarine is a product which unfortunately tends to replace butter.
What we especially require, is pure food; and between the two, there is no hesitation of choice. I think we should even protect the poor or the workman against this substitute which certainly has not the value, nor the taste of good butter. We are told: Canada is the only country in the world that prohibits the sale of oleomargarine and all the other countries, even those that produce butter in large quantities, have permitted for a great number of years the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. I think we should be thankful that our country has never adopted legislation to that effect. After all, we are perhaps in the infancy of the development of this great dairy industry, we therefore need to encourage it the more. That is the reason why we should not cast aside any means that are apt to help in its development. We cannot compare ourselves to the European countries, to Denmark for instance, who for a number of years past, has not ceased to work for the development of its dairy industry, the source of its wealth. Here, we are in the earliest stages; we live in an agricultural country where we find natural resources in abundance, where we can produce more than any other country, butter and cheese, for exportation. We cannot compare with Denmark or Switzerland so far as

this is concerned, but let us wait. We are the owners of vast territories, numerous rivers, magnificent and large lakes and the richest soil. For that reason, I state that we should be more drawn towards the development of this great dairy industry and that we should oppose energetically the thought of allowing the manufacture of oleomargarine.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this amendment is based on the premises that the suspension of the legislation preventing the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada was a war measure, and therefore being a war measure was by inference of a temporary nature, and that the suspension should now come to an end. It is true that the war >-over, but with the end of the war we did not settle the question of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine. We must now deal with it as an economic question The conditions, let us admit, permitted ol temporary action during the war, but conditions at the present time demand something more. They demand that this House and this parliament face the question of whether or not oleomargarine should be manufactured in and imported into this country as a permanent measure.

speechtext:
But the people of the Yukon I am quite sure though proud of their dairy herds do not wish to prevent the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in that country or other parts of Canada where such sale will be of great benefit to the majority of the population. It is subterfuge to say that because we dealt with the matter temporarily during the war we should not deal with it now at all. Supposing the action during the war was temporary, that does not relieve this parliament of its obligation to deal with the matter now one way or the other. It is purely an economic question. It is not a matter of sentiment in any respect. Both at the last session of this House and at this session the government has shown itself decidedly averse to taking a stand on this question, although I think it is fair to say that at the last session, represented by the Minister of Agriculture, the government tentatively pledged itself to deal with the matter this session. In support of that I shall quote
354E

Oleomargarine-Mr. Black (Yukon)
briefly the words of the Minister of Agriculture when the bill of last session was before the House. Excusing himself for not being in a position at that time to deal finally with the matter of oleomargarine the Minister of Agriculture said:
We have had before this House evidence indicating that it was more nutritious and also evidence that it was less nutritious than butter. I want to know which is the fact and other conditions in connection with oleomargarine before a permanent bill is brought down if that is found to be desirable. I want time during the recess-
That was the past recess, so he has had the time.
-to find out if it is desirable to bring down a bill, and, in that event, to know exactly what I am doing. That I could not know at the short time at my disposal. Hence I bring down-
In the classic words of the Minister of Agriculture.
-this rotten old bill that my hon. friends have passed 'on three or four occasions.
That is how the minister speaking for the government described the oleomargarine bill of last session. I say that the government through its Minister of Agriculture tentatively pledged itself there to deal with the matter at this session. A bill was brought in at this session. Evidently the Minister of Agriculture did inform himself for he brought in a bill dealing very copiously with oleomargarine, but suddenly and for some unknown reason the government, represented by the Minister of Agriculture, experienced a change of heart and withdrew and washed out from the slate this' bill dealing with oleomargarine upon which the Minister of Agriculture has taken the recess to inform himself. Strange to say, the explanation given to the House for the change of heart was that some law officer or departmental clerk without the minister's knowledge and against his wish had so altered and tampered with the bill after it had passed its' first reading that the government could not follow it and was obliged to destroy it. Truly an extraordinary situation for the head of a department to find himself in.
It is also true that the Prime Minister expressed his disapproval of the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture in sending out, through his department, anonymous communications seeking to influence those in receipt of such communications against legislation favouring the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. Perhaps the minister will * protect himself in this instance, as he did in regard to the mutilation of this bill, and say that some clerk in his department improperly, unlawfully, without his authority and against his wish, took the stationery of the Department of Agriculture and issued this appeal against oleomargarine. Otherwise he will have to take the responsibility for it.
Now, to ask us to believe that the government consider themselves bound by any pledge, made or implied, by any former government is to put too great a tax on the credulity of the members of this House, too great a tax on the credulity of the public, having in view this government's record in the matter of observing their pledges and carrying out their platform. However, be that as it may, I say this is an economic question to be dealt with now in the best interests of the public. The evidence is that oleomargarine is a good wholesome food composed of nourishing ingredients. It is manufactured under regulations ensuring cleanliness and sanitation. To allow its manufacture will build up an industry with all its attendant advantages, including increased employment in Canada. To allow its importation will provide revenue by applying a tariff charge both to the finished article and to the ingredients which enter into its manufacture. A man of straw is built up to be knocked down by opponents to the legislation in favour of oleomargarine by saying that it will hurt the dairy industry. The evidence is that in the countries allowing the manufacture of oleo the dairy industry does not suffer from that cause. Why should we suppose that the dairy industry will suffer in Canada? That being so, what argument is left against the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine? It would be just as reasonable to prohibit the manufacture and use of homemade bread in the interest of bakeries because the use of homemade bread lessens the consumption of baker's bread. That would be just as reasonable as to prohibit the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine because it might be used in some instances instead of butter. The importation of butter from Denmark and New Zealand gives the Canadian butter makers much more effective competition than the use of oleomargarine, but we hear no agitation to prohibit the importation of butter.
Beyond all question oleomargarine is a health giving food. It is a fact that the Canadian corps overseas were fed on oleomargarine, they were not fed on butter. They got oleomargarine and plenty of it, and they were a healthy lot; there were no healthier men on the face of the earth. Oleomargarine did not injure their health in the slightest, any more than it will injure the health of the people of this country. And it must be remembered that oleomargarine was supplied to the troops
3546	COMMONS
Oleomargarine-Mr. Black (Yukon)
under conditions that permitted of adulteration to a far greater extent than do the conditions of the present day. I say that to admit the quality of oleomargarine cannot be controlled and its use regulated, is to admit inefficiency on the part of those in charge of the administration of the laws of the land. For my part I say: Encourage its manufacture as a Canadian industry, allow its importation, and regulate it, as in the case of any other food, under the pure food laws of this country. I say let the people use it according to their needs, whether as a substitute for axle grease or for food.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
On the 15th of May, 1922, the question of oleomargarine was discussed in this House at considerable length and a clear-cut declaration of position on the question was made. The resolution proposed at that time read as follows:	.
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that in the best interests of the dairy industry, and of the public generally, the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine should be discontinued in Canada after September first, next.
That resolution was negatived by a vote of 83 to 57, 95 members of the House being absent. It appears to me that was a clear-cut and distinct declaration of position on the part of this House as to what, in the opinion of parliament, should be done in the matter of further prohibiting the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. That is how the question appears to me, Mr. Speaker, and may I say that I represent a farming community in Ontario second to none. But. if that farming community expects me to contend for the protection which I find embodied in the motion before the House they have got entirely the wrong individual to further any such scheme, which I regard as the rankest demonstration of protection that has been witnessed in the House since I became a member of it.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: But did you not vote for greater protection?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE

The hon. gentleman, as usual, is ever ready with a side remark. He is absolutely right in that statement but it merits, in view of the form in which it is made, a little explanation. I find that for these many years protection has existed with respect to very many, altogether too many, walks of life. I find that protection, with the bright	lights of the	industrial prosperity of those protected has attracted too many of our young men and young women from the farms of Canada. It has brought them to the towns for the pur-
[Mr. G. Black.\
pose of continuing a protection which, in my opinion, is wrong and should never have been tolerated. But I am not ready, as the representative of an important constituency in this House, simply because I believe that the principle of protection is absolutely wrong, first, last and all the time, to bring industrial or business chaos to Canada by saying that we are going1 to wipe out at one fell swoop all the protection that exists in Canada to-day. Holding that view, Mr. Speaker, I am not ready to quietly acquiesce in encouraging a species of protection which, in my
10 p.m. opinion, is less justifiable than any other protection we have had in this country in the years gone by.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I will try to come to that logically and in sequence. I was much interested in noting the efforts made by two of my hon. friends across the aisle to my right, one of them, the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica) intimating that he was against protection, but that he would vote for this amendment because oleomargarine w'as not sold and put before the consumer on its merits. Then the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) also was in favour of the amendment because oleomargarine is an imitation of butter. These seem to me very plausible apologies for overlooking the rank feature of protection embodied in the matter that is before the House to-night. If the view of the hon. member for Strathcona with regard to the imitation feature is correct, why should this House to-morrow or the next day not legislate against wooden legs and glass eyes and go the whole length in respect of preventing imitations.
Some hon. members referred to the fact that the women of Canada were in favour of continuing the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. I think that great and

Oleomargarine-Mr. Murdock
undue stress has been laid upon the fact that this was a war measure which permitted, in the first place in 1918 and since that time, the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. I want to place before the House the views of part of the community of Canada, whose views I think should be given consideration. Under date of April 22, 1922, there came to me on the letterhead of the Great War Veterans' Association, a letter addressed to the Minister of Labour, reading:
Dear Sir,
I have the honour to submit herewith attached resolution adopted by the convention representing the Province of Ontario Great War Veterans' Association when in session at Ottawa the 21st April, 1922, respectfully urging that legislation may be enacted to permit the continued manufacture and sale of oleomargarine within the Dominion of Canada, which product has proved a boon to large families with small earnings and to those suffering distress through unemployment, as well as the provision of a channel for continued employment of a number of our citizens.
This resolution has been submitted to the Hon. Prime Minister of Canada.
I beg to remain, Sir, yours very obediently.
J. V. Conroy,
Secretary, Great War Veterans' Association, Toronto district.
This is the resolution:
Whereas oleomargarine is widely known as a good and palatable food of high nutritive value and obtainable at all times at a considerably lower price than butter, and,
Whereas its sale is freely permitted in all parts of the British Empire (except the Dominion of Canada) and in other countries so long as it is sold on its merits, and
Whereas by a conservative estimate there were last winter 200,000 unemployed persons in the Dominion (of whom 17,000 men, three-quarters of them married with dependants, were reported in Toronto) to whom the lower price of oleomargarine was undoubtedly a benefit, and
Whereas members of the Great War Veterans' Association, Inc., know from experience that oleomargarine is a hygienic food which furnishes the necessary fats required in the diet, and
Whereas there is reason to fear that the present regulations permitting manufacture and sale in Canada may be allowed to lapse in September next:-
Be it resolved that this Ontario Provincial Convention, Great War Veterans' Association, respectfully and earnestly urges the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and the members of the Dominion government promptly to take steps to assure the continued manufacture and sale of oleomargarine within the Dominion so that housewives may be enabled to continue freely to purchase oleomargarine for their families if they so desire.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
The editorial of the Labour Leader in part says:
A product which was considered a good palatable food in war times by all competent authorities has a right to be so considered in times of peace. A glaring example of government by orders in council is reflected in the way permission to manufacture, import and sell this product has been granted. Yearly extensions have been made and undoubtedly several manufacturers who would equip their plants to make a- high-class product have hesitated to make the outlay and thus create industry because of the uncertainty.
To allow this right to lapse would appear to be class legislation by protecting dairy interests at the expense of the wage earner. Oleomargarine has won a definite place in our commerce and so long as Canadians desire it, they should not be denied the privilege of making their own choice.
I could not in any way add to the statements made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), when he pleaded for the poor family and the working man, that they be permitted to purchase oleomargarine. We have heard to-night, for the first time so far as I know, that a distinct assurance was given at the time when the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine was suspended, that such suspension was but temporary and a war measure only. I should like to inquire why it was that last year when this question was discussed and when by a majority of twenty-six it was, in my judgment, decided that the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine would continue, the question of such assurance was not raised? Is it conceivable that because on the 15th May, 1922, the House passed judgment on this question adversely to those who now desire to prevent the continued sale of oleomargarine, this is an after-thought of an assurance given in 1918, and that they are now trying to bring this forth, as some hon. member suggests, from a camouflaged viewpoint in order to influence this House to make good on some alleged agreement that w*i given in 1918.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Murdock
It seems to me that the House should do to-night what was done on the 15th day of May, 1922; it should pass upon this question on its merits, and on its merits alone. A great deal of literature has been read to-night in regard to the comparative food values of butter and oleomargarine. I have before me a statement which it has been stated is an analysis of the energy values of food and which was published by the British government. The author is R. H. A. Plimmer, D.Sc. who was attached to the Directorate of Hygiene of the War Office, and in this analysis the following statement appears:
Butter, margarine, dripping, lard: As is well known, these foodstuffs consist essentially of fat and their energy value is entirely due to this constituent. The amount of protein present in butter and margarine is a negligible quantity. Butter and margarine have a lower energy than dripping and lard, owing to their content of water and salt. It is owing to the variability in amount of these two constituents that there are differences in the proportion of fat.
It is not necessary to enlarge further on this because I realize, from the documents that have come to my hand during the past few weeks, that it is possible to get a view either one way or the other on this particular question, and you can obtain all sorts of expert advice and decisions in regard to it. But let us come to the real question of protection involved, which is now being advocated openly for the dairying interests of Canada. In my judgment they want protection in its most glaring form. And how much protection is involved? Let us analyze the matter and see. Some of the figures were given to the House this afternoon by the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), but there were not submitted all of the comparisons which I desire to draw therefrom. In 1916, there was produced in Canada-I am just giving the millions and thousands-26,966,000 pounds of butter, while there was imported into the country 2,091,000 pounds. In the same year we exported of this product 7,787,000 pounds. In 1917, there was produced 34,274,000 pounds of butter; we imported only 466,000 pounds and exported 4,-
344,000	pounds. The tendency was gradually to increase the ratio until 1921, when we find that there was a production of 128,784,000 pounds of butter in Canada, while in that same year there was imported into this country 4,-
018,000	pounds and exported from Canada
9,132,000	pounds. Last year, 1922, we produced in Canada 146,863,000 pounds. But that was not sufficient; 6,396,000 pounds of butter was imported into the country, while we exported 21,504,000.
As to the production of oleomargarine, I have here a report of the Canada Food Board for 1918, which gives in detail the results of
IMr. Murdock. 1
its work as a food board for the months during 1918 in which it was in operation. At page 57 of the report reference is made to the enormous amount of business over which the board exercised control, and the statement is made that oleomargarine was imported to the extent of 1,000,000 pounds monthly during the year 1918. In 1919, the production of oleomargarine in this country was 10,084,000 pounds, while during the same year we imported 5,221,000 pounds. * In 1920, we produced in Canada 10,565,000 pounds of oleomargarine and exported 5,553,000 pounds. In 1921, we produced in Canada only 3,824,000 pounds of oleomargarine, while during the same year only 2,057,000 pounds was imported. Last year, 1922, the production of oleomargarine was 2,326,000 pounds, while the importation was 1,032,000 pounds.

speechtext:
In this matter of oleomargarine there is involved a simple question of principle. There has also been indicated in the debates of the House a desire to serve political expediency. Some hon. members represent dairy constituencies; many of them are sincere in their advocacy of the total prohibition of importation or manufacture of oleomargarine. But I suggest that most hon. members are impelled to their conclusions against oleomargarine largely by political considerations. How can it be argued for a moment that it is within the proper authority of parliament, that it is one of the functions of parliament, to prohibit the manufacture or importation of a food which has been demonstrated to be wholesome and useful to the community? The consumer, I submit, is the person to be primarily considered in this question. I know of no better argument on the subject than a few lines contained in the circular issued by the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, part of which has been read to the House and part of which I will now read. This circular presents the views of the Grocers', Butchers' and Provision Dealers' sections of the association throughout Canada. They say:
We have no interest to serve, only that of serving the public with what they want, and the fact that
the demand from the consuming public for oleomargarine for the past year has been greater than that of any previous year is the best evidence we can offer you that the people want it.
Now, if the people want it, what right has parliament to prevent them from using it? Then the circular continues:
Before our members undertook to offer it for sale to the general public we made exhaustive inquiries as to the ingredients it contained and its method of manufacture. We consulted with the Chief Analyst for the Dominion government and he pronounced it a perfectly good food, and he stated that it contained no harmful ingredients, and, as on each package is stamped the approval of the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion of Canada, our retail grocers, butchers, produce dealers and general store merchants throughout Canada felt perfectly justified in stocking it and offering it for sale. If our customers did not want it there would be no sale for it, but our experience shows that they do want it, and, seeing that it is a non-injurious and palatable product, and^ contains nothing that is unhealthful, we are of the opinion that they should be allowed to buy it if they so desire, and no law should be passed to prevent them from having it.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in that simple statement we have all or most that can be said in favour of the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. Every country in the civilized world permits it. On what principle does the parliament of Canada deny the people of this country the right to use oleomargarine if they want it? The dairyman's gain, I submit, would be microscopic, even if the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine was eliminated. I have figures on good authority which show that in value there was about $800,000 worth of oleomargarine consumed in Canada in 1922, and about $74,000,000 worth or a little more of butter, or less than 4,000,000 pounds of oleomargarine and about 240,000,000 pounds of butter, including both dairy and creamery butter. If you calculate these figures you will find that of the spread on bread about II per cent in value is oleomargarine and 98f per cent is butter. I inquired from several dairymen who are members of the House as to the profit per pound on butter and I was informed that there is no profit or only a very small profit. This whole proposition I submit simply comes down to this, that the small amount of profit on the $800,000 worth of oleomargarine is not a factor which should cause the government of Canada to put that small profit in the hands of the dairymen and deny the working classes of this country the privilege of obtaining a species of butter fat which is perfectly wholesome, and which otherwise they could not have. If this question is considered on the basis of principle, on the basis of fair play, on the basis of the liberty of the subject, on the basis of the right of
Oleomargarine-Mr. Ladner

a man to buy what he wants provided it is healthful to him, and considering the infinitesimal advantage there would be to the dairy interests and the great loss to many of the poor people of this country, I cannot understand how any hon. gentleman could deny the citizens of this country this right which is accorded in every other civilized country of the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Acting Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
There are one or two words only that I would like to address to the House on this question with a view to explaining what my position is in regard to it. I come from a constituency in the Maritime provinces which was a, pioneer in the dairy industry in our part of the country. I know how important the development of the dairy industry is to the farmers of eastern Canada, and I am sure the experience that ' we have had there has been equally felt in all parts of this country. There has been no development along agricultural lines which has been so satisfactory and of such benefit to the agricultural people of our part of the
[Mr. Ladcer.l
country as the development of the dairy industry during the last ten or fifteen years.
All parties in this country down to 1917, about the middle of the war, apart from any question of free trade or protection, had decided that in the interests of the Canadian people from every standpoint there should be a prohibition of the sale and importation into Canada of oleomargarine. That was the situation, and nobody ever questioned it. But solely and only on account of the situation that was created by the war the government of the day under the War Measures Act, without the consent of parliament, without asking parliament anything in regard to the matter, proceeded to pass an order in council which expressly recited the circumstances under which this prohibition was to be removed. It stated that it was due entirely to the abnormal demand for butter, and that as high prices would prevail for this product for some time to come it granted permission for the sale and importation of oleomargarine under regulations to be enforced and take effect "for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue, the conclusion of such period to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council."
When the provisions of the War Measures Act and the orders in council that were passed under it ceased to * have effect, by reason of the fact that abnormal conditions still continued in the country, a statute was passed extending the provisions of this order in council for another year, then later another statute was passed extending it a further year, and last year a third statute was passed extending the permission for the temporary manufacture and importation of this article to the 31st day of August, 1923, and the offering of same and having possession for sale was permitted up to the 31st day of March, 1924.
Now the matter comes to this House by my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) bringing forward a resolution in which he asks the House to reverse the policy of the Canadian parliament and people which has obtained ever since confederation, and to permit the importation and sale of oleomargarine in this country without restriction except in so far as the regulations of the act provide. We have an amendment moved to that resolution by my hon. friend from Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Kay) which I would interpret as meaning, if adopted by this House, and I hope it will be, that these temporary acts shall be done away with and that we shall revert to the condition of affairs that existed before the orders in council and these statutes were passed, and that oleomargarine shall

Oleomargarine-Mr. Macdonald (Pictou)
only be permitted to be manufactured until August, 1923, and ita sale permitted only until the following March.
The question is what ought we to do? It is all very well for my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) to argue about the virtue of consistency, but of what use is it for a man to congratulate himself upon consistency in voting today for something that he supported five years ago, when in this changing world with the varying conditions that we have seen in that period what would be in the interest of the country to-day might not have been in its interest five years ago? Consistency is not the only virtue a public man should possess. Again my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) undertook to give his lecture ex cathedra to the gentlemen who sit next to him as if he had had some holy principle committed to him alone and the Ark of the Covenant was in his charge. I submit that neither of these gentlemen is taking the proper position. Apart from either of their theories, our attitude on this question should be that which would be of the greatest advantage to and contribute to the advancement of the country as a whole.
Now, what is the situation that confronts us? We have the dairy industry developing in Canada in the manner in which it is, and bringing to those engaged in it the greatest amount of money, derived from any part of the agricultural system of Canada outside of that derived from the sale of wheat. Are we to say that it is not wise in the interests of this country to encourage the development of that industry still further? Because somebody says that oleomargarine is good to eat and somebody else says that it is not, are we to imperil that industry? Are we going to give notice to the people in those parts1 of Canada where it has not yet been developed that they must not co-operate for the purpose of building up this great industry to a greater degree, or that they are not to teach agriculturists proper methods for the production of butter? For myself I care not what theories may be advanced. I believe it is in the interest of the Canadian people that the dairy industry of this country should be encouraged. May I venture the statement, Mr. Speaker, that there is too much of a tendency on the part of many in this* House to indulge in theorizing. Why cannot we look every business proposition that is submitted to this parliament squarely in the face, and say honestly what we think in regard to it and whether it is in the interest of the Canadian people or not. If we are actuated by that idea when we approach the determination of this proposition we need
not care what theory may be violated or what maxim may be overlooked so long as what we decide upon is in the interest of our people. It does seem to me that this House would be wise and would be doing that which will be best for the country as a whole if we support the amendment which has been submitted by my hon. friend the member for Missisquoi.
The hon. member who immediately preceded me (Mr. Ladner) read from a circular issued by the Retail Merchants Association this statement:
The fact that the demand from the consuming public for oleomargarine for the past year has been greater than that of any previous year is the best evidence we can offer you that the people want it.
Now I find from an authoritative official statement that in the year ending December 31, 1920, the quantity of oleomargarine manufactured in Canada was 7,182,936 pounds. In the year ending December 31, 1921, the quantity manufactured was 2,632,250 pounds; and in the year ending December 31, 1922, the quantity manufactured was 1,964,243 pounds, or 5,000,000 pounds less in 1922 than in 1920. This shows that if there was a large portion of the Canadian people consuming oleomargarine they are getting heartily sick of it, and that the product is going out of use.

The fact that the unanimous opinion of parliament for so many years was against the use of this article should influence us in our decision. It was never pretended on the part of the then government that the act authorizing the use of oleomargarine was to be anything but temporary in its operations due entirely to the abnormal conditions created

(North Ontario): After all the discussion that has taken place in this House during the last four sessions on oleomargarine I had decided not to say anything on the present occasion, and I would not be taking up the time of the House now had it not been for certain remarks made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). However, what I have to say will only occupy a few minutes. The Minister of Labour professed to be speaking for the labour people of Canada, and he said it was not fair that they should not be allowed to buy oleomargarine instead of butter. I wonder if he was thinking of the thousands of labour men who work in the mines and in the lumber camps who do not want to eat oleomargarine but are forced to eat it under present conditions or else lose their job? Oleomargarine was allowed to be manufactured in Canada under the War Measures Act of 1917. Up to 1917 we heard no person complaining about the price of butter. Were there no poor in the country then? Prior to that time there was little or no oleomargarine used but we heard no complaints from the poor such as we have heard to-night made on behalf of labouring men.
My main reason for taking part in this debate is because of the allegation that the prohibition is desired for the purposes of protection. We are told that oleomargarine raises the price of beef cattle because of the use that can be made out of the fat of these animals. If I were to advocate the use of oleomargarine the Minister of Labour, with as much truth, could allege that I was asking for protection for the farmers who raise beef cattle in this country. It would be just as appropriate for him to argue that by supporting oleomargarine I was advocating protection for the beef cattle industry as it is for him to say that by urging its prohibition I am recommending protection for the butter industry. It must be remembered that the legislation on this subject was passed during war time. The dairy industry of Canada made no protest against that legislation; they were willing to do anything that would help to win the war. The war has long been over, and all war time measures have gone out of existence with the exception of this. The oleomargar-
ine law has been extended year after year down to the present time.
It has been stated that oleomargarine is a good food. That is for adults. We do not hear it said that oleomargarine is good for infants. I would advise the manufacturers, therefore, not to eat any oleomargarine because their- industries are still in the infant stage-so they claim at any rate-and it would not be good for them. If we were advocating more protection for butter the protection argument might be brought in, but it is certainly far-fetched to say that any person who votes for the amendment is advocating protection for the dairy industry. When the manufacture of oleo was not permitted the labouring men of Canada were getting not more than half the amount they are receiving to-day. Still -we had no complaints. I think, Mr. Speaker, that under present conditions we should revert to the legislation which prevailed before the war. I am not saying whether I am in favour of the manufacture of oleomargarine or not. Let the
11	p.m. subject be fought out on its merits and give the dairy industry its just dues because the general belief is that the legislation on this question was only a temporary measure. I think, therefore, we should revert to the former status and give the manufacturers of oleomargarine on the one hand and the dairy industry on the other a chance to fight out the question on an even footing, because we know that this was the thin, end of the wedge that was introduced, and now the manufacturers of oleomargarine want to drive it home. Possession, we are told, is nine points of the law, although I do not know whether all the members who are lawyers will agree with that. These people have been permitted to come inside and now they refuse to go out. Let us put both the manufacturers of oleomargarine and the dairy interests on the same footing. I intend to vote for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be extremely brief. I am rising only for one purpose. I did not intend to say anything at all on this matter and I know how I am going to vote. I rise particularly to say that I object to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) or any other hon. member saying that he represents labour. There is not a member on the Liberal, Progressive, or Conservative side who does not represent all classes of citizens in his community and in the constituency which he represents in the Canadian parliament. Personally, I have organized unions in my constituency, and I happen to-

Oleomargariiie-Mr. Martell
be solicitor for those unions. I am not here as a Labour representative; I am not here as a Progressive; I am not here as a Conservative; I am here as a Liberal, and I believe that I represent labour just as truly as hon. members who sit in yonder comer and the Minister of Labour do. One of my chief objects in rising is to protest against certain men setting themselves up in this House as the supreme arbiters in all matters pertaining to the labour interests, so-called, in this country. We are all labourers when we get down to the final standpoint. Some may be lawyers, others doctors, merchants, men who have to take the pick and shovel; in fact, we are all labourers in our particular vocations in life. Personally, I have stood in court when I have defended members of labour unions without money and without price. I do not apologize for that; I am proud of the fact, and I am glad to say that these men, not foreign agitators, but natives of my constituency, are my friends and will vote for me when election day comes around. Therefore, I protest against the Minister of Labour and other members in this House arrogating to themselves the right to be called representatives of labour in this parliament.

speechtext:
When some of us

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
My hon. friend may have run on a Labour ticket; but what I regard as Labour is men who are willing to take their place in life amongst all the rest of the people without asking any particular favour, not men who run on a socialistic ticket and who advocate communism.
All I have to say in regard to the subject under discussion to-day is this. Most hon. members know that I am regarded as a radical. 1 do not apologize for that, but I do believe good radicalism is good Liberalism. My Liberalism is hereditary Liberalism fostered by the fact that my small education has convinced me that Liberalism is right. I am, however, ready to accord to people who cannot agree with me the right to have their particular views. I have particular views of my own; other people have particular views of theirs, but on the subject which is before us to-day, namely the matter of oleomargarine, some of us have been told that we are advocating protection. If protection is going to be the system in this country, then all industries should be protected. I am not saying that protection is the system of this country. What I say is that this is not protection in the way of tariff legislation; it is
simply preventing people from being able to put up against the dairy industry of this country a combination of fats, Heaven knows whence they come. I am prepared to say to the people of my constituency: If you want oleomargarine, you can have it, that is if my hon. friends opposite or some other people like the Minister of Labour want to give to the people of this country things that he will not eat himself. I am sure the Minister of Labour, if he had placed before him oleomargarine and good creamery butter such as is manufactured at Selma in the county of Hants, would not eat the oleomargarine. I am not prepared to stand in this House of Commons and give my vote for a conglomeration of Heaven knows what against the good creamery butter of Hants. Therefore, I am going to oppose the question of the admission of oleomargarine into this country.
I come from a seafaring race. When I was a boy at school, my great ambition was, when the summer vacation arrived, to go on a trip with my father on his old boat. After my parents had passed beyond the vale, I went to sea for a couple of years, and all the oleomargarine I saw was used as slush to slush down the masts of the schooner. Are we going to place before the people of the Dominion of Canada slush to eat rather than the good creamery butter manufactured at Selma and ether places in Nova Scotia?
I am opposed to oleomargarine primarily because it should not be permitted to come into competition with a natural industry. Oleomargarine is an artificial product; butter is a purely natural product, and if we are going to protect the people of this country, we do not want to protect the decrepit, the aged and those who have passed beyond the three score years and ten. We want to protect* the children of the country. As the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) has said, nobody has ever said that oleomargarine is a good food for children, and the children	are	going	to be	the peoplewho will govern	this	country in	the future.As I have said already, artificial products should not be permitted to come into competition with natural products. Let us protect the children who will be the people of to-morrow, and	not	those	who	should be
buried if they are not already buried.

If the Minister of Labour
was out of order, then, of course, I am out of order also. But if he was in order, I should think that I ought to be in order in explaining the point he raised. However, I must abide by the ruling of the Chair. I simply wanted to explain that the Labour members were absent because they had been in the Banking committee for six hours. If the government of which the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) is a member was not in such a hurry to put this Bank Act through we could have been here instead of in the Banking committee.
But to come down to the subject of oleo, from which I was led astray by the logic of hon. gentlemen opposite. In the first place, I am not opposed to freedom of trade of any description, nor am I opposed to the manufacture of anything that any person wishes to manufacture. At heart I am a free trader. I do not care what sort of stuff you manufacture or sell so long as the people want to buy it. Therefore in regard to the principle of this question I' am going to vote for oleomargarine. But I aidd this rider: I want to see oleomargarine so marked that these labour men-whom we are all so anxious about to-night-will not be paying for grease under the impression that they are getting butter. Therefore if those who are interested in getting an oleomargarine bill passed will kindly arrange the legislation so that when a labour man sits down in a restaurant and pays for butter he will not be served with margarine, I am prepared to vote for the bill.
That is all I have to say on this most profound economic question, Mr. Speaker. I think we might have settled it much more speedily. There is nothing involved in this



Oleomargarine-Mr. Stansell
simple principle that I can see, and I repeat that while for myself I want to have the privilege of eating butter, I am very much concerned to see such economic conditions prevail in Canada that our labour men will all be able to eat butter, I should like to see the margarine plants starved out simply because they could not sell the grease they are handing out instead of butter, and I appeal to the hon.
