subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the interests of the dairymen of Canada I think something should be said to place them in the light in which they wish to appear before the public on this question. There is a great deal of misconception as to the attitude of the dairy interests, and I think as president of one of our dairy breed associations I have a fair idea of what they really desire in this connection. I do not think our dairymen are anxious to say to the consumers what they shall or shall not eat. All they are desirous of getting is a fair deal in a matter that vitally concerns their industry.
I believe I can point out what is the real cause of complaint. I think it will be generally agreed that there has been no complaint on the part of the dairy interests over the manufacture of apple butter, peanut butter, maple butter or similar preparations because they each have their own peculiar flavour and are sold entirely on their merits. What dairymen complain of is the unfair competition from oleomargarine, which is made to taste and smell and look like butter-the article which it is aimed to supplant. The dairymen also feel that another element of unfairness in this competition is the respective restrictions applied to the manufacture of these two articles. The law requires that butter must contain pure butter fat to the extent of at least 80 per cent, with not more than 16 per cent of moisture and a small percentage of salt and other natural milk solids. Those proportions may not be varied, and if departed from the butter-maker is liable to prosecution. But on the other hand the manufacturer of oleomargarine may manufacture his commodity from any material he wishes and the only restriction is that it must be approved by a government inspector as being clean and sanitary. The public are not given the formula by -which the oleomargarine is made. A large proportion of the ingredients originate outside Canada and

are imported practically free of duty, there being a drawback of 99 per cent. The butter-maker is shut out of the country to the south by a duty of 8 cents a pound. Therefore he has to compete in his home market with an article which is imported free of duty.
I was interested in the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). He says he represents a farming constituency, and he added that he did not make known his views before his election, as he was adopted without any questions being asked. I could not help thinking that his was a case of being left on the doorstep for adoption when questions are not usually in good taste.
Something has been said in the course of this debate about settling this question once for all. I submit that this cannot be done, for there is nothing to prevent a resolution or a bill being introduced next session to provide for, or to prohibit, the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine.
This question may be considered from two points of view. We have heard a good deal about the relative values of butter and margarine from the health standpoint. I have noticed particularly that those who claim oleomargarine to be a wholesome product adduce nothing in support of their statement. I have yet to learn of any investigations either in this country or outside that have not shown conclusively that oleomargarine bears no comparison to butter as a life-giving food. I was interested in the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), in the course of which he quoted an authority to the effect that there were certain vitamines present in milk or butter which were not to be found in the product of the slaughterhouse. I think his statement ran something like this: He did not understand that nature would be so partial as to distribute these vitamines freely to the dairy cow and have them entirely wasted in the steer. Well, I need only remind the hon. member that the steer is not entirely a product of nature.
From the standpoint of health we have had many investigations and experiments made, all of which go to show that in food value oleomargarine is so far inferior to butter that it can scarcely be compared with it at all. As something has been said about this question being viewed from the women's standpoint, let me quote from the remarks of one who is regarded as an authority on the subject; I refer to Dr. Margaret Patterson. Summing up this question she states:-
Which do we want in Canada-health for the many or wealth for the few? When one sees the question in writing it looks too foolish to be regarded seriously; yet as a people we act as if we were more interested ir

Oleomargarine-Mr. Stansell
producing a few foreign millionaires than in giving our Canadian children a chance to grow into strong, healthy citizens. We have long since accepted the truism "that every child has the right to be as healthy as knowledge can make it." The knowledge gained in the research laboratories has shown us that milk (whole milk) is an absolute necessity for proper development, both physical and mental, of the child, yet we allow the importation and sale of substitutes for dairy products.
Reference has also been made to the manufacture and consumption of oleomargarine in Denmark. Attention has been called to the fact, too, that when its use was very general in war time, considerable difficulty was experienced through illness of children and it was found that the only way to effect a cure was to have a resumption of the diet of butter fat. I would like to mention one more experiment that was not referred to either last session or this in the progress of the discussion on this subject-one that comes closer home. It is from the same authority that I formerly quoted, and it says:
An indisputable demonstration of the necessity of butter to the growing child was given us quite near home. It was during the war, when both as a matter of patriotism and economy, oleomargarine often replaced butter. In an orphanage for boys the board ladies decided to reduce expenses, and also save butter to be sent overseas, by serving the boys in the orphanage oleomargarine. Shortly after the butter was stopped there was a great deal of illness. The children seemed to have no resistance and contracted every disease with which they came in contact. The teachers began to complain that the children were not making progress in their work as they had previously done and were restless and inattentive. The nurse also noted that the increase in weight had either stopped or very markedly decreased. The doctor made careful inquiry and when he learned of the butter substitute he at once thought that this was the cause. But he could not make the board ladies believe this, for they had heard a lecture on the food value of oleomargarine. They had even heard a doctor say that it contained more calories to the ounce than butter, therefore the theories of the orphanage doctor were all wrong. Fortunately, the doctor had been keeping abreast with the findings of the research workers. He asked the ladies to allow him to provide butter at his own expense for the boys in one of the cottages. This he was allowed to do, and in the course of a few weeks the difference was so marked that even the board ladies were convinced and the supporters of oleomargarine will find no market for their product in that school.
But you say: Does not the importation of oleo keep the price of butter from soaring away beyond the reach of the labouring people? I believe it has the opposite effect. It tends to spoil the market for our home dairy product. It is not fair to ask our farmers-
Mark you, this is from a woman not engaged in farming.
It is not fair to ask our farmers with dairy cows to compete with the product of the American slaughterhouses, nor can we expect our Canadian farmers to keep up an expensive dairy herd unless they are assured of a home market for their produce. When we educate our people to the value yea, the absolute necessity of plenty of milk and butter in the daily diet, we will have a constant demand for the products of the dairy farm. This will ensure an abundant supply. The question of demand and supply always regulates the price. When the farmer is sure of a market for all
227J
he can produce he will produce more and at a reduced cost. The price of butter will be lowered to the consumer. Butter is cheap food at any price, for it contains that which is essential to health, and which money cannot buy as a separate product.
This is the	opinion	not	of the dairy interests but	of	a noted	lady physician in the
city of Toronto who has the welfare of growing children and the rising generation at heart. What she points out is the result of investigation.
A great deal has been made of the argument that	we	should	not	say what a manshould eat	or	drink.	But	we must confess
that we are saying it by legislation all the time. There are many countries in which articles of food that we ban are in common:' use. We believe that horse meat is not fit for food, but there are some countries in which this form of meat is very largely consumed by the people. I presume it might at least be considered fit to eat if the horse had been in good condition and free from disease, but we in Canada do not recognize it as wholesome food for the people; therefore we say that this form of meat must not be offered for sale. Now, we could argue on behalf of the man who came from a foreign country and who wished to partake of his favourite article of diet, as our friends argue on behalf of oleo, that parliament has no right to forbid that man from having the food to which he has been accustomed and which, in his case, has proved to be wholesome. So that considered from the standpoint of health we have a perfect right at least to give the benefit of the doubt to the consumer, especially to the children, in an effort to protect them as far as possible by giving them the most wholesome product we have at our disposal. If there is to be any doubt, let us err on the side of safety.
A great deal has been said about the poor man in this connection. I have personally asked a good many questions on this point, and I have yet to hear of anyone who was pleading for the poor man and his family who would admit that he used oleo for himself. It is always a case of someone giving advice for the benefit of the other fellow. It is very much like the argument of those who say, "Go back to the land;" they always want the other fellow to go back. In my own experience we have not had any complaints from labouring men or poor people; we have not had any requests from them for the continuance of the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. We have had complaints from the lumber interests and from the Retail Merchants' Association. It has been claimed that the manufacture of oleomar-
Oleomargarine-Mr. Stansell

garine is on such a small scale that it does not affect the dairy interests. But I believe that once the oleomargarine interests were assured that they would not be disturbed they would quickly take steps to put the business on a very dangerous competitive basis. In a local town, where dairying is the chief industry, oleomargarine has practically for the first time made its appearance in the local stores. It was featured very strongly in window displays and I asked the proprietors why this was done. Invariably the answer was that they would make a larger profit for themselves in handling oleomargarine; therefore they were pushing the sale of it. In other words, the profits allowed them were greater than they could obtain in the sale of butter.
I am not going to express an opinion as to what should be done as the result of promises. But I believe I can say this, representing the daily interests, that it was generally understood by the dairymen that if they submitted to this as a war measure it would be regarded as a temporary measure only. Rightly or wrongly they have come to that conclusion and they have been waiting with a good deal of patience for the time when abnormal conditions would be considered as safely past and they would again have possession of the home market that they are so well fitted to supply. The statement has been made that if it was in the nature of a promise the present government could not be expected to carry out promises made by the former one. I have nothing to say regarding that, except that the present government might well take a little warning :from the experience of the former one. Whether a promise was made or not, let us consider it from this point of view: It has been amply brought to our attention in this House that the present condition of farming is anything but rosy, and especially is that true of dairy farming. We have a large staff in our agricultural colleges, and we have heard a good deal in various parts of the country, as well as in this House, urging people to take up dairy farming, because it returns more fertility to the soil, enables the employment of more labour and is generally the most satisfactory method of farming. With all of that I can quite agree.
There is no use encouraging an industry unless you can provide a market for its output. We must admit that the condition of European countries is not now such as to enable them to buy the amount of exports we would like to send them, and the home market has been invaded by many of these coun-
JMr. Stansell.l
tries. We are therefore faced with the problem of finding a market for what we produce at present, rather -than of how to encourage greater production. Even if oleomargarine only displaces butter to the extent of four or five million pounds a year that is a market well worth catering to, and the money invested and the thousands of men and women engaged in the dairy industry should be sufficient I think for this House to have some concern for its welfare. It it comes to a choice between encouraging an industry based on importations from tropical or foreign countries and encouraging an industry at home, surely there can be only one answer from this House.
If we consider this question from the health standpoint, if we are to believe the results of investigations so far, there is no question as to the advisability of feeding our Canadian boys and girls butter in preference to oleomargarine. I will go further and make this statement, that if the food values of the two are carefully analyzed it will be found that at present prices, although oleomargarine can be bought cheaper, a dollar's worth of butter contains very much more food value than a dollar's worth of oleomargarine. Because the competition of oleomargarine is unfair, for it trades on the reputation of butter, because I believe it is in the interests of this country to encourage our people in the use of the best product and because the condition of the dairy industry is such that it needs every encouragement we can possibly give it, I have only one choice and that is to oppose, as at present regulated, the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine in every legitimate way.

As a representative of a rural constituency wherein the dairy industry is of great importance I wish to give a few explanations before I cast my vote. On the other hand I also wish to give the assurance to the House that my remarks will be very brief. This debate has been long, and I could add very little to what has been said. .
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that most of the speakers who have addressed the House have treated this question as being one where high principles are at stake. I do not think that any high principle is at stake in this matter. The question is very simple, and should be treated in a very simple way: Should butter be preferred to oleomargarine? In my opinion good fresh butter should be given the preference.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Cannon
We are told that we cannot vote in favour of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) without being considered high protectionists. That argument was made by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). But how can that argument be seriously put forward? How can it be high protectionist to support an amendment that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is opposing? Is there a man in this House who can be considered more of a protectionist than the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition? He has fought for protection since his entry into this House. He has fought for protection on the floor of parliament whenever the occasion has arisen, and to-day therefore can I be considered a protectionist if I vote the other way from him?
Another argument which has been brought forward is that by voting for this amendment we interfere with the freedom and liberty of the citizens of this country. Can this argument be seriously considered, Mr. Speaker, when it is brought forward by the hon. gentleman, for instance, who represents Swift Current (Mr. Lewis), who is a strong prohibitionist? Is it interfering more with the liberty of the citizen to prevent him from eating oleomargarine, which may be most unhealthy, than it is to prevent him from drinking beer or wine if he wishes? I say that these arguments have nothing to do with the question. It is not a matter of protection; the attitude of the leader of the Opposition proves it. It is not a matter of the liberty of the citzens of this country; the attitude of the hon. member for Swift Current proves it.
It has been said that the dairy industry is of great importance. I do not wish to add to the arguments which have been brought forward in support of this industry. It is an important industry, and it should grow every year in Canada. I am quite sure that every member of this House will give to that industry the encouragement that it deserves. An argument was brought forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) this afternoon that struck me particularly. The amendment mentions that we should revert to the condition of things as it existed before the order in council was passed under the War Measures Act. The hon. Minister of Finance said that parliament was in no way bound by acts or orders in council passed by former governments or by former parliaments. With all due modesty, with all due respect for the hon. gentleman's opinion on account of his vast parliamentary experience, I say that if there is one thing which is important
in Canada it is political consistency. Can one government undo what former governments have done? Can one parliament undo what former parliaments have done? Constitutionally, yes, but as a matter of political expediency, if that course were followed, where would be stability?

Now, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion let me say (hat before the French Revolution there was a class of philosophers who wanted to replace God by nature. subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I would feel more at ease dealing with this question of oleomargarine in my mother tongue, but I believe there are no more converts to be made among the French speaking members of this House. Consequently, I crave your indulgence. Mr. Speaker, and that of the House whilst I add my remarks to this debate. The fact that this matter of oleomargarine covered more than seventy pages of Hansard last year, and will cover about the same number of pages this year, Tenders it hard for a new member to be original on this question. I am glad, however, to raise my voice in this debate and to summarize the reasons which induce me to oppose the motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) and to vote in favour of the amendment.
In studying the history of oleomargarine, Mr. Speaker, we find that it was- introduced shortly before the Franco-Prussian war, and that in 1870 Mege Mouries was awarded a prize for his invention by Napoleon III. From this it will readily be seen that the introduction of this article of diet was essentially a war measure, and was naturally looked upon with favour at a time when rats were at a premium for eating purposes. At first oleomargarine was made entirely from animal fat,

principally fresh beef. Gradually the proportion of animal fat was decreased and replaced by vegetable fats such as cocoanut oil, cohune oil, cotton seed oil, kapok oil,
and sometimes by fish oil.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Coal oil. Whale oil.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
That is why we have
to be selfish and protect ourselves against the oleomargarine. These oils are transformed into hard fats by a process known as hardening, or hydrogenating. This is accomplished by treating liquid oil with hydrogen in the presence of a catalytic agent, such as nickel, or its oxides, or salts, or other agents. It is generally agreed that a small quantity of the catalytic agent often remains in the finished product. Practically all oleomargarine is emulsified in skim milk or in cream, in order to give it the flavour of butter. In considering any article of diet, its nutritive value is a most important factor. Any food to be efficient must not only provide heat and energy but must also promote growth. Recent researches in nutrition have demonstrated that certain elements known as vitamines are essential to promote growth. These same researches show that while butter contains a very high percentage of these essential vitamines, oleomargarine is almost entirely, if not wholly, deficient in them. From this we may logically deduce that compared with butter, so far as its nutritive value is concerned, oleomargarine is an inferior article of diet. In this connection, I may well quote the following from Dr. McCollum's book entitled "The Newer Nutrition," which is recognized as an authoritative treatise on this subject.
The vegetable fats and oils such as olive oil, cottonseed oil, peanut and cocoanut oils, although good energy yielding foods, do not furnish this dietary essential. The body fats of animals such as lard, beef fat, etc., are not important sources of the fat-soluble A.
Practically all of McCollum's findings have been endorsed by the Lister Institution of Great Britain and the British Medical Research Committee. I would not like to tire the House with the quotation from Dr. McGill's statement as the hon. mem-12 m. ber for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) has already given it. This all tends to prove, however, that in the last analysis, nature has endowed the cow with the best process for producing good edible fat.
The supporters of this resolution have given the impression that the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine is a benefit to the poorer classes. This argument is poorer than the poor to whom it refers. No one in this House I am sure has more sympathy

Oleomargarine-Mr. Bouchard
for the poor than I have, being one of a large family brought up on a small farm where the conditions were very hard and where many sacrifices were necessary to secure my education. I know by experience the meaning of privation. If cheap food is required for poor people, as undoubtedly it is in many cases, why should we not induce them to eat raw materials similar to those from which the oleomargraine is derived such as good refined lard or good oils, both of which are just as nourishing and almost twice as cheap as oleomargarine. "Poor people" they say, and yet by legislation they would invite them to pay a tribute of 10 cents to 20 cents a pound tc manufacturers and distributors of oleomargarine. "Poor people"-this sounds well at first, but would it not be better if the poor people, instead of getting two pounds of oleomargarine, bought one pound of lard and one pound of genuine butter for about the same amount of money?
"Poor people!" and we are to make them and the country poorer by legalizing the sale of a food so evidently deficient in vitamines. If any class of people requires good butter, full of vitamines, it is surely the poorer class who have not the means to indulge, in fresh green vegetables all the year round, and whose staple article of diet in the winter time is potatoes which, as hon. members know, are very deficient in vitamines and many other things.
The statement has been made that the competition 'of oleomargarine vdth butter would tend to keep down the price of butter. When we consider, however, that our Canadian butter has to compete on the world's market, the weakness of this argument will at once be realized. As a matter of fact, if the Canadian supply of butter was insufficient to meet the needs of the home market

a condition of affairs which would naturally tend to raise the price-New Zealand or some other butter producing country would soon send its products to Canada and this would reduce the price at once.
Let us now glance at the history of legislation concerning oleomargarine in Canada since 1886, when this question was first discussed. From that date until 1917, oleomargarine was absolutely excluded from the Canadian market. In 1903, the Hon. Sydney Fisher, Minister of Agriculture in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's cabinet, reiterated the viewpoint of the government on this subject.
Following this, in 1914, the Hon. Martin Burrell, Minister of Agriculture when the Conservative party was in power, took exactly the same stand, and in the debate which was aroused he made the following statement:
I am not saying that oleomargarine is not a wholesome product to eat but if you allowed the sale of a substitute looking exactly like butter although not made of the same ingredients you would have a tremendously large staff of inspectors to prevent men from selling it as butter. They have had a great difficulty in the United States over that, and I believe the general opinion of this country would be against it.
Of course at that time there was not much question of the vitamines. In 1917, however, an order in council was passed, and as this order in council has been fully quoted, 1 would call the attention of the House just to the following words:
Such regulations to be in force and to have effect for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue. . . . and as a war measure only.
That is, we see that oleomargarine was invented as the result of a war, and was also introduced into Canada under similar circumstances. Thus doth history repeat itself.
When the division comes on this resolution, the responsibility for saying whether the promise made to the farmers of Canada in 1917 was only another scrap of paper or not, rests with the hon. members of this House. My Progressive friends will readily agree with the statement that agriculture is the backbone of the economic structure of this country, and that dairying is one of the most important parts of the agricultural industry. It is recognized that this industry must be developed upon a much larger scale, and this has already been pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and other hon. members. How can we expect, however, that prospective investors will put money into an industry over which there hangs such a sword of Damocles as is represented by the unfair competition of an inferior substitute for butter?
It may be said that this is only another form of protection; but my Progressive friends have already admitted, in principle, that growing industries need protection, and when we consider the highly specialized state of the dairy industry in New Zealand, Denmark, Holland, we cannot do otherwise than admit that here in Canada, this industry is still in its infancy. Admitting this principle, let us begin by protecting our basic industry, an industry which should appeal to you as it does to me, as l'industrie par excellence. Let me quote a statement which I read recently:
The decline in dairying, an industry which more than any other farming industry maintains best our soil fertility, would have an unfavourable effect upon farm practice in all sections where dairying is now practised and extending.
If this resolution is carried, and a law permitting the importation and manufacturing of oleomargarine is placed upon the statute books,
Oleomargarine-Mr. Neill

the door will be opened for numberless frauds. In this connection let me quote from the Journal of Agriculture, Quebec, under date of July, 1917:
The question of controlling the manufacture and sale of margarine involves so much, a small army of inspectors would be required. Even then frauds will be numerous. In England, where, I think, they usually observe laws perhaps better than we do, there are two cases of prosecutions weekly for offences against the Margarine Act.
I would not have hon. members infer from this that every manufacturer and importer of oleomargarine would sell his product for other than what it is; but it must be remembered that much of the margarine wihch is sold goes to boarding houses, lumber camps, and so forth, where workmen are boarded and where they are supposed to be given butter.
In conclusion, and before resuming my seat, let me emphasize again the following points: First, that oleomargarine is a very inferior substitute for butter, and while possibly deceiving the eye, the palate, and even the stomach, will never deceive the physical nature, and especially that of our children who will be unable to find in it the vital elements of real food; secondly, that its importation and manufacture have been prohibited by all previous governments; and that it is a real menace to the development of the dairying industry.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I will not detain the House, Mr. Speaker; I promise to introduce no arguments that have been advanced by any other member, which at this stage of the game will be a somewhat diffcult undertaking. I wish for a moment to deal with the position of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). He told us that he represented a dairy constituency; that his views-shall I say his sinister views?-on the oleomargarine question had not befen put before the electors prior to his election; that he had not put them before those people since, but that he intended to carry out those views, as he believed in them, without any regard to his constituents. Now, I think I can best leave the electors of the county of Kent to deal with that situation.
I have seen in another House a member coming from an election where he did not have to fight for his seat and proclaiming in that House his indifference, his aloofness, his absolute independence of the men that presumably had sent him there. I have seen more than one man do that, but I have never seen the same man do it more than once. I think it is Solomon who describes this situation somewhat aptly. He says:
[Mr Bouchard.]
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof is death.
I am sorry that the minister devoted so much time to a consideration of this agricultural question, with which he is evidently only imperfectly acquainted. I do not, of course, blame him for that ignorance because the matter does not come within the scope of bis ministry. It is regrettable, however, nevertheless, that he spent so much time on the subject, because there is a field that opens directly in his own department which presents a much larger scope of undeveloped territory demanding instant attention. There was a pledge, we are told, in connection with oleomargarine; there was also a pledge in connection with labour. In the Treaty of Versailles, and confirmed by labour conventions later on, there was a very definite pledge given to labour, by virtue of and in reward for their services during the war, that a certain definite schedule of labour reforms would be aimed at, and carried out at the earliest possible moment. Canada was one of the signing parties to the agreement, and that was five years ago. So far as I know, not a single iota, jot or tittle or these reforms have been carried out in this country. So that this is a matter that presents great scope for a man of the energy of the Minister of Labour, without his delving into these remote subjects of more strictly agricultural concern.
Now, there is no need for me to go into the merits of the case, and I do not propose to do so, especially seeing that I spoke at great length on the subject last year, and in view of the fact that the amendment of the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) has limited the discussion entirely to the question of a pledge given and the desire to fulfil that pledge now. I can only say, in order to save time, that I entirely and heartily endorse the stand taken, first by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke), and secondly, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It would be painting the lily and adorning the rose for me to try to add anything to the able way in which those hon. gentlemen have dealt with the subject. There is no question that the pledge was given. The conditions have passed away and now the time has come -in fact, it has long since passed-when that pledge should be fulfilled.
The right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) stressed to some extent the point that the order in council was of a temporary character, and he indicated that the government of that day only had power to pass, under the War Measures Act, legislation

Oleomargarine-Mr. Neill
for a temporary purpose. That, no doubt, is true. But the order in council went further than that, for it not only took certain action but it specifically stated that there would be a time when the suspension of the prohibition would cease to take effect. Not only did it say when that suspension would cease; it even went to the trouble and the precision of defining the body who would decide when this condition had arrived; the conclusion of the period of suspension was to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council. It is true that the order in council no longer exists; we are aware of that. But the temporary character of its enactment was carried on into legislation, because we find the word "temporary" apears in the title of the act into which the order in council was later crystallized.
I desire for a moment to turn to a consideration of the stand taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who asked us more than once, when or where a pledge would end. He told us that a government had no business, or was not bound-I think that was the precise word-to carry out the undertakings of its predecessors. While that is technically true, it is so only in a very limited sense. There is no doubt the government of to-day can cancel the laws of yesterday; they can cancel their own laws. But a government cannot cancel contracts without providing some compensation therefor. That is the difference between changing a law with the consent of parliament and cancelling a contract or repudiating a pledge, legally or even morally given, with all its obligations. The Minister of Finance asked us again and again, when does a pledge end? I think the answer is obvious: a pledge ends when it is fulfilled. A promise ceases when it is carried out. Let us consider a few illustrations.
Any hon. member of this House who has been under the necessity of -pawning his watch in a case of temporary financial embarrassment will understand what I mean. This experience has never occurred to me, because in the many periods of my financial disability I have never had a watch worth pawning. But one can realize if he did find himself in that position, that he would not get his watch back until the pledge was redeemed in the ordinary way. Or take a more businesslike illustration-a mortgage, say. I am speaking now of a hypothetical case under British Columbia law, which follows the English law, and may or may not be different from the law in the province of Quebec. In a mortgage, the outstanding feature, the gravamen, is personal obligation. There is a phrase indicating a promise to pay to So-and-So the
sum borrowed. That is the centre, so to speak, of the mortgage. Of course, the bondage of the land is also valuable, but that is only as collateral security, and if that security diminishes in value and does not realize the amount of the mortgage, then a personal obligation rests upon the man who borrowed the money to repay it out of whatever other funds he may possess. In other words, his pledge continues until he has paid back the money. The same thing is true in reference to a note. I am not aware that our note wears out like a suit of secondhand clothes, if you have it long enough. There is, it is true, a statute of limitations with regard to debts. But who would suggest that we should invoke the statute of limitations in connection with the moral or legal obligations of a government?
I think the example cited by the hon. member for Missisquoi was a very good one, that
is,	in connection with the British government. The case there was even stronger than it is here. In the matter of the removal of the embargo on cattle, the British government had no order in council that could bind them; they had no legislation that could compel them to do what they did. It was a simple fulfilment of a promise given by a British statesman across the table to a Canadian statesman. But the British government made good on it. The British government did not want
it,	the people did not want it, and they held an election on it and said, "We do not like it, it is going to hurt us"-they thought it would at any rate-"but we have made a promise and we must stick to it." For my part I am proud to be associated with a government and a parliament that will follow the very best traditions of British public men in this regard.
I should like to say a word regarding the Progressive party in this House-not by way of commendation, Sir, for that would be presumptuous on my part, but the man on the outside sometimes sees conditions from a somewhat different angle to that from which they are viewed by those immediately concerned. I do not think that up to date the party has done anything that will strengthen them more in the confidence and esteem of the country than by the action they have indicated they are going to take on this measure to-night. It will be years before they will have a very great-shall I say?-clientele outside the farmers. It is to the farmers of the country that they must look in the first place. They have been accused in the past of being one-sided, parochial, short-sighted, but the action they intend to take to-night, as expressed by the leader of their party and by many of those who follow him, will show
Oleomargarine-Mr. Neill

that they are capable of taking a broad, national view of this subject, and as a consequence they will secure the esteem and support of fanners from one end of Canada to the other-the first occasion I think on which they have received it.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Well, at any rate I am sure that this action will be favourably received from one end of Canada to the other and will materially increase the standing of the party in the country. I am safe in saying that. They have deserved the name which is given to them of the National Progressive party, for their attitude shows that they have taken a national and also a progressive view in the best sense of the word in regard to this subject. I have criticized them in the past, and therefore I am glad to be able, on behalf at least of the dairy farmers of my constituency and, I believe, of British Columbia generally, to thank the National Progressive party for the stand they are taking to-night.
Referring to the original motion moved by my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), I think hon. members will find that if they look at the amendment introduced by my hon. friend from Missisquoi (Mr. Kay), which I think the right hon. leader of the Opposition described as clumsy, they will find I think that it is clear-cut and distinct, for it indicates exactly what is proposed to be done under it. But let me refer for the moment to the original motion. You will find there a strange confusion of ideas. In the first half dozen lines it provides that despite certain acts-and it is quite proper to express it in that way-such and such shall happen, that the offering for sale and so on of oleomargarine shall henceforth be permitted. So far as that goes you understand clearly the position. It says, in defiance of certain acts to the contrary, that henceforth the sale and manufacture of oleomargarine shall be permitted. Had it stopped there it would have been intelligible, but the motion goes on to say, "subject to the provisions of the said Oleomargarine Act." Well, the said Oleomargarine Act-there is only one, which has been extended from time to time-says that oleomargarine shall go out of business on the 31st day of August. So while in the early part of the motion the hon. gentleman expresses a determination that its sale and [DOT] manufacture shall henceforth be permitted, he also says that it shall be "subject to the provisions of the said act." If it is subject to su,ch provisions, the manufacture and sale . of oleomargarine will automatically cease on

the 31st August. Had the hon. member put in the words, "in other regards" or "subject otherwise to the provisions of the act," that would have expressed a different meaning. But as it stands the motion is vague and confusing and ultimately binds the government to nothing and is in sharp contrast with the distinct meaning which is expressed by the amendment.
The hon. member who introduced that motion has, as we all know, a high legal standing in his profession. He is a man of repute in his profession, and we all know his ability as we have seen it expressed in this House-and I am not saying this in sarcasm at all, I am speaking the sober truth. However, believing that as I do, it is impossible for me to so impugn the hon. gentleman's motive as to suggest that he drew that amendment wrongly by accident, blunder or incompetence. While it might be in order for me to so assume, I do not believe it is justified by what we know of his ability and his reputation. Therefore I think I am justified in concluding that he drew it in that way of deliberate intent; and, if so, I am pleased to say that I am proud of his action in that regard. If he did so of deliberate intent, why then he put that abortive, or at least noneffective, resolution on the order paper presumably to stop other resolutions that might be more effective, and he has taken this method to show-and I honour him for it- that the Swift Company of Chicago have overdone their lobbying in this House and he has shown this House I hope that he possesses -and I always thought he did- a rugged independence that would never allow him by any means to be put in a position where it might be suggested he was the man Friday of any alien corporation in the States or anywhere else. Now, I have sat in this House for over four months and watched with a good deal of interest and a certain amount of disgust the persistent lobbying in this House of these alien interests from Chicago. They have camped in the galleries, they have haunted our rooms, they have slept on our doorsteps, so to speak, and one of their main arguments has been their desire to give the poor workingman of Canada a wholesome food at a cheap price. I have sometimes wondered when I have seen the lobby that is carried on whether, if they succeed in establishing oleomargarine permanently in Canada, that poor workingman would not ultimately have to pay the price of this lobby, because you can easily conceive that when conditions are such that there are only two companies allowed to

manufacture oleomargarine in Canada it would be easy, once its manufacture was permanently established, to so manoeuvre and manipulate prices that the cost of this extensive lobby would be amply repaid out of the pockets of the poor workingmen for whom the Swift Company of Chicago profess to take such an altruistic interest. I have sometimes wondered when I have seen all this going on whether it was these paid lobbyists or whether it was we ourselves who took the oath of office when we came down here that we would act in the best interest of our constituencies and the country. It is not they who took the oath, it is we. We have got to answer to our God so far as our oath is concerned, and to our constituents for the pledges we made before election and since. Therefore I would suggest that we throw aside all these paid arguments and address ourselves to the consideration of this subject animated only by the oath we took and the pledges we gave that we would one and all of us legislate in the best interests-putting it on the lowest basis-of our constituents. If we do that I think the aggregate result will also be in favour of the best interests of the people of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I was about to rise before this amendment was proposed, and I was about to say that I did not like the amendment. I do not like its head; I do not like its body, and now that it has got a tail I do not think that it is improved thereby.
My intention in rising was to make a word or two of explanation, because I intend to vote against the amendment, and now against the amendment to the amendment. I think it is always easier to make an explanation before one votes than afterwards. I do not envy the position of some hon. members who will have to explain themselves afterwards.
I do not wish to impute any motives to those who are responsible for this amendment or who support it, but I have observed certain things in the debate that have raised questions in my mind. For instance, I have thought that some of the hon. members have been supporting the amendment from purely humanitarian motives, a kind of inverted Benthamism, the least good for the least number. Now, I do not take very much stock in humanitarian arguments on economic questions. I think that all good economics, all just economics, are fundamentally humanitarian and that you do not need to be continually dragging in the widow and the orphan and the poor workingman. I have a great deal of respect for the poor workingman and the widow and the orphan, but for the purpose of rational discussion it might be just as well if we abolished them. I think we could even afford to bury them in wool or, perhaps still better, in butter, I do not, as I say, take any stock in that kind of argument. We hear it frequently in discussions of questions of this kind but I do not think it deceives anybody.
Now, another thing occurred to me, I hope I am not going out of my way to impute motives, but it seemed to me that this amendment was not so much an amendment as a convenient sand-hill in which political ostriches might hide their heads for the time being, until somebody made a definite move in the matter. It seems to me that everybody is waiting for somebody else to declare himself on this question. I do not know whether or not this is general, but it is a type of procedure which I personally object to. I think hon. members ought to be willing to say "no" or "yes" to the motion on the order paper without all this seeking of convenient refuges and putting it up to somebody else to take the first step in the matter.
Then, again I have thought that perchance some moralist had invented this amendment in order that the sanctity of pledges might

Oleomargarine-Mr. Bird
be observed. I think that pledges from parliament to parliament ought to be observed and held in veneration, and also pledges from one party to another. That is, pledges of governments or parties when in power and out of power ought to be held sacred, too. If we are going to talk about pledges let us talk	about pledges per se-in
themselves. I do not think there is a great deal in the moralistic side of this argument. I cannot persuade myself that there is much sincerity in it. I do not think this parliament is greatly concerned in the keening of pledges. 1 cannot say that any hon. gentleman sitting opposite can claim to be specially interested in the sanctity of pledges. There have been those who have referred tc this amendment as a piece of protection for the farmers, and I honour the frankness of the hon. gentlemen who take that position, because I think it is the only straightforward position to take. I am standing here to-night not as one who is a hard and fast believer m consistency. I do not draw that distinctic-between expediency and principle which the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) does. For instance; I believe that expediency is principle, or a kind of principle. It all depends on how you use it. If you use it openly and with a declared purpose and without any intent to mislead or deceive, I think that is justifiable. I have a great deal ot sympathy with some hon. members on my own side of the House who imagine that by prohibiting oleomargarine they are doing a service to the cause of agriculture. However, I have been watching this process very keenly, and I hope with some foresight, and it seems to me that the farmers of this country are beginning to nose around the protection trough, they are beginning to sniff around it. They have seen other people in it for fifty years and they have been shoved aside or have been persuaded to keep aside. But tonight the farmers of Canada, it seems to me, are beginning to see the attractions of that trough and some of their old time prejudices are being held less firmly than before. Will any man stand up in this House and say that they are to be blamed for that, that they are swallowing their principles? Why, what are principles for but to be swallowed:
A marciful Providunce fashioned us holler O' purpose thet we might our principles swaller.
It is not the swallowing that is wrong; it is the inopportune time that we choose to swallow. This is a very opportune time for the farmers to swallow their principles, because they will go down very easily with oleomargarine-or butter. I want to point out
IMr. Bird.]
this, and I hope I do not need to point it out because everybody with his eyes open will have seen it before now, that the farmers of this country are of the same flesh and blood as farmers elsewhere in the world, and we have seen the British farmer go to his government with the plea for protection; we have seen the United States farmer go to his government with the plea for protection, and we have seen the Canadian farmer to-night not exactly asking the government for protection but just hovering around and trying to hint to the government' that they would like some protection if they dared give it to
them.	That is the position. Now where are we coming to? We are coming to this position; we are just beginning to get in the thin end of the wedge and by and by you are going to have a Farmers' party in Canada that will be one hundred per cent protectionist. They will all be in the trough
then.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: You are getting in it to-night, those who are going to vote for this amendment. I am laying down lines of logic, and those who say "never" will be up against something in the future. I am not speaking against any gentleman in the Farmers' party to-night who thinks he ought to vote against eloomargarine to protect the farmers' interests. That is what we are all coming to. For fifty years the farmer has been wedded to a theory, and where has it got him? He trusted to a free trade party to' bring him relief, and where has that got him? The farmers of Canada cannot afford to go on for anothei fifty years on the same principle. They must have something more to live on than simply professions. I was wondering to-night how much difference it would have made to this debate if someone could have given us an authoritative definition of what a dairyman is. Supposing Mr. Speaker could have settled for this House what a dairyman is. Is it the man that milks the cow, or the man that milks the man that milks the cow? That is what we are up against to-night, and that is why all the parties are divided because they do not know whether they are supporting the farmer or the manufacturer, and we are slithering around all over the place on this question of oleomargarine simply because we do not know whom we are supporting.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I am speaking for myself and I think I am speaking for a good many more too, if they would only get up and say so.

Oleomargarine-Mr. Putnam
Some hon. gentlemen are very eloquent from their seats in this House, but we rarely see them on their feet to express their opinions.
I foresee the time, and you can judge whether I am speaking ironically or not, when this party here will ha,ve lost all the faith they ever had in the free trade party in this country. I do not think they have lost it all yet. We are still hoping we will get some support from the free trade party in this country, but our faith has been badly shaken and I think it has pretty nearly got to the vanishing point. What are we going to do? There is a party at the other end of this House, the high protectionist party, and what are we going to do when he have lost faith in the party across the way? We are going to turn to this party at the other end. We are all going to be high protectionists. We are going to turn to them and say: "Get out a scheme, you protectionists, and you manufacturers' associations, and come and hold conferences with the long-suffering farmers of Canada and see if we cannot get some remedy for the position we have been in for the last fifty years. We have to do something. We cannot live in a vacuum. We have got to have actual benefits." That is economics. We are not here to prate about theories or anything of that kind. You cannot live on theories. Who is the theorist in this House anyway? Who is the expedient man in this House? Why I was amazed today and I rubbed my eyes when in another place I saw a high protectionist quoting Adam Smith as a sound economist. I thought that was about the furthest I could get, but to-night I rubbed my eyes again when I saw sound free traders advocating high protection, and protection as somebody has said, in its worst form, but I would say in its most naive form. It reminds me of the story of the deputation of orange growers that went to McKinley to get a duty on bananas. He said, "We do not grow any bananas in America," but the deputation said, "We know that, but we calculate like this: We think if the people get their stomachs full of bananas they will have no room for oranges." That seems to be about the position of the advocates of the elimination of oleomargarine. They seem to be afraid that if the people get their stomachs full of oleo they will not have room for butter. I say that is the most naive kind of protection you can think of. Where are we getting to? Our principles are all up in the air together. We are none of us on solid ground, and therefore we have to get together as all sensible men should and try and arrange a practical solution for the difficulties of the dairyman, however you may
define him, and for the farmer generally in this country. I am only throwing out a hint to the party to my right. I leave it to them to work it out as best they can.
One hon. gentleman said to-night that this was the first time that the Progressive party had ever done right. That is a very significant remark that I would like the members of the Progressive party to think about. It seems to me that is where the confusion of right and wrong comes in. His right is our wrong and our wrong is his right. This is the first time we have done right, which means to our way of thinking, the first time we have ever done wrong.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: I did not intend to delay the House and would not have risen but for some rather remarkable statements which in the last few moments have fallen from the last speaker, the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). From his occupation and training I had hoped for a logical speech; I had expectation of a charitable speech, but as far as any attempt on his part to interpret my reasons for casting the vote I shall give is concerned, he was utterly uncharitable, and therefore I must occupy a few moments to make myself clear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman seems to imply that I had some direct implication with regard to himself. I have not heard the hon. gentleman speak.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I did not intend to imply that, but I take up his imputation of motives. He professed some lingering faith in the Liberal party and some hope in the Conservative party but he showed an absolute lack of that greatest grace of charity towards many of us who are voting for this amendment from a special reason. The hon. gentleman professes his inability to distinguish a humanitarian from an economic question, and he gave the concrete and instanced or implied that those of us who are voting on this question on the basis of child welfare were not sincere, and he said in terms that only those who approached it from the standpoint of protection for the farmer were doing so with any straightforwardness, or words exactly to that effect. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that two hon. gentlemen in this House the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) and the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard), based the major portion of their speeches on the argument of child welfare, and I for one found my information in that regard very much supplemented and buttressed by the excellent speeches of these two honourable members, and I cannot thank the
Oleomargarine-Mr. Putnam

hon. member for Nelson for telling us that the
only straightforward vote from those opposed to oleomargarine will be on the part of those who are frankly for protection for the farmer.
I was impressed, Mr. Speaker, with the humanitarian aspect of this question which the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) professes so frankly to ignore. In this country we have rather a unique climate. It is very rigorous in the winter, it is in many parts very severely warm in the summer; and while, for the moment, I cannot recall exact figures it is a tremendously unfortunate fact that infant mortality in Canada is comparatively heavy. That infant and child mortality is heavier in the Canadian cities. I am not going to say that solely because the children in the country have plentiful access to the products of the dairy the mortality there is less. But, Mr. Speaker, that fact stands as a very obvious circumstance in connection with an unfortunate situation. Now while the hon. member for Nelson professes to ignore the humanitarian aspect of this question he has done nothing to dispute, or dispose of, or disprove the statements and the arguments of two or three hon. members of this House who at least did base their case upon the welfare of the little child who cannot even say what is palatable always-the little child of the poor man. That child should have access as freely and openly as possible to products of the dairy during his growing years. It is not disputed that oleomargarine lacks the vitamines which are necessary for the bringing of that child to a healthy maturity. Oh, you may say, he will get them elsewhere, he will get them from vegetables. But let us remember that those fresh vegetables are just the very things that the poor man in the cities cannot always afford, that he gets but a very small quantity, and in many cases none at all. Mr. Speaker, we are confronting a problem as to how we shall get immigrants to this country. Mr. Speaker, I have very few words to say in reply; I shall confine my remarks now to a consideration of the order in council passed in 1918. It has been stated that the order in council as drafted contains a pledge to the dairymen of the country that the manufacture of oleomargarine would be prohibited at the close of the war. I say that there is no such pledge in the order in council; no pledge of the kind was intended when that order in council was drafted. The order in council simply conformed to the usual order passed under the War Measures Act of 1914. I believe it was passed in August; and when hon. gentlemen make any assertion of the kind that has been put forward in this debate, they are evidently doing so without having fairly read the order in council and the act based thereon. I was not a member of the House at that time, but I have no doubt in the world that the dairy interests of this country were never approached in the matter, and never approached the government, because I do not think that the government of that day made known to any interests in Canada, daily or otherwise, any order in council which they intended to pass based upon the War Measures Act of 1914.
Some hon. gentlemen say that for fifty years oleomargarine has been kept out of Canada. Yes, Sir; and for five hundred years the franchise was kept from the people of England, but they ultimately got it; and for sixty-five years responsible government was kept from the Canadian people in some provinces, but
they, too, ultimately obtained their right. So that this is no argument whatever against the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada. The manufacture of this butter substitute is not an imposition on anybody in this country; it absolutely is not. On the other hand, it undoubtedly is an imposition on the Canadian people to deprive them of oleomargarine if they desire to have it. You are not imposing on any people in this country by allowing the manufacture of oleomargarine, because you do not compel anyone to eat it or even to have it on his premises. The member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) had a few kind words to say about myself, and no doubt he meant them. But I do resent the latter part of his speech wherein he talks about paid arguments in this House. So far as I am concerned, I want to assure the hon. gentleman that my arguments are not paid for except by tne indemnity I receive. And when the hon. member goes on to refer to certain interests staying around doors, I should like him to look around the galleries to-night and say who, apparently, are taking more interest in this matter-the paid servants of the dairy industry, or those whom he pretends to see there, and whom I have not seen, as representing the oleomargarine interests of the country. My hon. friend from Missisquoi in his opening remarks said that I was less belligerent to-day than I was on the last occasion this subject was before the House. I am never very belligerent, Mr. Speaker, but sometimes I am spirited; and I shall continue to be spirited so long as hon. members break the rules of the House by using in reference to myself language which you, Sir, declare to be unparliamentary. Before I sit down, I hope that hon. members will give to this question a fair meed of consideration. If they do, I believe they will vote for the main resolution and against the amendment.

I desire to state, though, that while I agree to the validity of the sub-amendment offered by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) I am compelled to oppose it. Did the sub-amendment stand alone, the principle it embodies would receive my support. I feel it is quite consistent with the amendment, and should be added if the amendment is to carry. In other words, if the amendment is a correct statement of fact and principle and goes into effect, it should be followed by action on the part of the government. I cannot support it because it is an addition to and incorporated with the sub-amendment. The subamendment I regard as a false statement as the



Oleomargarine-Mr. Meighen
official imprimatur of this parliament, a false implication to the people of Canada. Consequently, no matter what is appended to it, I must vote against it.
Anyone who believes the amendment I cannot understand voting against the subamendment. I disbelieve the amendment; I believe it is a subterfuge, admirably described by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) as camouflage. It is only a means of escape from an affirmative or a negative answer to the main motion. The amendment states that assurances were given at the time of the prohibition of oleomargarine that the suspension was but temporary. The implication is that some contractual assurance was given certain persons that at the expiration of the temporary measure parliament would not be free to enact such legislation as it liked. No such assurance was given. Nothing was done save the passing of legislation, first by order in council and subsequently by this House. It is passing strange to me, Mr. Speaker, that this House of Commons, which last year knew everything it knows to-day, which last year	knew	all	that was	embodied in the	order	in	council, whichlast year knew	every	word of the	statute, and which	last year	felt itself	perfectly free to enact a prohibition of oleomargarine or to enact art abolition of such prohibition, should now after twelve months find that it had tied its hands behind its back four years before it deliberated last year. Nobody has ever insinuated that there was anything in the world in the way of an assurance that was not contained in the order in council and in the legislation. We knew of the order in council last year, we knew of the legislation. Then how is it that we felt perfectly free last year, and now we find ourselves fettered and shackled? Really to assert to any person that parliament is not free at the close of temporary legislation to do as it feels right in the interests of the people of Canada is an affront both to its intelligence and to the intelligence of the nation.
I make an appeal to hon. members of this House to face this as we ought to face any situation. Leaving aside the question of government policy-and I think the government should have a policy-the matter is now before parliament. Then let us be honest, do not let us try to escape a clear yes or no under an assertion of an assurance, which assurance never existed. That is my appeal to hon. members. I make no further argument on the main motion or on the question that we ought to get finality. I make an appeal that we

sweep aside these subterfuges and get to the question, and that hon. members vote yea or nay upon it. I have stated my position upon it alreadjr and I will buttress it by no further argument.
Hon. members who are opposed to oleomargarine, who believe it is bad for the dairy industry and for the nation in general, who think it is going to hurt little children and all the rest of the community, let them sweep away the arguments and push oleomargarine aside. Why should hon. members put this amendment between themselves and oleomargarine? Why does the hon. member whose heart is bleeding for the little children and who thinks they are going to be hurt argue against the merits of oleomargarine behind an amendment of this sort? Is the man who believes that oleomargarine is an unsound food, that it is deleterious to health, that it is condemned by medical authority-is he going to stand up and say that he is not free to express his opinion because of an assurance given by a government or by a parliament five years ago? Could anything be more absurd? Were it not parliamentary I would say: Could anything be more cowardly? I can understand hon. members being opposed to oleomargarine. I am free to admit that I am myself opposed to the unrestricted manufacture and importation of oleomargarine under conditions as they are to-day, and I can understand hon. members being opposed to oleomargarine under any conditions. Such a position may be right; I do not think it is. But I cannot understand hon. members who have opinions upon the subject at all seeking to hide the expression of those opinions and their reflection by a vote in this House behind an amendment which, I repeat, is an affront both to the intelligence of the House and of Canada.

I have heard something with respect to the order in council which permitted the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. I have a very distinct recollection of the time it was passed and from that time down to the present I have been strongly opposed to the regulations which were issued in pursuance of that order. I have stated repeatedly that I was not opposed to the manufacture and importation under proper regulations, but the regulations which have been in effect are such as have never been in effect in any other country in the civilized world. The manufacturers and importers of oleomargarine have been given a freedom and a liberty such as has obtained in no other country, I care not where you go, and it was for this reason that I have so bitterly opposed the continuation of the permissivt legislation.
A year ago we had a lengthy address from the hon. Minister of Agriculture in relation to this matter. He is a practical farmer and realizes the unfairness which was done to those engaged in dairying by reason of the legislation which has been renewed from year to year. We have heard a good deal during this debate with regard to the injurious effects of oleomargarine on the health of the people, and we have also heard claims made that it is a splendid food and the people should not be debarred from using it. But these statements of the wholesomeness and food value of oleomargarine have never been supported by any conclusive evidence. Notwithstanding that this has been a bone of contention during the past four or five years, and that we have to-day a Department of Health and officials by the thousand to enforce the law, there is not a member of the government who can tell parliament what oleomargarine really is-not one.
If there is a minister present who can give such information, I should like to hear from him. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) told us about the poor man and his children, about the families of the soldiers who went overseas and did not return, about the man who was earning a small wage, and the importance of a cheap substitute for butter. Let me call attention, Mr. Speaker, to something that may open the eyes of my hon. friend in regard to this matter. In 1919 valuable evidence with regard to the manufacture of oleomargarine was secured by a cost of living committee of the parliament of that day, and it was brought out how highly coloured June butter was purchased to be mixed with these other ingredients in order to make the product look like butter and thus deceive the people. When the question was asked, "Why do you go to all this trouble and expense; if oleomargarine has the virtues you claim for it, why not sell it on its merits?"-the reply came " Oh, it would be like eating lard; the people would not eat it at all." So that shows there has been a deliberate attempt on the part of the manufacturers of oleomargarine to deceive the people and induce them to consume this article by making it look and taste like butter. We are voting millions of dollars to the Department of Health, yet not a particle of evidence is laid before parliament to show whether this stuff that has been consumed in this country has or has not any merits. It is impossible for a private member to secure this information, but it is not impossible for the Minister of Agriculture and members of the government to secure it.
