Minister of Agriculture in 1922 before the Ayrshire Breeders' Association in the city of Toronto. The report states:
On the question of the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine, Mr. Motherwell said that, being introduced as a war measure, it had served its purpose and would do well to die a natural death. "All that we want to do with oleo is to do nothing at all," the speaker said. The legislation expired on September 1, 1922, and it would be up to the other fellow, he said, to make the next move.
[Mr. Sutherland.!
I have been wondering since who the other fellow was. I remember about a year ago the Minister of Agriculture frantically waving above his head a bill he was moving the House to adopt and characterizing it as "this rotten old bill." The "rotten old bill" is evidently going to be revived again because the government have not enough courage- or shall I say backbone?-to take a decided stand on this matter. They are fooling away the time-perhaps that is too strong a term to use; the time of parliament is being taken up day after day and year after year when everyone knows that there was in the order in council passed in 1918 an implied promise that the measure then passed was to be a war measure and a war measure only. The order in council said:
-to be in force and to have effect for the period during which the present abnormal conditions continue, the conclusion of such period to be determined by His Excellency the Governor General in Council.
Yes, His Excellency the Governor in Council can decide this matter at any time; why has it not been done? Why all this subterfuge? Why all these attempts to make it appear that this is democracy, that the government are placing the responsibility upon parliament? When I saw the bill which appeared in the name of the Minister of Agriculture about a week ago, providing for the reinsertion of the suspended clause of the act of 1914, I thought the government were going to have the courage to deal with this matter, but when it came up in the House, the minister, to my amazement, asked leave to withdraw the bill. The hon. member for Cape Breton South, a private member (Mr. Carroll) has had this motion on the order paper since the second of March. Now, that is surely not democracy. It is certainly not responsible government but an evasion of responsibility.
Just a word in regard to what has been said about this being a protective measure. People are inclined to think that anything that savours of protection is not to be encouraged in this country. We have from the Atlantic to the Pacific a staff of officers who are preserving order, who are protecting the people; and the farmers are entitled to protection just as well as any other class. They contribute their quota toward the government of the country; I venture to say that no other class contributes as much as they do to the prosperity of Canada. When you look through the list of bills that has been introduced this session and last session you can come to no other conclusion than that the government are making it as difficult as they can for the farmers to carry on and do business. Is any attempt being made to

Oleomargarine-Mr. Sutherland
see that the farmers are enabled to manufacture dairy products profitably? We have a protective tariff of three cents a pound on butter

why do they not put on a specific ad valorem duty as in the case of agricultural implements and other manufactured articles. When it comes to agricultural implements the duty on these implements is doubled, when the price is doubled; consequently, the protection on them is doubled. But in the case of butter when it is at 25 cents a pound the duty is 3 cents a pound under the British preference if it comes from the British Empire as it does, and if it goes up to 50 cents a pound the duty remains at 3 cents a pound but the protection is reduced by one half with an ad valorem duty such as the manufacturers of agricultural implements enjoy, their duty is doubled, but in the case of the other product it is decreased. This is the opportune time for the manufacturer of oleomargarine to get in his work. The cost of peanut oil, cocoanut oil, cottonseed oil and all these other things does not fluctuate as does the price of butter, and he takes advantage of the opportunity and comes in as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) has pointed out, and he quoted figures here tonight from year to year showing that sometimes the cost of oleomargarine in this country was up to 40 and 45 cents a pound. What is the price of butter to-day? It is quoted in Montreal at 34 and 35 cents a pound. So is there any injustice being suffered by the people of this country?
Take the price of cheese, 18 cents per lb. If the same price was obtained for butter to-day on a butter fat basis, it would be selling at 39 cents a pound when you compare the values of the two commodities. The manufacturer of cheese to-day has a great advantage over the manufacturer of butter, and this is why there is no progress being made in the manufacture of butter in this country. I know that in western Ontario 'many of the creameries have been closed up, and let me point out there is nothing so important and so essential to carrying on successful agriculture in this country as the butter-making industry. There you have the very fundamentals which are necessary in order to carry on agriculture successfully. We have seen in old Ontario, farms that have been cropped for many years and finally practically abandoned, and there has been a great effort and an immense amount of labour has been applied and money spent in trying to bring them back to a successful state of agriculture. The same thing applies to western Canada at the present time, where in many sections they have cropped and
cropped year after year and now the farms are congested with weeds, the fibre of the soil has been exhausted, and it is drifting everywhere to-day. You cannot bring this land back to a copdition where you can operate it successfully without going back to the primary agricultural industry, that of butter-making. In that case you raise the young stock on the farm. You engage in the raising of cattle, hogs and all these other things, and the product of the farm is converted into a product that is easily exported and that is much cheaper to export than is grain. In that way and that way only can this be brought about. But what do you find? You find during the past few years that the very things that are so essential to carrying on agriculture in this way have been lost sight of.
I hope I have done my utmost to see that parliament would put into effect some regulations whiph would protect the farmer with regard to the thing which is so necessary for feeding the young animals he is endeavouring to raise on the farm. The pollution of the mill feeds of this country as they have been and as they are being polluted to-day is a crime against the farmers of Canada and is responsible for driving thousands of them from the farm. The farmers of this country are entitled to protection and to something different from what they have been receiving from this government and from preceding governments. You may talk about the importance of having the farmer stay on the land, but how can you expect the farmer to stay on the land? They go in the mills and feed stores and purchase a load or a carload of mill feed so polluted with poisonous seeds- yes, and this information is all in the Department of Agriculture, that thousands of animals have died from the effect of the poisonous seeds found in these mill feeds, and no steps being taken to remedy this condition of affairs. Now we are asked to permit the continuance of a condition with regard to something that is going to be used as the Minister of Labour has pointed out to regulate the price of butter in this country. Yes, it is going to be a very convenient thing. It is a matter of small importance to him in view of present conditions, although nearly $400,000 has been handed back to the two manufacturers of this article during the past four years in a rebate on the customs duties collected upon the ingredients which go into the manufacture of this article, and some years there has been a great deal more imported for which rebates have been granted than there have been pounds of oleomargarine manufactured in this country, notwithstanding the fact

Oleomargarine-Mr. Sutherland
that from 15 to 20 per cent of the article manufactured is made of skimmed milk. It is a very clever scheme that has been devised of recent years, particularly in the United States, where the chemists now extract the butter fat from milk and put back into it cocoanut oil, peanut oil and other extracts of that kind and then put the product on the market in competition with its genuine article.
Much has been said and particularly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding)-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
I know hon. members are getting anxious, but there is no particular hurry. The Minister of Finance a year ago in reply to the speech made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture, said:
So it is that we are setting ourselves up against the civilised world if we adopt this resolution.
A little further on he says:
The whole question is this: Here is a commodity that is traded in by every country in the world except Canada. Surely there is no reason why it should not be traded in in this country, unless our people are lacking in the intelligence that we believe they possess. It is because I believe they are intelligent, because I believe they are able to know what they want and able to make a distinction, because I believe they are not going to be so easily fooled and humbugged into having oleomargarine pawned off on them as butter, that I am going to oppose the motion made by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).
I was surprised to get a certain piece of information from the Minister of Agriculture to-night. I have always understood that Canada was a dairying country. I have been down in the eastern townships of Quebec and have heard eloquent speakers declare that there was no finer agricultural, grazing or dairying country in the wide world than those eastern townships of the province of Quebec, but to-night I learn from my hon. friend that that is a mistake. It is a country in which the dairying interests are in such a perilous condition that at any moment they may be destroyed by the butter which is being brought up from the Argentine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext: It sounds a pretty good speech.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CARROLL TO PERMIT MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION AND SALE
speechtext:
A pretty good speech. He talks about the civilized world and Canada being the only country where the farmers are afraid to come into competition with conditions as they find them here.
I have here some of the regulations which are in effect in some of the states of the union where dairying is carried on even more successfully and scientifically than we are doing it in Canada. For instance, in the state of Minnesota the regulations provide:
The use of milk and milk products are forbidden in the manufacture of oleomargarine; the manufacture of oleomargarine in imitation of, or in semblance of butter of any shade of yellow, even by the selection or proportion of any fat or other ingredient which

may color the product, shall be taken as an intent to deceive or defraud the consumer or purchaser thereof; labelling of receptacles and packages is very strict, and package must show, with substantial accuracy, percentage of each ingredient and the name of each animal or vegetable from which the fats or oils are derived.
Why is it that the government has absolutely refused to specify on the containers the ingredients of the oleomargarine sold in this country? Yet that requirement is insisted on in the case of many other articles. The ingredients are supposed to be placed on containers of mill feed. Even in the case of the mill feed to which I have been referring you will find printed in small letters on the bottom of the container "screenings not exceeding mill run." In the case of fertilizers it is necessary to enumerate the articles and percentage of which they are constituted. But when it comes to an article of food consumed by the people the manufacturers are given the absolute right to put into it anything they see fit providing it is something that is not absolutely putrid. So far as the actual ingredients of oleomargarine are concerned the consumer knows nothing about them. In regard to the splendid speech delivered by the Minister of Finance, who dilated upon the conditions prevailing throughout the world, let me say that the value of dairy products in the state of Wisconsin in the year 1919 was $144,655,000 and they have this provision in their regulations:
Any person manufacturing, selling, offering or exposing for sale any commodity or substance in imitation or semblance of butter, the product of the dairy, shall be deemed guilty of a violation of this section-
And so on. Note this also:
Under this section if, in the manufacture of any oleomargarine, fats, oils, or other ingredients are selected and used in such proportions as to cause the oleomargarine so manufactured to resemble butter of any shade of yellow, such fats, shall be prima facie evidence in any prosecution under this section that such oleomargarine was manufactured with an intent to deceive or defraud the. consumer or purchaser thereof.
What do we provide? We permit manufacturers to colour their oleomargarine and to put it in pound prints the exact size of butter prints, and we allow that product to be sold in the retail stores by the retail merchants of this country. On the other hand in many other countries it is not permitted to be sold in the same retail stores where butter is sold. In France, for instance, the retailing of oleomargarine is not permitted on the same premises in which butter is being sold; and in Wisconsin the name of each ingredient in the oleomargarine must be printed on the container, also each animal or vegetable from

Oleomargarine-Mr. Sutherland
which the fats or oils are derived. Many-other states of the American Union have recently passed very stringent regulations with regard to oleomargarine. There is no article of food in which such a great amount of fraud has been perpetrated, and is still being perpetrated as in the case of filled milk and oleomargarine. Consequently I think it would be much more satisfactory and in keeping with good administration in this country if a proper stand had been taken by the Minister of Agriculture and the government on this question. I am satisfied that the Minister of Agriculture realizes the seriousness of the situation, he has given evidence of that, but it appears that his influence with the government has not been sufficient to enable him to get their consent to refusing to take any action and allowing the law to revert to the condition in which it was prior to 1917. We export butter, at an enormous expenditure, to about seventeen different countries to-day. We are in a position to manufacture much more butter than we are manufacturing at present, and it is idle for anyone to argue that what is proposed in regard to oleomargarine is a measure of protection for the consumer, or for the poor of this country. I venture to state that in nine cases out of ten those that are asking for the continuance of the oleomargarine regulations are not those who intend to use the commodity, or have any desire to do so. We have had requests from Lumbermen's Associations and from retail merchants' who are anxious to retail oleomargarine at a profit. We have had requests from women's organizations-some of them even in this city-the members of which would not touch oleomargarine if they knew it for anything. These are the people who are. so solicitous about the poor of Canada. Nevertheless they are not taking any steps to see that the poor are not being imposed upon, or to put them in a position where they can purchase an article of food and know what they are paying for. It is a deceptive counterfeit which is being placed on the market. If this article is good and wholesome why not come out and let the people know what it contains. Strict regulations are enforced with regard to the manufacture of butter. Is there not a necessity for still more rigid regulations with respect to oleomargarine. I almost feel impelled to speak at length owing to the attitude of the government on this question. I cannot conceive of any government pursuing such a policy as the present government is adopting with regard to oleomargarine. We have had differing statements from various members of the cabinet. They have no mind on the question; they say it is
one for parliament to decide. That is something new in the way of parliamentary government in this country. If the government are going to shirk all responsibility for the measures they originate that may possibly account for the length of the session, and for the numerous special committees that are sitting and which have not yet reported. The fact that these committees have not reported precludes the possibility of dealing with many questions which ought to be dealt with, some of them having a direct bearing on this matter. It is all very well to be ruled out of order on the ground that committees have been sitting and hearing evidence but have not yet reported. I venture to state that there are committees which have dealt with every possible thing that will come before parliament during the present session. One committee in particular has taken a stack of evidence, and it will be the end of the session before the report is brought in. In the meantime we cannot do anything until the report is presented. Yet the government continues to sit here day after day refusing to accept the responsibility which belongs to them, and to take a definite stand on this question.	.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend be in favour of putting into force in Canada regulations corresponding to the Wisconsin regulations?

speechtext:
I would be heartily in favour of it. I have advocated that for years back. Do not permit any milk or milk products to be mixed with other ingredients in view of the strict regulations which are in effect respecting dairy products. Why should it be possible, when dairy products are subject to such strict regulations,
2 a.m. to take those products into some packing houses, manufacture them into an article and place it on the market? Moreover the country to the south of us has placed a tariff barrier of 8 cents a pound on butter. We have also a similar duty on oleomargarine, which is absolutely prohibitive. If this is a good thing for the country and if the people want to use it, let them use it by all means, but let them know what they are doing. Let us put a proper protective tariff on it. It is all very well to talk about protection and free trade. That is a beautiful theory; but it is not a theory with which we are faced in this country, it is an actual condition, and this condition prevails to-day by reason of the tariff which has been erected against us by the United States. We must take action according to conditions with which we are confronted and deal with them

It is moved in amendment by Mr. Kay:
That all the words after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor,-
"In view of distinct assurances given at the time the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine was suspended by order in council in 1917 under the War Measures Act of 1914, that as such suspension was but temporary and a war measure only it should now be removed and the question left, without prejudice as to its merits, in the same position as before the enactment of the said temporary suspension."
It is moved in amendment to the amendment by Mr. Good:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following words:
"And that the government do before the end of the present session submit to parliament such legislation in the premise as may be deemed advisable."
I do not wish to contravene the wishes of the House when I insist upon putting the question, but the putting of the question is probably the most important function of the Speaker. Of course, at the beginning of the proceedings, when the Speaker orders that the members be called in, the formal reading of a motion may be dispensed with. But when the vote is being taken the Speaker is bound by the rules of the House to put the question.
